children.translated_text: Therefore, the cognition of non-difference preceded by the apprehension of difference is the faultless refuge in the acceptance of universals (<s>jāti</s>) in diverse [particulars].
This [chapter] named '<s>Jātinirṇaya</s>' (Determination of Universals) was composed by <s>Śālikanātha</s> of accomplished intellect;
this chapter resolves manifold disputes — [study it] with great attention.

<s>Pūrvapakṣa</s> (the opponent's position): The <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) say that the very substratum, namely substance (<s>dravya</s>), of the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is non-existent.
For indeed, the universal is not regarded as residing in the four kinds of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) — earthy, watery, fiery, and airy — because of the absence of cognitions of the recurring form (<s>anuvṛttākāra-pratyaya</s>).
Where a universal (<s>jāti</s>) is to be recognized as non-different among things that are different, there the cognition that reflects the recurring form is the sole basis.
No being has, even with the most subtle examination, a cognition reflecting the recurring form arise regarding atoms which are far beyond the range of the sense-organs.
Even the cognition 'this is an atom' is conceded even by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> to be caused by the quality characterized as sphericity (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>).
Earthiness (<s>pṛthivītva</s>) etc. too are not the basis for the cognition of earth etc., which obtains its self-nature merely through the inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) of the distinctive qualities such as smell.
Nor could a universal inhere in gross substances, since these very [gross substances] are difficult to establish.
Indeed, the origination of gross substances does not work. For thus: the origination of gross substances is stated to proceed by the sequence of dyads (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>) etc., but first, we consider that the very origination of substance is not well-established.
For a single atom does not originate [another substance] in that manner, since it is impossible for a single substance to be the producer of another gross substance.
And there is nothing that is another producer apart from each individual substance.
Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) too between those two is simply untenable. For it inheres neither in individual substances nor in multiple substances. Because in the absence of individuals beyond each one, there is no plurality.
And thus, when inherence in each individual substance is absent, inherence in multiple substances is also impossible.
By this very reasoning, the possibility of a triad (<s>tryaṇuka</s>), which is to be produced by three dyads and which possesses the quality of magnitude, has been eliminated.
Thus the discussion of the origination of larger composites (<s>avayavin</s>) has become remote.
Moreover, regarding the composite: does it subsist in each part wholly (<s>kārtsnyena</s>) or partially (<s>vyāsaṅgena</s>)? This must be considered.
We do not perceive it subsisting wholly, since it cannot be apprehended as residing in each individual part.
And if vibration or color in a single part [entailed] the perception of vibration or color of the entire composite...
Similarly, in another part where vibration or color is absent, since there would be the consequence of simultaneous presence and absence of vibration-color, the composite would enter the contradictory state of vibrating and not vibrating, being colored and not colored.
Nor does the composite subsist partially in the parts, because of the absence of the other parts.
For a partial subsistence is reasonable for something possessing multiple parts — subsisting in one place with one part, in another place with another.
Moreover, since it does not subsist in each individual location, there is simply non-subsistence, because there is no plurality beyond each individual.
Furthermore, the composite would necessarily be known only upon grasping all parts, but that is not possible, since some parts conceal others.
Nor can it be said that it subsists in some other manner, since such another manner is untenable.
And the composite, whether differentiated from or non-differentiated from the parts, does not agree with any valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>).
If differentiated, it could sometimes be perceived even without perceiving the parts. For there is no rule that different things must be perceived together, as with a pot and a cloth.
Similarly, the composite, being different, would not necessarily be perceived together with the parts alone. In some state, even without the parts being experienced, it could be experienced.
But no one perceives the composite without experiencing the parts.
If non-differentiated, then saying 'it does not exist' has been stated merely as a mode of expression.
Thus, the composite substance, when examined by reasoning, entirely dissolves.
How then should the cognition reflecting grossness be explained? Thus: atoms generated in an uninterrupted series of upper and lower, having attained the specific state of competence for generating sense-organ-based cognition, are directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).
For one who comprehends them as thus constituted, the mental conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) of grossness, arising from the force of that [cognition], manifests — just as the cognition 'forest' arises when trees in uninterrupted succession are perceived from a distance.
Therefore, since the substances accepted as gross substrata do not exist, the universal too, which supposedly resides in them, does not deserve to be admitted.
Moreover, the universal is also not perceived as an object of sense-cognition, since it is admitted to be eternal (<s>nitya</s>). For nothing eternal is adequate for producing any effect; since if it were of the nature of capacity, the effect would always arise.
And being of the nature of incapacity, being eternal and indubitably incapable, something eternal would never produce anything.
And what does not generate [sense-cognition] does not experience the domain of sense-cognition.
For that object which causes the cognition of its own presence and absence to follow along is what is directly perceived.
Moreover, when one who has just opened his eyes, after a long time having turned his mind from other objects, directly perceives a black cow (<s>kālākṣī</s>) or an auspicious one (<s>svastimatī</s>) standing before him — no universal appears separately.
Furthermore, this universal does not arise together with the individuals, nor does it perish [with them]. If that were admitted, there would be loss of its essential nature.
And this one universal is claimed to reside in multiple substrata — if it were subject to origination and destruction, it would be different [at each occurrence], since the superimposition of contradictory properties leads to differentiation.
This eternal universal, perceived in a particular individual that has arisen, has not come from elsewhere, being without action (<s>niṣkriya</s>). Nor was it there before, since it was not perceived earlier. Nor is abiding reasonable — for the individual alone is its locus, not space etc., and if the individual has not yet arisen, where would the form (<s>ākṛti</s>) abide?
Nor does it abide even in the [individual] yet to be produced.
Thus this universal abides and does not abide — a predicament has arisen.
Moreover, should the universal be held to be identical with, different from, or of both natures with respect to the individual?
Here, it is not identical — for if so, the consequence of loss of essential nature through arising and perishing together with the individual has been stated above.
And if one accepts mere individuals, 'what is the difference between our position and this one?' — let the opponents torment themselves thinking about this.
Therefore, those who accept non-different universals have merely rendered assistance to those who maintain that only the individual is the reality.
Even in the case of difference, there would be the consequence of perceiving [the universal] without perceiving the individual.
And in the perception of both, the consequence of perceiving the relation would arise.
'But [the relation] does exist!' — this is a great perversity. Who indeed would accept the cognition 'in this cow there is cow-ness,' apart from you who have discarded all sense of propriety?
In the case of difference too, the mode of subsistence is simply impossible to determine — is the subsistence partial or wholly complete in each?
If complete in one, it would not subsist in another — and again the consequence of loss of essential nature.
Partial subsistence too is untenable with respect to individuals existing in all three times.
And the cognition 'this is a cow, this is a cow' with respect to each individual would have to be accepted as mere conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>).
Nor [is there] both natures, because of contradiction.
Nor is it clever [to say] that based on the strength of perception the contradiction simply does not exist, because such perception is itself inconceivable.
For ordinary people consider that what is the object of a cognition of identical form is non-different, and what is the object of cognition of different forms is different.
If at the time of perceiving different forms two entities appear with different forms, then at the time of non-difference-perception one form must be experienced — does that belong to the universal portion? Then this would be the double appearance of one thing, not the appearance of non-difference of universal and individual.
If the view is that even different forms are cognized as identical — here too one must ask: what is this 'identity' (<s>tādātmya</s>)? If one says 'being of one form,' then the same objection stated before has been embraced.
If co-referentiality of words (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) is identity? That is improper, because co-reference is seen even without identity, as in '[he is a] cow-[keeper], [he is a] water-buffalo-[keeper]' etc.
'That is figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>)' — in this case too, proponents of different universals consider it merely figurative.
We, however, consider that words, being dependent merely on the speaker's intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>), are not capable of establishing the nature of reality anywhere.
How then does the cognition reflecting a recurring form arise regarding individuals that are actually diverse, as 'cow, cow'? For this reason we shall infer the cause of this cognition's firmness.
There exists some distinguishing attribute (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>) by whose influence this cognition, which discerns identity among different things, arises.
But that too does not suffice to prove universals. For this cognition, being an effect, when it invokes a cause, posits as its cause only that which immediately precedes it, and does not additionally posit anything else that is not perceived.
And this [cognition] arises immediately after the perception of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), and thus those very individuals, manifesting themselves in cognition, generate through that channel the cognition reflecting one form.
And it is not unreasonable that among utterly different individuals, some have this power and not all.
Just as the eye, light, and mental contact (<s>manassaṃyoga</s>), though utterly different from each other, when falling together in one aggregate, produce the effect characterized as the arising of a single cognition — so too, why should individuals not produce [this]? This is not hard to understand.
And this [cognition], by its own form, concealing the difference of even utterly different individuals through non-difference, is therefore celebrated as conventional (<s>saṃvṛti</s>).
And this cognition does not take the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) as its object, since that appears vividly [in direct perception], while this [conceptual cognition] has the character of reflecting content fit for verbal designation (<s>abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogya</s>).
Since verbal designations are incapable of reflecting a vivid form, and through mere verbal designation such perception does not arise —
Therefore this [conceptual cognition] does not reflect a clear form.
'But this is contradicted by perception! In the cognition "this is a cow," there is vivid appearance!' —
We reply: we do not deny vivid appearance. But that is due to the grace of the simultaneously occurring non-conceptual cognition (<s>nirvikalpaka-pratyaya</s>) which grasps the particular; in its absence, such vividness is not perceived.
Nor should it be said: 'How can the very same entity be experienced vividly by the senses and non-vividly through words?' — for even when the means of cognition differ, the impossibility of difference in what is cognized does not follow.
The particular with its determinate form and the conceptual form (<s>vikalpākāra</s>) with its indeterminate form both shine in this cognition.
Thus, even though the particular and the conceptual form are different — in terms of vivid/non-vivid and determinate/indeterminate — conceptual cognitions, being directly or indirectly born from the perception of the particular, arise with the self-confidence of grasping the particular.
Therefore, directing a person [to action] regarding that [particular], they serve as auxiliaries to practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>).
Through indirect connection with the object, even what is not a [real] entity becomes connected, like the cognition of a gem regarding the gem's luster.
For just as the cognition of a gem regarding the gem's luster, when the gem shines — that cognition of the gem, though inaccurate in not reflecting the difference, being connected with the gem — becomes the means for obtaining the gem.
Similarly, this [conceptual cognition] too, though not grasping the particular, being connected with the particular through the perception from which it arises — through perception, then conceptual construction — serves to lead to the particular.
And this is said to be memory (<s>smṛti</s>), since it brings about [acquaintance with] the particular apprehended by non-conceptual perception.
And for this very reason, since it grasps what has [already] been grasped, it is not a [valid] means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>); otherwise, being object-directed and leading to the object, it would be a valid means of knowledge just like inference.
And this form that appears in it is not of the cognition itself, since it appears as external.
Nor does it belong to the object, since it has been rejected by the stated reasoning.
But this [form], though non-existent, appears following the cognition, like an echo follows a sound.
And the philosophical analysts (<s>śāstracintaka</s>) distinguish this, but ordinary practitioners, identifying the seen and the conceptualized objects, relying only on the external, engage in practical activities, and having engaged, consider themselves in accord with reality through the attainment of the object.
How then is there the judgment of identity between the seen and the conceptualized? Through similarity arising from the exclusion of what is not that (<s>atadvyāvṛttatā</s>) — just as the seen has exclusion of what is not that, so too does the conceptualized.
Therefore the cognition of universals is mere conceptual construction; in ultimate reality, there is no such thing as a universal.
Moreover, the universal is admitted to inhere in substance (<s>dravya</s>). But we do not perceive any substance apart from smell etc., since the eye etc. operate only with respect to color etc. individually — thus is the summary of the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s>.

<s>Siddhānta</s> (the established view):
Here it is said: Cognition alone, that blessed one, is the refuge for establishing the existence and nature of objects.
Regarding cows etc., a cognition resting on the gross form arises — this is undisputed.
And in the course of our reasoning (<s>nayavīthī</s>) it has been determined that both valid cognition and memory are our means of knowledge.
'But that itself is considered non-existent, because composites etc. are entirely untenable!' —
We reply: there is no impossibility regarding what is directly observed.
'But the impossibility of the composite has been stated, because of the absence of a producer!' —
This impossibility is itself impossible. An effect that is perceived is the evidence for inferring its cause. An effect that clearly appears cannot be denied merely because the cause has not been determined. Therefore the parts themselves, having acquired the shared quality characterized as conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), will be the producers of the composite.
And conjunction, being one, extends to many — since the cognition 'conjoined' does not arise in each individual; even in the absence of a plurality beyond each one, the two in conjunction are themselves the substratum of conjunction. So there is no fault.
'But when substance itself arises thus and generates the conceptual construction of conjunction, there is no distinct quality called conjunction beyond it' —
Not so, because the two substances are recognized (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) when they persist. And this occasional state of theirs is observed — thus the establishment of their difference is confirmed.
And recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) has been established in the <s>Mīmāṃsā-jīvarakṣā</s>.
Therefore, the parts themselves, supported by the non-inherent cause characterized by the shared quality of conjunction as assisting cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>), are established as the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of the composite.
And the fault stated regarding the mode of subsistence of the composite — that too is untenable when the perception of the composite has been established.
The composite subsists partially (<s>vyāsakta</s>) in the parts, not complete in each one like a universal.
And even without the other parts, there is some capacity of the composite such that, being one, it pervades many parts — why should this not be posited?
And although the composite does not subsist in each individual part, there is no fault of non-subsistence. Because the parts are producers only in conjunction with conjunction — since for inherent causes, being a substratum is through being a producer. For this very reason, conjunction having a dual substratum is not faulty.
And the perception of the composite does not depend on perceiving all the parts, because the composite is different from them.
Nor, therefore, is the objection of perceiving it even upon grasping a single part justified, because the inference of causes follows the requirements of the effect. For the cause is posited for the sake of establishing the effect, not for destroying it. Therefore, the perception of the composite arises from grasping however many parts, and the understanding of just that many parts is its basis — this is to be accepted on the strength of observation.
Regarding [the objection about] difference: the very rule of co-perception follows, because of the relation of end and means. The composite is the end; the parts occupy the position of means. But their non-co-perception with respect to each can also be stated, since when the composite possessing other parts is also grasped, the exclusion of other parts is also easily seen.
And this is the reasoning for establishing difference: the distinctness of an entity is ascertained by agreement and difference (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>); and the composite, even while being perceived, does bring about a cognition of a distinct form.
For the composite comes to mind as a single large entity, while the parts are smaller and more numerous.
And this composite is perceptible by the eye or by touch, being large and possessing color — whether earthy, watery, or fiery. An airy [composite], however, being large and possessing touch, is perceptible only by touch.
But a dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>), even though consisting of all four elements, is imperceptible because it is not large — its lack of largeness being due to the absence of plurality of parts, largeness, and specific accumulation, which are the causes of the quality of largeness.
But space (<s>gagana</s>) etc., even though large, are not objects of perception because they lack color and touch — but enough of excessive elaboration.
'But since the composite resides in all its parts, when some parts are hidden, how does it come into contact with the sense-organ? And it is not reasonable to claim that an external sense-organ can cognize something without being in contact with it, since even parts, when not in contact with the sense-organ, are not cognizable' —
This has already been answered: since the composite is different from the parts, even without conjunction with some parts, the cognition of conjunction with the composite is established — as is established for cloth etc. — so the sense-contact of the composite is established.
Thus, by this approach, the substratum substance of the universal (<s>ākṛti</s>) has been abundantly established.
'But it was said that no substance is perceived apart from color etc.' — what is this blindness of one who is seeing? For a composite substance different from color etc. is indeed perceived.
For this very reason, even a crystal substance whose color has been overpowered by the proximity of a <s>japā</s> (hibiscus) flower is recognized (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>). How could what has not been grasped be recognized?
Moreover, from the grasp of a single object by both seeing and touching, a substance distinct from color and touch is more clearly perceived — it is not proper to deny it.
For this very reason, in forests etc., the inference of [individual trees] does not extend because of the force of a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka-pratyaya</s>) — [there] the non-difference usage operates, caused by the non-grasping of intervals due to distance.
But regarding the composite, there is no sublating cognition — as has been pointed out previously.
Therefore, the denial of the universal on the grounds of the absence of the substratum substance is mere prattle — this is established.
As for the statement 'the universal, being eternal, is not capable of generating sense-cognition' — that too has been answered in the section refuting momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>), through the elaborate demonstration that eternal things are capable of producing effects.
Or let it be that the universal did not generate its own cognition. Even so, how is it imperceptible?
Let it be imperceptible if you wish.
Or rather, there is no mandate that only the cause need be directly perceptible.
Whoever is the object for whichever cognition — that is its object. This [principle] is entirely extraordinary.
'But even direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is a valid means of knowledge only insofar as it is non-deceptive' —
Non-deception is through obtaining its own nature from that [object]. But from your [Buddhist] standpoint, even in the absence of the actual entity, since the [mis-]appearance of it is possible, there is no certainty of accordance — therefore, as should be accepted even by a child, the cause itself is the object of direct perception.
And for this very reason, direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>) are the only two valid means of knowledge, since only they are non-deceptive regarding objects.
Direct perception is directly connected with the object; inference is indirectly connected, being generated by a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that is connected with the object.
But that which has no direct or indirect connection with the object — for that, validity is not appropriate, since there is no certainty of its accordance with that [object].
And people who wish to act practically rely on a means of knowledge that is non-deceptive regarding objects.
This wish would be fulfilled if the non-deception dependent on some other cognition were sought.
But whatever cognition is of whatever object, when the object has been presented by that very cognition — there is no seeking of non-deception based on another cognition.
And even a cognition not connected with an object, presenting the object by its own power, operates non-deceptively.
Therefore, cognition requires external assistance only for its origination, not for its validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) characterized by non-deviation from the object.
Thus it is established that even scriptures etc., though devoid of connection with objects, possess validity.
For this very purpose, in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> it has been taught: 'All cognition is non-deviating from its object.'
Therefore, even regarding the eternal universal, the validity of direct perception is established.
As for the statement 'when one perceives a black cow or an auspicious one with a single-pointed mind, there is no perception of the universal' —
That is unproven. For the universal is the form (<s>ākāra</s>); when the form is perceived, if its recurrence is not ascertained due to the mind's preoccupation with some other matter at that time, [this does not disprove it].
A universal that is recurrent does not cease to be recurrent [merely because its recurrence is not noticed].
And even without grasping a property, the grasping of the property-bearer is not impossible.
For this very reason, when another individual is subsequently encountered, a cognition reflecting the previous form arises — this is called recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>).
As for the statement 'the universal, having no substratum [before the individual arises], not having previously existed there, not coming from elsewhere being without action, and not arising together with the individual because of loss of essential nature — how does it experience relation?' —
This is merely a fright-inducing illusion that disturbs ordinary folk.
For conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is produced either by the action of both [parties], as with two wrestlers; or by the action of one, as with a post and a hawk; or by another conjunction, as the conjunction of cloth with the loom-beam produced from the conjunction of threads with the beam.
And this [conjunction] requires either action or prior proximity.
But inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), being different from conjunction, requires neither action nor prior existence.
From the very [cause] from which the individual arises — the inherent cause — from that very [cause] the inherence of the universal with that [individual] also originates.
And we do not, like the followers of <s>Kaśyapa</s> (the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>), maintain that inherence is eternal.
Even when the individual has perished, the universal does not go elsewhere, nor does it remain there, nor does it perish — merely, its inherence with that individual ceases, and thereby it is not perceived.
For: it does not go, because it is without action; it does not remain, because its substratum is only the individual, and in the absence of that, abiding is impossible; and it does not perish, because it is recognized in other individuals.
Destruction is defined as the absolute non-perception — this will be explained in the <s>Amṛtakalā</s>.
Therefore there is no predicament whatsoever.
As for the refutation of the non-difference of universal from individuals and of both-natures — that has merely aided our position. For what sane person would establish the recognition of a distinct entity on the basis of non-difference? Or who would assert two mutually contradictory natures for one thing?
The doctrine of difference, however, is accepted by us too.
Nor is the consequence of independent perception (<s>iha-pratyaya</s>) a fault [for our view]. For one would perceive the relation only after perceiving the substratum and what subsists in it.
And no form is perceived without perceiving the form-bearer. Therefore, since the universal is graspable by the same sense-faculty, the universal enters into the perception of the individual — so there is no possibility of independent perception.
Regarding action (<s>karman</s>), however, which is inferred, there may indeed be independent perception.
Regarding the mode of subsistence, we must accept complete presence [of the universal in each individual].
Nor is there the fault of non-subsistence elsewhere, because subsistence is established by direct perception.
Since recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) has been established.
Separate perception of the universal, however, is simply not proven. For the universal, perceived in another individual, manifests while excluding the previous individual. But the exclusion of the later individual at the time of cognizing the previous individual is already established.
Thus, with all difficulties resolved, the truth of universals (<s>jāti-tattva</s>) — established through the experience of a common form in cows etc. — has been demonstrated.
And the perceptibility of the universal has been established, since it is perceived in accordance with the operation of the sense-organs.
The sense-contact (<s>sannikarṣa</s>) characterized as 'conjoined-inherence' (<s>saṃyukta-samavāya</s>) is also not untenable.
'But the cognition "this is a cow" extends, reflecting the object most vividly!' —
Not so, because there is no evidence for that. Through mere words, perception of a form grasped solely by a [prior] form [is non-vivid], and because of the non-appearance of another form, it is indeed non-vivid.
But in sensory cognition, there is vivid understanding due to the appearance of the abundant forms of the parts — so there is no consequence of the object being merely internal.
'But this perception of the universal, arising while cognizing diverse individuals as non-different — is an error, not a valid means of knowledge!' —
But this error would be groundless, and so the universal is inferred as its ground, along with its inherence.
For a cognition resembling fire-form is observed regarding a heated iron ball infused with fire-particles transmitting heat.
'This has already been answered!' — we think: the fault of forgetfulness leads to the repeated objection.
For the universal is perceived as different. We do not consider the form and the form-bearer to be one and the same. Only regarding word-usage must the justification be stated.
And in that regard, ordinary usage itself is the authority. And the usage is not untenable through either literal meaning (<s>śruti</s>), secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), or figurative meaning (<s>gauṇī</s>) function.
As for inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) — let it be inferred when the entity it relates to has been independently established, since it is not perceived through direct perception.
But the form (<s>ākṛti</s> / universal) is established by the valid means of direct perception and is not to be inferred.
And inference too cannot be pursued regarding the followers of <s>Śākya</s> (Buddhists) who deny real connections — but enough of excessive elaboration.

Refutation of <s>sattā</s> (being) as a universal:
Here some, like [the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>], following the analogy of cows etc., accept the universal of being (<s>sattā-jāti</s>) also in substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), and action (<s>karman</s>), saying that there indeed arises the recurring cognition 'existing, existing' in all things.
This is rambling upon rambling by those who have not grasped the true nature of universals.
If a cognition resembling a prior form arises, then a universal should be admitted. But in substances of diverse kinds such as mustard seeds and mountains, or in diverse qualities such as smell and taste, there is no common-form experience.
It is merely the word 'existing' (<s>sat</s>) that is applied.
And there is word-usage like 'cook,' '<s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>' etc. even without a universal.
'But even so, word-usage does not work without some single basis!' —
True. There is indeed one qualifying condition (<s>upādhi</s>) — the fitness for connection with a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa-sambandha-yogyatā</s>).
Thereupon, another who considers himself learned objects: 'This is improper, for in all cases, having cognized the difference of qualifying conditions, a cognition pervaded by the conditional word arises — not beforehand, nor simultaneously. Here, the means of knowledge itself, as it arises, arises precisely as "exists." This [yogyatā] should come only after the arising of the means of knowledge.
Moreover, even when there is connection with a means of knowledge, something is cognized as "exists," something as "existed," and another as "will exist." Since the connection with the means of knowledge is present [only now], there should be the cognition of present being in all cases. But in the case of a being distinct from that [connection], its threefold arrangement justifies the threefold appearance.
Moreover, regarding objects buried in the ground, existing for a very long time, with all knowing persons gone, devoid of marks etc. — even when all means of knowledge have ceased to operate, there is doubt of present existence. And that is untenable without a being (<s>sattā</s>) distinct from the connection with the means of knowledge.'
This, from one who has not considered the opponent's words, is mere throat-clearing.
We have said: the fitness for connection with a means of knowledge is the qualifying condition. If we had said that the connection with a means of knowledge is the condition, then such a criticism would be apt.
But fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>), being distinct from the actual connection with a means of knowledge, is ascertained by a means of knowledge — so the cognition 'it exists' arising from the means of knowledge is justified.
And since that [fitness] pertains to all three times, the threefold cognition too is justified.
And doubt about it too is justified.
What then is this fitness for connection with a means of knowledge?
'Is not the great universal (<s>mahā-sāmānya</s>) merely accepted under another name?'
Not so at all. For even those who affirm the great universal called <s>sattā</s> also accept the intrinsic existence (<s>svarūpa-sattā</s>) of entities. Otherwise, regarding hare's horns etc. and things that have not yet arisen or have already passed — if asked 'why should they not have connection with the great universal?' — what answer could there be?
Therefore, it is intrinsic existence itself that constitutes the fitness for connection with a means of knowledge. For that which has its own nature is determinable by a means of knowledge. The three-time dimension too pertains to intrinsic nature itself, not to the great universal, since it is eternal.
Similarly, doubt too pertains to that [intrinsic nature] — and no one doubts being (<s>sattā</s>) when the intrinsic nature is not in doubt.
'But what relation does even the eternal <s>sattā</s> have that would be three-temporal?' —
The three-temporality of that itself — whence? There is no answer here other than 'from the three-temporality of intrinsic nature.'
Therefore, the word 'being' (<s>sat</s>) operates based only on the qualifying condition of intrinsic existence, and there is no single form called <s>sattā</s> belonging to substance, quality, and action.
Moreover, it is also the position of the followers of <s>Kaśyapa</s> (<s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>) that regarding universals, inherence, and particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>), the word 'being' operates based solely on the qualifying condition of intrinsic existence. Let the same apply to substance, quality, and action.
Thus, having refuted the great universal called <s>sattā</s> — which is distinct from the intrinsic nature of entities — [the Buddhist's argument that] 'there is a direct perception solely of being' has been thoroughly dismissed, [since it was] established by the force of sophistry fashioned by their own intellect.
By this very reasoning, <s>śabdatva</s> (word-hood) too should be understood as refuted. For no cognition reflecting a single recurring form arises regarding [the sounds] 'ka' and 'ga.'
Even the word 'śabda' (sound) itself operates based on the qualifying condition of being grasped by the ear — so it never serves to posit a universal.
Thus, what they say — '<s>Śabdatva</s> (word-hood) alone, by being the object of various non-common manifesting sounds, serves the understanding of this or that meaning through diverse phonemic forms' — has been refuted.

Refutation of <s>brāhmaṇatva</s> etc. as universals:
By this same approach, the universal of <s>brāhmaṇatva</s> etc. is also rejected. For no cognition manifesting a single form as something distinct arises regarding diverse male and female individuals.
Even after the most prolonged investigation, no one comprehends a single form that is present in all <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and absent from <s>kṣatriyas</s> etc.
As for what they say — 'Even if <s>brāhmaṇya</s> is not ascertained by a cognition arising at first glance, still, in the cognition born from the investigation of the relation with parents who are <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, it shines forth' —
That too contradicts one's own experience. Even while investigating the parental relation, who is able to comprehend a single form?
And the illustration offered — 'Just as clarified butter dissolved [in oil], though not distinguishable from oil, is cognized as different by the eye aided by smell-perception' —
That too is not sound. For at that time there is no surplus in the object of visual cognition; rather, there is merely an inference of the ghee. And one who has sharp vision, capable of seeing even the subtlest form, perceives the nature of ghee by the eye alone, without depending on smell.
'But then much is left unaccounted for: what is the basis for the eligibility of certain persons and not others for rites such as the <s>āhavanīya</s> fire etc.? And what is the basis for the determinate application of the word "<s>brāhmaṇa</s>"?'
Here it is said: In beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, certain lineages (<s>santati</s>) of men and women are established in the relation of parent and offspring. Individuals born from their mutual intercourse are designated by the word '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>.'
Since the lineage has no first beginning, all who have fallen in that lineage have the established designation '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>.'
Therefore, being born from a specific lineage is the qualifying condition (<s>upādhi</s>) for the application of the word '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>.' Those born from that [lineage] alone have eligibility for [specific] rites — so nothing is left unaccounted for.
'But what are those specific lineages?'
They cannot be enumerated and specified, but are to be understood as well-known from common knowledge. And thus, when the birth [from that lineage] is known, people apply the word '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>.'
'But how can that birth be known with certainty, given the possibility of women's transgressions? For there are unchaste women who are unfaithful to their husbands.'
We reply: It has been stated that the non-perception of what should be perceived is itself absence. Regarding those women for whom, when the complete conditions for perception are present, no transgression is observed — for them there is simply no transgression. This is established by the authority of common knowledge.
Moreover, women should be guarded by the vigilant — for those [thus guarded], there is no room for the suspicion of transgression.
But for those regarding whom there is [suspicion], let there be no certainty of lineage-birth for their offspring. And this does not mean that where certainty is possible, uncertainty [should also be assumed].
As for what some maintain — that the universal of flame-hood (<s>jvālātva</s>) is the object of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) among many flames dependent on a single wick —
Our teacher does not accept that either. He examined the matter thus: a cognition that cannot be otherwise accounted for is the seed for positing a universal.

children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, the fourth chapter named '<s>Jātinirṇaya</s>' (Determination of Universals) is concluded.
The fourth chapter named '<s>Jātinirṇaya</s>' (Determination of Universals).
Statement of the subject-matter of the chapter:
In many ways,
the learned dispute regarding <s>jāti</s> (universal);
according to the view of <s>Prabhākara</s>, the refutation of those [views] is stated here. [1]

children.translated_text: Still others hold it to be both different and non-different.

children.text: tathā ajātāvapi jātivyavahāro bahulamupalabhyate keṣāñciditi tannirākaraṇāyedamārabhyate /
children.translated_text: Moreover, since the usage of <s>jāti</s> is widely observed even in cases where there is no <s>jāti</s> according to some, this [chapter] is commenced for the refutation of those [views].
The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>): <s>Jāti</s> (universal) is different from its substrata and is within the range of perceptual knowledge (<s>pratyakṣa</s>);
it is recognized through the recollection of a prior form — this is the view of Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>. [2]

Some declare that <s>jāti</s> (universal) is merely an elaboration of conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>). Others accept that <s>jāti</s>, even as something real, is non-different from its substrata. Yet others say it is different [from its substrata] but only inferable.

children.translated_text: But this [cognition of sameness] is explained by non-apprehension of difference, like the cognition of silver in a shell — so it does not suffice to establish a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>).

children.text: tena bhedagrahaṇapurassaramabhedajñānaṃ bhinneṣu jātyabhyupagame śaraṇamiti niravadyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the cognition of non-difference preceded by the apprehension of difference is the faultless refuge in the acceptance of universals (<s>jāti</s>) in diverse [particulars].
This [chapter] named '<s>Jātinirṇaya</s>' (Determination of Universals) was composed by <s>Śālikanātha</s> of accomplished intellect;
this chapter resolves manifold disputes — [study it] with great attention.

The opponent's position (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>): 'But the Buddhists (<s>Saugatāḥ</s>) say that the very substratum — substance (<s>dravya</s>) — of universal (<s>jāti</s>) is non-existent.' For indeed, universal (<s>jāti</s>) is not considered to reside in the four kinds of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) — earthy, watery, fiery, and airy — since there is no recurrent-form cognition regarding them. The basis for postulating an undifferentiated universal in different things is indeed only cognition that manifests a recurrent form. No being has a cognition manifesting a recurrent form with regard to atoms, which are far beyond the range of the sense organs, even upon the most careful examination. Moreover, the cognition 'this is an atom' is also acknowledged by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s themselves to be caused by the quality characterized as sphericality (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>). Earth-ness (<s>pṛthivītva</s>) and so forth are also not the basis for cognition of earth etc., which obtains its existence merely through the inherence of distinctive qualities such as smell in each respective element. Nor does universal inhere in gross substances, since those very substances are difficult to establish. Indeed, the production of gross substances does not work. For it is stated that gross substance-production proceeds through the sequence of dyads (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>) and so on. But in that account, we hold that even the production of composite substance is not well-established. For a single atom does not produce anything just by itself, since it is impossible for a single substance alone to produce another gross substance. And there is nothing other than individual substances that serves as a further producer. Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) too between them is simply impossible. For it does not inhere in each individual substance, nor in multiple substances — because in the absence of individual substances, there is no multiplicity. And thus, in the absence of inherence in each individual substance, inherence in multiple substances is also not possible. By this very path, the possibility of the triad (<s>tryaṇuka</s>), which should be produced by three dyads and possesses the quality of magnitude (<s>mahiman</s>), has been refuted. Thus the discussion about the production of grosser composite wholes (<s>avayavin</s>) is far-fetched. Moreover, one should consider: does the composite whole exist in its parts entirely (<s>kārtsnyena</s>) in each, or partially (<s>vyāsaṅgena</s>)? We do not find it existing entirely in each part, since it is not apprehended as being in each individual part. And if it were present in each individual part, then when there is trembling or coloring in one part, the consequence would be cognition of trembling or coloring of the entire composite. Likewise, when there is absence of trembling or coloring in another part, the composite would enter an anomalous state: 'it trembles and does not tremble, is colored and is not colored.' Nor does the composite whole exist partially in the parts, because of the absence of other parts in each location. For a partial existence would be intelligible only if the composite, possessing other parts, existed somewhere through one part and somewhere through another. Furthermore, since there is no existence at all in each individual location, there is simply non-existence, because of the absence of a multiplicity beyond individual parts. Moreover, the composite whole should be known only when all parts are grasped, but that is not possible, since some parts are concealed by other parts. Nor can one say it exists in some other manner, since such an alternative mode is impossible. The composite whole, whether postulated as different from or non-different from the parts, does not accord with any means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>). If different, it would sometimes be apprehended even without perceiving its parts. For there is no invariable co-perception of different things, like a pot and a cloth. Likewise, the composite whole, being different, would not necessarily be perceived along with its parts. In some state, it would be experienced even when its parts are not experienced. But no one perceives the composite whole without experiencing the parts. If non-different from parts, then saying 'it does not exist' has been stated by a mere turn of phrase. Thus the composite substance, when investigated by logical arguments, entirely dissolves. Then how is the cognition that appears as gross to be explained? Thus: atoms produced in unbroken vertical succession, having attained the specific state of being capable of generating sense-organ-produced cognition, are perceived directly. For one who apprehends them in that condition, a mental conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) of grossness, arising from that force, expands — just as the cognition 'forest' arises when trees standing close together are experienced from a distance. Therefore, since substances admitted as substrata of grosser things do not exist, the universal (<s>jāti</s>) residing in them should also not be accepted. Moreover, universal is not perceived as an object of sense-knowledge, since it is admitted to be eternal. For nothing eternal is sufficient for any effect; it is not of the nature of capacity, since otherwise the effect would arise perpetually. And being not of the nature of capacity, being eternal, undoubtedly powerless, an eternal entity would never produce anything. And a non-generator is not experienced as the object of sense-cognition. For a sense-object is one whose presence and absence correspondingly produces and prevents its cognition — that is what is directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Furthermore, for one whose eyes have just opened, whose mind has long been diverted by attending to other objects, and who directly perceives a fair or dark cow before him — universal does not appear as something separate. Also, universal does not arise together with the individuals (<s>piṇḍa</s>s), nor perish with them. If so accepted, there would be the consequence of loss of its own nature. And if the one universal is declared to reside in multiple substrata, then if subject to origination and destruction, it would be different in each case, since the superimposition of contradictory properties leads to differentiation. This eternal universal, when perceived in a newly arisen particular (<s>vyakti</s>), has not come from elsewhere, since it is without action (<s>niṣkriya</s>). Nor was it there before, since it was not perceived previously. Nor is continued existence logically tenable — for its locus is only the particular, not space etc., and since the particular has not yet arisen, where would the form (<s>ākṛti</s>) abide? Nor does it abide in something yet to be produced. Thus this universal abides and does not abide — a predicament has arisen. Moreover, is the universal to be maintained as non-different from the particular, or different, or of both natures? It is not non-different; for in that case, arising and perishing with the particular, there would be loss of its own nature — as stated above. And if only particulars are accepted, let the opponents consider what difference there is between their position and ours. Therefore, those who deny a non-different universal have actually assisted those who accept only the particular as reality. Even if different, there would be the consequence of perception without perceiving the individual. And if both are perceived, there would be the consequence of perceiving the relation. 'It exists!' — if one says so, this is great willfulness. Who indeed, other than you who are free from shame and restraint, would accept the cognition 'cow-ness in this cow'? And if different, the mode of existence is truly difficult to determine — is it partial or complete in each? And if complete in one, it would not exist in another — again the consequence of loss of own-nature. Partial existence too is impossible in particulars existing across the three times. And in each case, the cognition 'this is a cow, this is a cow' would be admitted to be mere conceptual construction (<s>vikalpamātra</s>). Nor is the nature of both, because of contradiction. Nor is the clever response 'there is no contradiction at all, by force of perception' valid, since such perception itself is inconceivable. For ordinary people think that what is cognized through a non-differentiated form is non-different, and what is cognized through a differentiated form is different. If at the time of differentiated cognition two things appear with differentiated forms, then at the time of non-differentiated cognition one form should be experienced — is that the portion of the universal? Then there would be a double appearance of one form, not a non-differentiated appearance of universal and particular. If one holds that even different forms are determined as identical — then one should be questioned: what is this identity? If one says 'having one form,' the previously stated objection applies. If 'co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of words is identity,' that is wrong, since co-reference is seen even without identity, as in 'the cow is a draft-animal.' 'That is figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>),' one may say; but those who advocate distinct universals also consider this to be merely figurative. We, however, hold everywhere that words, being dependent merely on the speaker's intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>), do not serve to establish objective reality. 'Then how does the cognition arise in diverse particulars, tracing a recurrent form, as "cow, cow"? By that very firmness of this cognition we shall infer the cause. There exists that qualifying property, by whose influence this cognition arises, tracing a non-differentiated form in different things.' But this also cannot establish universals. For this cognition, being an effect imputing a cause, posits as cause only that which immediately precedes it, and does not set up anything further that is not cognized. And this cognition, arising immediately after perception of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) — those very particulars, self-manifesting, generate cognitions and through them bring about that cognition which manifests a single form. And this glory belongs to some among the utterly different particulars, not to all — what is impossible in that? For just as contact with the eye, light, and mind, though utterly different, when occurring in one causal complex produce the single effect of one cognition's arising, so too can particulars — this is not difficult to understand. And this cognition, by its own form concealing the difference of particulars that are in fact utterly different by non-difference — this is what is celebrated as 'conventional reality' (<s>saṃvṛti</s>). And this cognition does not have the particular as its object, since that manifests clearly, while this manifests content fit for verbal association (<s>abhilāpasaṃsargayogyārtha</s>). And since words are incapable of manifesting a clear form, in the absence of such cognition through words alone — therefore this does not manifest a clear form. 'But this is stated contrary to experience, since in the cognition "this is a cow" there is a clear appearance!' We reply: We do not deny the clear appearance. But that is due to the grace of the simultaneous non-conceptual cognition (<s>nirvikalpapratyaya</s>) that grasps the particular; in its absence, such clarity is not found. Nor should one say: 'How can the same thing be experienced clearly by the senses and unclearly by words?' — for even when the means of cognition differ, it does not follow that the cognition of what is to be known must differ. And the particular with its determinate form, and the conceptual form with its indeterminate form — both shine in this cognition. Thus, even though there is a difference between the particular and the conceptual form in terms of clarity versus unclarity and determinacy versus indeterminacy, conceptual cognitions arise — directly or indirectly — owing to perception of the particular, and thus claim to grasp the particular. Therefore, directing a person toward that object, they serve as a means of practical activity. And through indirect connection with reality, even what is not the real thing becomes connected, like the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem. For just as the cognition 'gem' in the luster of a gem, though inaccurate, being connected with the gem, serves as the means for acquiring the gem, so too this conceptual cognition, though not actually grasping the particular, being connected through the chain — from the particular to perception to conceptual construction — is connected with the particular and serves to attain it. And because it leads to the particular known through non-conceptual cognition, it is called 'memory' (<s>smṛti</s>). And precisely because it grasps what has already been grasped, it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). Otherwise, by being directed toward a real object and leading to it, it would be a valid means of knowledge just like inference. And this form that appears is not of the cognition itself, since it appears as external. Nor is it a property of the object, since it has been refuted by the stated argument. But this, being utterly non-existent, appears following the cognition, like an echo follows a sound. The philosophical investigators (<s>śāstracintakāḥ</s>) discern this; but practical people, identifying the seen and the conceptualized as one, pursuing only the external, engage in practical activities and, having engaged, consider there to be no discrepancy due to obtaining the object. How then is the determination of unity between the seen and the conceptualized? Through exclusion of what is other (<s>atadvyāvṛtta</s>): the seen, being excluded from what is other, resembles the conceptualized, which is also excluded from what is other. Therefore the cognition of universals is merely conceptual construction (<s>vikalpamātra</s>), and in ultimate reality there is no such thing as universal (<s>jāti</s>). Moreover, universal is held to inhere in substance. But we do not perceive any substance apart from smell and so on, since the eyes and other sense organs function only with respect to color and so on' — thus ends the summary of the opponent's position. The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>): Here we reply — It is indeed the blessed cognition (<s>saṃvid</s>) that is the refuge for establishing the existence of objects. And it is undisputed that with respect to cows and so on, cognition arises grasping a gross form. And it has been determined in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> that both perception and memory are <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) for us. 'But that very claim is unsound,' the opponent thinks, 'since composite wholes and so on are absolutely impossible.' We reply: There is no impossibility in what is observed. 'But the impossibility of the composite whole has been stated, due to the absence of a producer.' — This impossibility is itself impossible; an observed effect is the valid means for inferring a cause. An effect that is clearly manifested should not be denied merely because the cause cannot be ascertained. Therefore the parts themselves, having acquired the common quality characterized as conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), will be the producers of the composite whole. And conjunction, being one, exists in many locations; since the cognition of conjunction does not arise in each individual substance separately, even in the absence of a multiplicity beyond each individual, the one substance accompanied by another is the locus of conjunction — so there is no fault. 'But when substance is produced in that manner, a conceptual construction of conjunction appears — there is no separate quality called conjunction.' That is wrong, for the same two substances are recognized as persisting while conjunction comes and goes. And this occasional state of theirs is seen to differ — thus the establishment of difference is accomplished. And recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) has been established in the section on the defense of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>'s vital principle. Therefore, the parts themselves, grasped by the non-inherent cause characterized as conjunction, are established as the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of the composite whole. And the objection raised about the mode of existence of the composite whole — that too is untenable when the perception of the composite is established. The composite whole exists partially in the parts, not complete in each one like a universal. And that is some glory of the composite — that a single entity pervades multiple parts — why should this not be postulated? And although the composite does not exist fully in each individual part, there is no fault of non-existence. For the parts are producers only in association with conjunction; being substrata precisely because of being producers — since the inherent cause is the substratum of the effect — therefore conjunction having a paired substratum presents no difficulty. Nor does the perception of the composite depend on perceiving all parts, since the composite is different from them. Nor is the objection appropriate that it should be perceived even when only one part is grasped, since the inference of cause is proportional to the effect. For the cause is postulated for the establishment of the effect, not for the effect's destruction. Therefore, to the extent that parts are grasped, to that extent the composite is perceived — this is to be accepted by the force of observation. 'Even if different from parts, there should be invariable co-perception' — precisely because of the means-end relationship. The composite is the end (<s>upeya</s>), and the parts are the means (<s>upāya</s>). But for the parts individually, non-co-perception with the whole can certainly be stated, since when a composite whole possessing other parts is grasped, the exclusion of other parts is also easily perceived. And this is the reasoning for establishing difference: difference of objects is determined through co-presence and co-absence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>); and even when perceived, the composite engenders cognition of a different kind. For the composite comes to mind as one gross thing, while the parts are smaller and more numerous. And this composite, because of its grossness and possessing color, is either visual or tactile — either earthy, watery, or fiery. An airy composite, because of grossness and possessing touch, is tactile only. A dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>), though composed of the four elements, is not perceptible due to lacking grossness. And its lacking grossness is because the causes of the quality of magnitude — namely multiplicity of parts, pre-existing magnitude, and specific accumulation — are absent. Space and other vast entities, lacking color and touch, are not objects of perception — enough of excessive elaboration. 'But since the composite depends on all its parts, and some parts are concealed, how can it contact the sense organ? And it is not correct to maintain that the external sense organ perceives without contact.' This has already been answered: since the composite is different from the parts, even when some parts are not in contact, the contact of the composite with the sense organ is established, just as conjunction-cognition is established in cloth and the like. In this way, the substratum substance of form (<s>ākṛti</s>) is established as extensive. 'But it was said that substance different from color and so on is not perceived!' — What is this robbing of the perceiver? For the gross composite is perceived as different from color and so on. For this reason, crystal (<s>sphaṭika</s>) substance is recognized even when its color is overpowered by the proximity of a hibiscus flower. How could what has not been grasped be recognized? Moreover, through grasping one and the same object by sight and touch, a substance different from both color and touch is perceived most clearly — that should not be denied. For this reason, in forests and the like, by the force of sublating cognition, such composite postulation does not proceed; the practical activity of non-difference is based on not grasping the intervals due to distance. But regarding the composite whole, there is no sublating cognition, as has been shown above. Therefore, the denial of universal (<s>jāti</s>) due to the non-existence of the substratum substance is mere prattle — this is established. As for the objection that 'because of eternality, universal cannot produce even its own cognition' — that too has been answered in the section on refuting momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>), by the extensive demonstration that eternal entities are capable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritva</s>). Or let universal not generate even its own cognition. Even so, how would it be imperceptible? Let it be imperceptible if you wish. Or rather, surely this is not a royal decree that only the cause must be directly perceived. Whatever is the object of a valid cognition is its object — this is the universal principle. 'But even perception is a valid means of knowledge only insofar as it is non-deviating.' And non-deviation means obtaining one's own nature from that object. 'But from something that does not exist in that manner or whose nature is otherwise, the possibility of something existing entails no guaranteed correspondence.' — so the naïve must accept that the cause alone is the object of perception. For this very reason, perception and inference are the only two <s>pramāṇa</s>s, since only they are non-deviating from reality. Perception is directly connected with the object; inference is indirectly connected through being born from a logical sign (<s>liṅga</s>) that is connected with the object. That which has neither direct nor indirect connection with reality — validity is not appropriate for it, since there is no guarantee of its non-deviation from reality. And people who wish to avoid cognition that does not correspond to reality value valid means of knowledge. This wish would be fulfilled if non-deviation requiring dependence on another cognition were sought. But for that cognition whose object is precisely what it presents, when that very cognition presents that very object, there is no need for non-deviation grounded in another cognition. And even cognition not connected with the real object, presenting an object by its own power, operates non-deviantly. Therefore, cognition depends on something else only for its origination, not for its validity characterized by non-deviation from reality. Hence, the validity of scriptures (<s>śāstra</s>) and other verbal testimonies, which lack connection with the object, is established. For this very purpose, in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> it was demonstrated that 'all cognition is non-deviating from its object.' Therefore, even regarding eternal universal (<s>jāti</s>), the validity of perception is established. As for the statement: 'when mentally apprehending with single focus a fair or dark cow, there is no separate cognition of universal' — that is not established. For the universal is the form (<s>ākāra</s>); and when the form is cognized, if due to incomplete examination its recurrence is not determined — that is not evidence against it. And universal, being recurrent, is not non-recurrence. And even when a property is not grasped, the grasping of the property-bearer is not impossible. For this very reason, upon the acquisition of another individual, the cognition referring back to the previous form arises, which is called recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>). As for the objection: 'being without substratum, the universal was not present there before; being without action, it does not come from elsewhere; and not arising together with the particular due to the consequence of losing its own nature — how does the universal experience a relation?' — this is merely an attempt to generate bewilderment and agitation in ordinary people, like a magical illusion. For conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) arises from the action of both, like two wrestlers; or from the action of one, like a post and a hawk; or from another conjunction, like the conjunction of a cloth with a loom arising from the conjunction of threads with the loom. And it requires either action or prior proximity. But inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), being different from conjunction, requires neither action nor prior existence. From the very source from which the individual arises — the inherent cause — from that very source the inherence of the universal in it also arises. And we do not, like the followers of <s>Kāśyapa</s> (Buddhists), hold inherence to be eternal. And even when the particular has perished, the universal does not go elsewhere, nor remain there, nor perish. Merely the inherence of the universal in that particular ceases — that is why it is not perceived. For it does not go elsewhere, being actionless; it does not remain, being located only in particulars, and in their absence there is no possibility of remaining; and it does not perish, since it is recognized in another individual. 'Destruction' means absolute non-perception — this will be explained in the <s>Amṛtakalā</s> section. Therefore there is no predicament whatsoever. And the refutation of the non-difference of universal from individuals, and of its having both natures — that actually assists our position. For what sensible person would establish recognition of something as different through non-difference? And who would maintain two contradictory natures for one thing? The doctrine of difference, however, is accepted by us too. And in that case, the consequence of separate perception is not a fault. For having perceived the substratum and the superstratum, one may then perceive the relation. And no form is perceived without perceiving the form-bearer. Therefore, being perceptible by the same sense organ, the universal too enters into the cognition of the particular — so there is no possibility of separate cognition. But for action (<s>karma</s>), which is to be inferred, there is indeed separate cognition. As for the mode of existence, complete existence in each is what must be accepted. And there is no fault of non-existence elsewhere, since existence is established by direct perception, and recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) has been established. But separate perception of the universal is not at all established. For the universal, when perceived in another particular, manifests itself with the exclusion of the previous individual. And the exclusion of the later individual at the time of grasping the previous individual is already accomplished — thus, having resolved all impossibilities, the reality of universal (<s>jāti</s>), established through the experience of a common form in cows and so on, has been demonstrated.

children.text: iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyaśālikanāthamiśrapraṇītāyāṃ prakaraṇapañcikāyāṃ jātinirṇayo nāma caturthaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam /
children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, the fourth chapter named '<s>Jātinirṇaya</s>' (Determination of Universals) is concluded.
Now, the sixth chapter named '<s>Pramāṇapārāyaṇa</s>' (Comprehensive Treatment of the Means of Valid Knowledge).
The first section: on perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Statement of the subject-matter of the chapter.

children.text: svarūpasaṃkhyārthaphaleṣu vādibhiḥ yato vivādā bahudhā vitenire /
children.translated_text: Since disputants have extensively spread manifold controversies regarding the nature, number, objects, and fruits [of the means of valid knowledge],
therefore, for the purpose of illuminating those [topics], we commence the <s>Pramāṇapārāyaṇa</s> (Comprehensive Treatment of the Means of Valid Knowledge). [1]
