children.translated_text: But these two arise only by ascending upon memory.

children.text: saṃjñini hi dṛśyamāne prāganubhūtau tau smṛtimārohataḥ /
children.translated_text: For when the named object (<s>saṃjñin</s>) is being perceived, those two [the name and the named], having been previously experienced, ascend into memory.

children.text: ata evoktam--- saṃjñā hi smaryamāṇāpi pratyakṣatvaṃ na bādhate /
children.translated_text: Thus it has been said: For the conventional name (<s>saṃjñā</s>), even when being remembered, does not sublate the perceptual nature [of the named object];

children.text: saṃjñinaḥ sā taṭasthā hi na rūpācchādanakṣamā //
children.translated_text: For it stands as a mere bystander (<s>taṭastha</s>) to the named object, not capable of concealing its form.

What then is this thing called <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge)? First, non-deceptive cognition is not [a sufficient definition of] <s>pramāṇa</s>, because memory (<s>smṛti</s>) too would have that character.
If it is held that memory, being of the nature of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), does not apprehend the ultimately real particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), but merely outlines a form that exists only conventionally (<s>saṃvṛtisat</s>) and is non-substantial — like the cognition of a double moon and so forth — and is therefore not non-deceptive:
Even so, inference (<s>anumāna</s>) would not be <s>pramāṇa</s>, for it too is of the nature of conceptual construction. If then inference, being conceptual in nature and having a non-substantial object, is nonetheless determined as though it had a substantial object, and is thus <s>pramāṇa</s> by virtue of being non-deceptive with respect to the particular that is determined as substantial — then memory too would be the same, for memory too arises as determining a particular.
Moreover, how can inference be non-deceptive when, like the cognition of shell-silver, it determines its own non-substantial object as substantial? Furthermore, if inference, being conceptual in nature, does not apprehend the particular, how then does it even determine it? For there is no determination apart from apprehension. A form that is not apprehended — how could it even be determined?
This claim that 'memory, like inference, does not take an external object as its content' contradicts experience, since even for those two, which are conceptual, the experience of apprehending objects perceived by direct perception is established.
If it is said: 'We do not mean by non-deceptive that which apprehends the object as it really is, but rather that which leads to the attainment of a real thing capable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsamartha</s>). For when a cognition has shown a thing as it is, and one who acts [on that basis] obtains that very thing as it is — then that non-deceptive cognition is called <s>pramāṇa</s>.' As stated: '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is non-deceptive cognition; causal efficacy is its ground; non-deception is...' [<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> 1.3]. And also: 'For one who, having ascertained the object through those [cognitions], engages in purposive activity, is not deceived.'
Even so, the unwanted consequence of memory being <s>pramāṇa</s> follows. If it is held that one who acts upon remembering an object does not invariably obtain it — even so, inference about a past object would not be <s>pramāṇa</s>, for there is no attainment of the object shown by it [when the object has ceased to exist].
If it is said: even though there is no attainment of the past real thing cognized by inference, still, since inference arises from a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that is bound to that thing, there is at least the fitness for attainment, and to that extent it has validity — even so, memory would turn out to be <s>pramāṇa</s>. For memory too, like inference, is indirectly bound to the object through a chain: from the particular of fire arises the particular of smoke, from that arises the perception of smoke, from that the concept of smoke, and from that inference — thus inference, being indirectly bound to the object, is non-deceptive and capable of leading to the object. Similarly memory: from the object arises experience, from that the dispositional impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and from that memory — so it too is bound to the object and would be <s>pramāṇa</s> by virtue of fitness for attainment.
If one thinks: even though fitness for attainment exists, the particular that memory would lead to has already been attained by experience itself, and therefore memory is not <s>pramāṇa</s>; whereas inference is <s>pramāṇa</s> because it leads to an unattained particular — even so, the bare capacity for leading to a real thing capable of causal efficacy is not the definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>; rather, a qualification must be added: 'Non-deceptive cognition that leads to what is unattained is <s>pramāṇa</s>.'
If it is said that there simply is no capacity in another cognition to lead to what is already attained — that is wrong. For 'capacity to lead' means being bound to the object, and that is not impossible for another cognition as well.
If it is said that validity requires not only the capacity to lead but also the capacity to prompt action, so that what both leads and prompts is <s>pramāṇa</s> — this too amounts to nothing. For the capacity to prompt action belongs to other cognitions as well. The capacity to prompt action is the capacity to show an object fit for purposive activity; and that belongs to memory of a real object just as much as to inference about a real object.
And if the capacity to prompt action enters into the definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>, then <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual) cognitions would not be <s>pramāṇa</s>, since they do not by themselves prompt practical activity. Rather, the conceptual cognitions (<s>vikalpa</s>) arising from them would alone be <s>pramāṇa</s> by virtue of leading and prompting.
And in the case of streaming cognitions (<s>dhārāvāhika</s>), the later ones would not be valid cognitions, since they have as their object something already cognized by the prior cognition. If it is said that their non-validity is indeed accepted — that is improper. For in ordinary experience, their status as <s>pramāṇa</s> is no different from the first cognition. And the validity recognized in ordinary experience should also be followed by critical philosophers.
If it is said that since the momentary instances of objects are distinct, all cognitions lead to unattained [instances] — that is wrong. Since the distinction of moments is not reflectively grasped, it is not relevant to the consideration of validity.
And the doctrine of momentariness has already been refuted in the <s>Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā</s>. Enough of excessive elaboration.

Refutation of the <s>Bhāṭṭa</s>-accepted definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>:
Nor is the definition '<s>pramāṇa</s> is cognition that apprehends an object not apprehended by perception and is non-deceptive' tenable, because it would exclude the later streaming cognitions from being valid, since they have as their object something already cognized by the prior perception.
Nor does validity hold by virtue of awareness of temporal difference, since the temporal difference, even though real, is not grasped due to extreme subtlety.
Moreover, what is excluded by the word 'perception' (<s>dṛk</s>)? If doubt-cognition — then what is this doubt? The <s>Tārkikas</s> (logicians) say: doubt is a cognition with an indeterminate particular regarding an object whose specific character is not ascertained, arising from perceiving a common property, from cognizing multiple properties in one thing, or from the disagreement of disputants who maintain different specifics. As in: when the specific character is concealed by darkness, seeing only uprightness, one doubts 'Is this a post or a man?' Similarly: 'The wind is perceptible, because it possesses touch, like earth.' And: 'The wind is imperceptible, because it possesses no color, like space.' And: when some say sound is eternal and others say it is non-eternal, doubt arises for one inquiring into the truth.
That is wrong. For the two properties that are doubted — this cognition does not arise as a single [cognition] of both; rather, these are two cognitions, namely recollections of the two qualifiers. And since there is no certainty of either qualifier in that substratum, the cognizer, unable to engage in determinate practical activity, becomes 'as if doubting' — thus the practical usage of 'doubt' obtains. And since those two recollections have their <s>pramāṇa</s>-status already negated by being apprehensions of what is already apprehended — what need is there for the word 'perception' [in the definition]?
The qualification 'non-deceptive' is also non-distinguishing, since all cognitions are non-deviant with respect to their objects.
But one sees the cognition 'This is silver' regarding a shell and mirror-image cognition as deviant. Not so. If the silver-cognition did not have silver as its object, then it would deviate from its object. But given that it has silver as its object, what deviation is there? But is not this cognition about the shell rather than silver? We reply: What is the meaning of 'having the shell as object'? Does it take as its object that very individual shell? Or shell-ness itself? First, the shell-individual cannot be its object, since the form and the thing bearing the form are different. Nor is it the case that a genuine silver-individual is not cognized by the cognition of silver-ness — how much less a shell-individual? And shell-ness, being non-manifest, cannot be the object. If it is said that objecthood means fitness for practical usage — even so, shell-ness is not the object. For it does not acquire fitness for practical usage. Being manifest is what constitutes objecthood. Therefore, silver-ness alone is the object. And since that is not possible in the thing before one, this is merely a memory regarding silver — whence its deviation?
As for mirror-image cognition, it presents the face and such, and has the face and such as its object. For when the visual ray, having fallen upon a bright mirror and such, is reflected back and connects with the face and such, it apprehends that very face and such.
But even so, the reversal of left and right, and the appearances of different location, different size, smallness, and largeness would be groundless. To this we reply: The location of the face is not apprehended, and there is non-apprehension of the mirror and such — hence the face and such appear as if in that location. Since the visual ray connects with the face and such as directly facing it, the reversal of left and right is indeed proper. And smallness and largeness [of the reflection] are due to the smallness or largeness of the mirror as the cause of ray-reflection, which being a defect causes non-apprehension of the face's true measure and apprehension of the mirror's measure — hence these appear in the face and such.
Therefore there is no deviation. Such matters have been more carefully demonstrated in the <s>Nayavīthī</s>. By this very direction, deviation should be rejected everywhere — thus this too is not a valid definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>.

The <s>Prābhākara</s>-accepted definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>:
Now [the author] states the definition of perception according to his own view: '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is <s>anubhūti</s> (direct experience).' And he shows that the unwanted consequence of memory being <s>pramāṇa</s> does not arise: 'It (<s>anubhūti</s>) is different from memory.' What then is memory? 'Memory is defined as cognition arising solely from the dispositional impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of prior cognition.'
Nor do streaming cognitions (<s>dhārāvāhika</s>) thereby become memory, since they arise from sense-object contact, like the first cognition. And by the word 'solely' (<s>mātra</s>), recognitive cognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) is not memory, since it arises from both the sense-organ and a dispositional impression as co-operating cause.
Why then is memory not <s>pramāṇa</s>? To this he says: 'Memory is not <s>pramāṇa</s> because it depends on (<s>apekṣā</s>) prior cognition.' For memory, arising in conformity with a prior perception to which it refers with the thought 'that,' does not independently ascertain the object — and therefore is not <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Then would forgetting (<s>smṛtipramoṣa</s>) be <s>pramāṇa</s>? No. That too depends on prior cognition, since its arising depends solely on the dispositional impression produced by prior cognition.
Then, in streaming cognitions, how are the later cognitions, which are no different from forgetting, <s>pramāṇa</s>? To this he says: 'But streaming cognitions are mutually non-dependent.' For when the causal complex of the prior cognition is still operative, the later ones also arise — thus the streaming cognitions do not surpass one another either in arising or in experience, and the validity of all of them is proper.
If mere <s>anubhūti</s> is <s>pramāṇa</s>, then the erroneous cognition 'This is silver' would also be <s>pramāṇa</s>. To this we reply: 'This is silver' is not a single cognition, but two cognitions — an apprehension and a recollection. There, 'silver' is a recollection, and since it lacks the character of direct experience, there is no unwanted consequence of its being <s>pramāṇa</s>. The cognition 'this' is of the nature of direct experience and is indeed accepted as <s>pramāṇa</s>. The erroneous character belongs only to the silver-cognition, because it is deceptive in practical usage by prompting the practical activity of apprehension.
Even those who maintain that this is a single erroneous cognition, by accepting that its falsity depends on a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka-pratyaya</s>), cannot declare the 'this' component to be false, since there is no sublating cognition with respect to it. For even in the state of sublation, the 'this' component continues unaltered. Thus it is entirely proper that even a single cognition, having distinctions based on its delimited objects, can be both <s>pramāṇa</s> and non-<s>pramāṇa</s>.
Then the cognition of a yellow conch and such would be liable to be <s>pramāṇa</s>. For in that case, both yellowness and the conch's own nature are directly experienced. For the yellowness, conditioned by the bile-substance in the eye, is indeed directly experienced — this has been more carefully demonstrated in the <s>Nayavīthī</s>. And the direct experience of the conch's own nature is indeed non-deceptive.
This is no fault. Who indeed says that the yellow-conch cognition is not <s>pramāṇa</s>? It is indeed <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it has a real object. But this is a pair of cognitions appearing in the common form of a single cognition; and through reflection on the form common to a single cognition, it prompts practical activity similar to that of a single cognition, and is thus deceptive in practical usage — therefore, though <s>pramāṇa</s>, it is called erroneous.
But where there is no deception in practical usage, error too is not attributed — as in the cognition of hot water. For there too, it is not the heat belonging to the water that is experienced, but only that belonging to the fire-particles. Since the production of heat in water through contact with fire is not accepted [as an inherent quality] — for a quality produced by heating is removed only by another heating. But the heat in water, not requiring another heating, ceases merely by the separation from fire-contact. For the fire-particles that have entered there, being mobile, when they depart elsewhere, in the absence of the movement of further fire-particles, there is indeed cessation of heat without requiring another heating — thus the hot-water cognition is not analogous to the yellow-conch cognition.
Therefore, that the yellow-conch cognition is indeed <s>pramāṇa</s> and also erroneous is faultless. But the <s>viparītakhyāti</s> theorist who says the hot-water cognition is non-<s>pramāṇa</s> and erroneous contradicts all ordinary experience.

Determination of the number of <s>pramāṇas</s>:
How many kinds of <s>pramāṇa</s> are there? To this he says: 'There, <s>pramāṇa</s> is fivefold.' By this, the counts of one, etc., and of six, etc. are excluded. What are those kinds? To this: '[Perception, inference,] scripture (<s>śāstra</s>), analogy (<s>upamāna</s>), and presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) — this is the view of the Guru [<s>Prabhākara</s>].'

Representation of the definition of perception stated by <s>Gautama</s>:
What then is the definition of perception? Some say: 'Perception is cognition born of sense-object contact, which is non-verbalizable (<s>avyapadeśya</s>), non-deviant (<s>avyabhicāri</s>), and of the nature of determinate judgment (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>).' The cognition that arises from the contact of a sense-organ with an object — that is perception. And that contact is of six kinds: conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), inherence in what is conjoined (<s>saṃyukta-samavāya</s>), inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined (<s>saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya</s>), inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), inherence in what is co-inherent (<s>samaveta-samavāya</s>), and the qualifier-relation of what is conjoined (<s>saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā</s>).
There, through conjunction, the perception by sight and touch of substances of earth, water, fire, and air. The eye operates through contact (<s>prāpyakāri</s>), being an external sense-organ like the skin. It is of the nature of fire (<s>taijasa</s>), since it is the cause of color-perception, like a lamp. Its rays, extending outward, conjoin with the substance. And since those rays are sharp-pointed, they reach even large substances.
But then, for a distant object, there would be no cognition-with-intervening-distance, since when contact is achieved distance is impossible, as with touch being a contact-requiring sense. Moreover, since conjunction depends on motion, and moving things go to near and far places sequentially, the simultaneous apprehension of both nearer and farther objects would not be possible.
We reply: Cognition-with-intervening-distance is accounted for with reference to the seat of enjoyment. As for simultaneous cognition, some explain thus: The visual rays, having reached all objects, becoming unified with the external fire-element present everywhere simultaneously, are the simultaneous cause of apprehension. Others criticize this: if contact is accepted in this manner, the apprehension of even extremely distant and obstructed objects would be unavoidable.
Others say: Due to the extreme swiftness of those rays, the temporal difference is not grasped, and hence the appearance of simultaneity. Others do not accept this either. For very proximate objects, the temporal difference in motion, like the splitting of a hundred lotus petals, may indeed not be discerned. But for objects thousands of <s>yojanas</s> apart on the ground and for the pole-star, the perpetual non-discernment of temporal difference does not satisfy the intellect.
But we say: There is no fault, because it depends on unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). Even when the external fire has merged with the visual rays, only that portion of it which has been employed as the cause of perception by the force of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> has the capacity for perception, not all of it — hence there is no perception of everything simultaneously, and the perception of earthly objects and the pole-star [is explained].
But if the eye-fire operates through contact, how is there perception when glass, clouds, cataracts, and darkness intervene? Because those do not obstruct the visual rays. But for those who say the eye operates without contact, the apprehension of obstructed and distant objects would be unavoidable. Even in proximity, even the most minute and beautiful objects would be apprehended at a distance. But when apprehension is through contact, due to the scarcity of fire-particles, the indistinct perception of distant objects and the non-perception of minute objects are proper.
But why are atoms, the subtle earthy substances and such, and space, time, direction, and the self not apprehended by perception? We reply: Largeness, being composed of many substances, and possessing a specific form of color — these, like contact itself, are causes of perception. Due to the absence of multiple substances, the atom is not perceived. Due to the absence of largeness, the dyad is not perceived. Space and the rest, due to being formless and being non-substantial substances, are to be understood [as imperceptible].
Here the following should be understood: Substance of three kinds is apprehended through conjunction by sight and touch. Through inherence-in-what-is-conjoined, the qualities such as color residing in that substance, and motions, are apprehended. Through inherence-in-what-inheres-in-what-is-conjoined, quality-ness, motion-ness, color-ness and such are [apprehended]. Through inherence, sound is apprehended — for the ear is the space delimited by the hollow of the ear-conch, and sound is its quality — this has been stated more carefully in the <s>Tattvāloka</s>. Through co-inherent-inherence, sound-ness is perceived. Through the qualifier-relation-of-what-is-conjoined, absence is apprehended, as in 'this branch is fruitless.'

Refutation of the <s>Naiyāyika</s> view:
This is improper. If largeness, being-composed-of-many-substances, and possessing-color are indeed the causes of perception, then wind would be imperceptible. And one cannot say 'that is indeed accepted,' since wind is perceived through touch. If only touch is perceived through that, not the wind-substance — [we reply:] since, when cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot touches are perceived, the substance is recognized through recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>). For when the warmth belonging to fire, the coldness belonging to water, and the neither-cold-nor-hot [touch] of wind are perceived by touch when the wind blows, one recognizes: 'It is indeed that same substance.' Therefore, it is not a perception of mere touch. Hence, possessing-touch, like possessing-color, should be counted as a cause of perception.
And the stated perceptibility of motion through inherence-in-what-is-conjoined is also improper, since motion is inferable through its effects of conjunction and disjunction. This has been elaborated in both the <s>Pañcikā</s> texts, and we shall also discuss it in the section on inference here.
And the accepted apprehension of quality-ness and such through inherence-in-what-inheres-in-what-is-conjoined is also improper, due to their non-existence. And the apprehension of sound-ness through co-inherent-inherence is similarly untenable. The apprehension of absence through the qualifier-relation-of-what-is-conjoined we shall refute here itself.
Moreover, why is not another type of contact called inherence-qualifier-relation (<s>samavāya-viśeṣaṇatā</s>) accepted? Just as the qualifier-relation-of-what-is-conjoined is accepted as a further contact for the perception of the mutual absence between a cow and a horse, so too, for the perception of the mutual absence between the sounds <s>ka</s> and <s>kha</s>, it is proper to accept a further contact characterized as co-inherent-qualifier-relation. Therefore, there are only three types of contact that are causes of perception: conjunction, inherence-in-what-is-conjoined, and inherence.
What is the purpose of 'non-verbalizable' (<s>avyapadeśya</s>)? To remove the suspicion of verbal cognition (<s>śābda</s>) for what arises from sense-object contact. For when one knows 'color as color' and 'taste as taste,' due to the possible occurrence of verbal designation, someone might suspect verbal cognition. To remove that, 'non-verbalizable' is stated. For in cognition born of sense-object contact, there is no functioning of words that would make it verbal.
This is incoherent. For the definition of perception should be stated — that form by which it is distinguished from cognates and non-cognates is the definition. Now, its difference from verbal cognition is already established by its being born of sense-object contact. The suspicion that perception accompanied by verbal designation might be verbal should properly be removed in the section examining verbal cognition, just as the suspicion of inference regarding all verbal cognition [is addressed there].
And the term 'non-deviant' (<s>avyabhicāri</s>), stated for the exclusion of error, is non-distinguishing since all cognitions are non-deviant with respect to their objects, as stated.
The character of 'determinate judgment' (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>) too need not be stated for the exclusion of doubt. For 'Is this a post or a man?' involves a pair of memory-cognitions; and since these are not born of sense-object contact, there is no unwanted consequence of their being perception. Moreover, the exclusion of doubt is already achieved by the term 'non-deviant,' since doubt too deviates from the object as it is being cognized.
Furthermore, non-deviation and determinate-judgment-nature are not the definition of perception, but of <s>pramāṇa</s> in general. Therefore, having first stated the general definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>, for its specific instance — perception — a particular definition capable of distinguishing it from cognates and non-cognates should be stated: 'That which is born of sense-object contact is perception.'
Even in this definition, the cognition of inference and such regarding oneself and regarding the cognizer would not be perception, since they are not born of sense-organs.

Representation of the definition of perception according to <s>Dharmakīrti</s>:
Others say: 'Perception is that which is free from conceptual construction (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>) and non-erroneous (<s>abhrānta</s>).' Conceptual construction is the association with universals (<s>jāti</s>) and such; cognition free from that is perception. The qualification 'non-erroneous' is stated lest even the cognition of hair-like floaters and such by those with eye-disease be considered perception.
This is of four kinds: sense-cognition, self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) of all mental states and their associates, mental perception (<s>mānasa</s>), and yogic cognition (<s>yogijñāna</s>). That which arises from the contact of the senses with the object is sense-cognition, fivefold regarding the five objects of color and such. Self-awareness of all cognitions is perception since it is free from conceptual construction. Pleasure and such, being of identical causality with cognition, are not different from it, and are thus also self-cognized. Mental cognition is produced by sense-cognition as a cooperating cause with respect to the moment immediately following its own cognized moment. And the moment immediately following the sense-cognition's object is its object. But at the time of the produced cognition, the producing object-moment has already passed — how then is the object perceptible? We reply: This very thing constitutes the perceptibility of objects — namely, their causal productivity and their imparting of their own form. Perceptual cognition bears the form of its object. Otherwise, how would formless awareness achieve the distinction of being awareness of color and such? For this very reason, conformity with the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>) is <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it alone is the cause of that distinction. The object produces conformity in cognition — not the sense-organ and such — hence those are not <s>pramāṇa</s>.
But since only one form is experienced and that resides in cognition alone, how is the object perceptible? We reply: That object which causes cognition to conform to its own form through positive and negative concomitance is perceptible — so there is no fault.
Moreover, the with-form nature of cognition must be accepted. Otherwise, in dreams and such, in the absence of an external object, whose form would appear? And how would a form that is external to awareness, whose nature is luminosity, appear — since the inert cannot be illuminated?
Also, the co-perception of object and awareness is invariable. This [invariability], being negated through the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader — namely, through the perception of [apparent] difference despite [actual] non-difference — persists in non-difference and thus leads to the inference of non-difference. But the appearance of difference should be imagined as being based on beginningless impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), like the perception of a double moon.
And yogic cognition arises at the culmination of the cultivation of a real object. When one who meditates on an object cognized by <s>pramāṇa</s>, even though it is remote, reaches the highest intensity of cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>), the cognition that arises with a direct, non-remote appearance — that is perception. Being free from conceptual construction due to having a vivid appearance. For a cognition pervaded by conceptual construction does not have a vivid appearance of the object.

Refutation of that:
This is untenable — because it would exclude from being perception those <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate) cognitions, namely sense-cognitions that arise through the association with universals and such.
If it is said: since universal and quality are not apprehended as different from substance, there is simply no difference. Therefore, cognition that arises by associating with universals and qualities, which do not exist, is not perception — that too is wrong. Because the non-apprehension of them as separate is unestablished, since they are apprehended in another substance when one substance is absent. Even in a single substance, when it is distinguished from another substance, the difference of universal and quality, which persist [while the substance changes], is cognized — this has been determined in the <s>Jātinirṇaya</s>.
But that the conceptual construction of motion (<s>karman</s>) is not perception is indeed accepted, since motion is inferable. However, the conceptual construction of substance, as in 'this has horns' or 'this has a stick,' does not transcend perceptibility, since it conforms to the functioning of the sense-organs.
Even the conceptual construction of names, as in 'This is <s>Devadatta</s>,' is perceptual, since it conforms to the functioning of the sense-organs. There, although the name consisting of phonemes is an object of memory, and the signifier-signified relation with it too is part of the memory complex, still the named individual (<s>saṃjñin</s>) does not lose its perceptibility. For the name, nor its relation, appears at that time as a qualifier in a single cognition.

children.translated_text: Such a cognition does not exist without the operation of the sense-organ.
Examination of the triad (<s>tripuṭī</s>).

children.text: samprati mātari mitau ca pratyakṣaṃ vyākhyātumāha--- "sarvavijñānahetūtthā mitau mātari ca pramā /
children.translated_text: Now, to explain perception with respect to the knower (<s>mātṛ</s>) and the cognition (<s>miti</s>), he says: "Valid knowledge (<s>pramā</s>) that arises from the causes of all cognition, with respect to both the cognition and the knower,
Is accepted as perceptual due to the commonality of direct agency (<s>sākṣāt-kartṛtva</s>)."

Thus, those who maintain that cognition arising from name-conjunction (<s>nāmayojanā</s>) is not perception — they too are refuted by this same reasoning, since name-conjunction is possible in sense-generated cognition. Moreover, for one who denies the perceptibility of <s>jāti</s> (universal) and <s>guṇa</s> (quality), no perception whatsoever can be maintained. For there is no cognition of a material thing that is devoid of form (<s>rūpa</s>). And <s>jāti</s> and <s>guṇa</s> constitute the form of material things. For every cognition arises as 'thus' (<s>evam</s>), and the mode (<s>prakāra</s>) is the meaning of the word 'thus.' And <s>jāti</s> and <s>guṇa</s> are the modes of objects. Therefore, all sense-generated cognitions arise in conjunction with these two — hence the phrase 'free from conceptual construction' (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>) is devoid of object. The word 'non-erroneous' (<s>abhrānta</s>) too [in the Buddhist definition] renders [perception] objectless for the Buddhists (<s>Saugata</s>s), since all cognitions appear as gross, and since they possess the distinction of apprehended, apprehender, and awareness. And what is called mental perception (<s>mānasa pratyakṣa</s>) — we do not consider it to be distinct from the continuous flow of consciousness (<s>dhārāvāhika-vijñāna</s>). One might think: when the activity of the sense-organ has not ceased, the cognition is sense-generated; but when it has ceased, the cognition arising in the immediately succeeding moment is mental. That is improper — because even when the cessation of sense-organ activity is granted, the result of direct object-cognition is possible, so [mental perception as a separate category] is unestablished. And what is said about mental [perception] having past objects as its domain — that too is improper, since the cognition is of a present form (<s>ākāra</s>). Nor is this form identical with awareness (<s>vitti</s>) itself; for what is to be known (<s>vedya</s>) appears as distinct from awareness, since awareness manifests as awareness by virtue of being awareness, and the form manifests as knowable by virtue of being knowable — so the identity of the two is untenable. And what was said, that the appearance of difference is error — that too is improper, due to the absence of a cause [for such error]. Nor is the distinction between object and awareness itself the cause of the difference, since even formless (<s>nirākāra</s>) cognitions naturally manifest as related to specific objects. And what was stated as the cause of determination — namely, similarity to the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>) — that is unestablished, since cognitions appear as gross while the object is atomic in nature. Furthermore, if that similarity is characterized by being cognizable at the time of [the cognition's] arising, then even the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>), being of similar form, would have to be cognizable. That even in dreams and such, the form of an external object manifests in memory — this was established in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> (Path of Reasoning). And what was stated as the cause of non-difference — that an inert thing cannot manifest — that too is improper. For it is precisely the inert that can have a connection with manifestation; identity [of object with consciousness], however, is not accepted at all. Moreover, if manifestation belongs only to what is non-different from cognition, then how is the difference of apprehended, apprehender, and awareness manifested? — since that [difference], being unreal [in their view], does not enter into the nature of cognition. And what was said — that from the invariable co-perception (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>), the form and awareness are non-different — that too is without substance, since even when awareness is different [from the object], the invariable relation of the object is tenable. For that very awareness is the apprehension of that very object — so how could it manifest without it? And what was said — that self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) of all cognitions is perception — that we accept. But what is maintained regarding pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and such — that self-awareness is accepted due to the non-difference of cause and hence non-difference [of cognition from its object] — that is untenable, because the non-difference of cause is unestablished; since the object is the cause of cognition, and cognition is the cause of pleasure and such; and since in dreams and such, pleasure and such are tenable from cognition alone even when the object is not present. And the view that yogic cognition (<s>yogijñāna</s>) is perception — that too is false. For perception is a specific type of valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). And yogic cognition, born at the culmination of intense meditation on real objects (<s>bhūtārthabhāvanā</s>), cannot even have the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s>, being of the nature of memory (<s>smṛti</s>). For the meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) that follows upon ascertaining a real object through a <s>pramāṇa</s> is merely a continuity of memory. And the cognition born at its culmination is merely a special type of memory — hence it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, nor perception. Enough with excessive elaboration. The refutation of the <s>Vṛttikāra</s>'s (<s>Śabara</s>'s) view by way of restatement: What some consider to be the definition of perception — '<s>tatsamprayoge puruṣasyendriyāṇāṃ buddhijanma sat pratyakṣam</s>' [<s>Mīmāṃsā Sūtra</s> 1.1.4] ('Perception is the cognition that arises in a person when the sense-organs are in contact with [the object], being veridical') — that too, being too narrow (<s>avyāpakatva</s>), is not a proper definition. For the cognition arising from <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) and such regarding one's own self is also accepted as perceptual, and since the perceptuality of all cognitions with respect to their own nature is accepted — what then is the meaning of saying 'contact with that'? It is replied: Those who assert perceptuality even in cognitions of shell-silver and such — they are being refuted. For in the world, regarding objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>), only that cognition is called perception whose object [corresponds to reality]. Thus, the cognition that arises in a person when the sense-organs are in contact with that [object] [is perception]. But the cognition of silver that arises when the eye is in contact with a shell — that is not of such a nature. Therefore, the cognition of silver is not perception. For the cognition of silver has silver as its object, but the sense-organ is not in contact with silver, since silver is not present there. Therefore, the cognition of silver is not perception. Rather, it is memory (<s>smaraṇa</s>) — to show this, this <s>sūtra</s> was composed; thus it should be explained. Definition of perception according to the Guru's (<s>Prabhākara</s>'s) view: He now states the definition of perception accepted by himself: '<s>sākṣātpratītiḥ pratyakṣam</s>' — 'Direct cognition is perception.' [Objection:] But then memory born at the culmination of intense meditation, being also of the nature of direct experience, would undesirably turn out to be perception. [Reply:] No, because [we are] in the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). Experience (<s>anubhūti</s>) is <s>pramāṇa</s>, and perception is a specific type of it — so there is no unwanted consequence of memory being perception. He states the objects of perception: '<s>meyamātṛpramāsu sā</s>' — '[Perception operates] regarding the knowable (<s>meya</s>), the knower (<s>mātṛ</s>), and the means of knowledge (<s>pramā</s>).' He distinguishes: '<s>meyeṣvindriyayogotthā</s>' — 'Regarding knowables, [perception] arises from the contact of sense-organs.' That perception which arises from sense-organ contact regarding substances (<s>dravya</s>), universals (<s>jāti</s>), and qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) — that perceptual cognition regarding knowables arises through the contact of sense-organs, through conjunction-inherence (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>), and through inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). What then are the sense-organs? The external ones are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear; and the internal one is the mind (<s>manas</s>). What then is the proof for their existence and their distinctness? It is replied: The cognition of objects is observed to be occasional; and the self (<s>ātman</s>) is its inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>). Without a non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>), an effect does not arise. And that non-inherent cause is proximate to the inherent cause. Proximity is observed to be of two kinds: inherence in the effect and inherence in [a] cause of the effect. For the conjunction with fire, inhering in the substance to be cooked, being a non-inherent cause, produces odor and such in that very substance. The colors of threads, inhering in the threads that are the causes of the cloth, are the non-inherent causes in the production of the color of the cloth. Now, since the self is eternal, there cannot be a non-inherent cause inhering in a cause [of the self]; therefore, a different quality inhering in the self itself must be resorted to as the non-inherent cause. There, in the case of <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> qualities residing in eternal substances, the conjunction with another substance alone has been ascertained as the non-inherent cause. Since in earthy atoms, color and such are observed to arise depending on fire-conjunction alone as the non-inherent cause, the quality called cognition (<s>bodha</s>) belonging to the self too depends on conjunction with another substance as its non-inherent cause. And since there is no proof for another substance serving as the substratum being a [gross] substance, it is ascertained to be a non-substance substance (<s>adravyadravya</s>). And the non-substance substance is of two kinds: that of supreme magnitude, like space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and such, and that of atomic nature. Now, if this other substance were accepted as supremely large, conjunction itself would be untenable, due to the absence of a cause of conjunction. For the conjunction that is directly perceived is either born from the action of one [of the conjuncts], or from the action of both, or from [another] conjunction. Since conjunction is known to have these fixed causes, in the absence of those [causes], it is ascertained that conjunction simply does not exist. And conjunction is not possible between two supremely large [substances] directly, nor can it be inferred — therefore, by elimination, atomicity alone is resorted to for that substance. And given atomicity, the arising of conjunction through its action is not untenable. And in the production of its action, the conjunction of the self possessing effort (<s>prayatna</s>) alone is the cause, like the action of the body. And in the absence of effort, the conjunction of the self possessing <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) is the cause, like the transverse motion of wind. Thus it is said: 'The upward flaming of fire, the transverse blowing of wind, and the initial action of atoms and mind are caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit)' [<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 5.2.13]. That other substance, to be designated by the word <s>manas</s> (mind), which is the independent cause of the experience of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, being assisted by the awakening of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) produced by prior apprehension in all memories — this should be understood. By this, the view stated by [the Buddhists]: '<s>ṣaṇṇāmanantarātītaṃ vijñānaṃ yaddhi tanmanaḥ</s>' — 'That consciousness which has just passed among the six is mind' [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s>, <s>Sthānakārikā</s> 17] — is also refuted, since conjunction with another substance alone has been observed as the non-inherent cause in the production of <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> qualities residing in eternal substances. Since in the apprehension of color, light possessing color is observed as the instrumental cause, so the sense-organ too, like that which possesses color, should be postulated as the instrumental cause of color-apprehension. Similarly, that which possesses odor alone is the instrumental cause in the apprehension of odor. Similarly, that which possesses touch is the instrumental cause in the apprehension of touch. That which possesses taste is the instrumental cause in the apprehension of taste. That which possesses sound alone is the instrumental cause in the apprehension of sound — this should be understood. Therefore, the earthen organ of smell (<s>ghrāṇa</s>), possessing odor, is the cause of odor-apprehension; the watery organ of taste (<s>rasana</s>), possessing taste, is the instrument of taste-experience; the fiery eye (<s>cakṣus</s>), possessing color, is the cause of seeing color; the airy organ of touch (<s>tvak</s>), possessing touch, is the cause of touch-apprehension; and the spatial organ of hearing (<s>śrotra</s>), possessing the quality of sound, is the cause of sound-apprehension. And since even an object in contact with the sense-organ is not cognized when the mind is engaged with another object, the dependence of the sense-organs on contact with <s>manas</s> (mind) is accepted. Therefore, in the apprehension of internal [objects] such as pleasure and such, two proximities are the cause: the proximity called the conjunction of self and mind, and the proximity of pleasure and mind characterized as conjunction-inherence (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>). And in the apprehension of external color and such, a fourfold proximity is the cause: the proximity of self and mind, the proximity of mind and sense-organ, the proximity of substance and sense-organ, and the proximity of color and sense-organ. He states the classification of knowables: '<s>dravyajātiguṇeṣu sā</s>' — 'It [perception] operates regarding substances, universals, and qualities.' That cognition arising from sense-organ contact operates regarding substances (<s>dravya</s>), universals (<s>jāti</s>), and qualities (<s>guṇa</s>). Substance that possesses touch and magnitude is of four kinds amenable to the senses: earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>), watery (<s>āpya</s>), fiery (<s>taijasa</s>), and airy (<s>vāyavīya</s>). The cause of the arising of such substances, and the proof thereof, were determined in the <s>Jātinirṇaya</s> (Determination of Universals). The existence of <s>jāti</s> too was stated in the <s>Jātinirṇaya</s> itself. And the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) that are perceptually apprehensible are: color (<s>rūpa</s>), taste (<s>rasa</s>), odor (<s>gandha</s>), touch (<s>sparśa</s>), number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>), separateness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>), remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), and effort (<s>prayatna</s>). Sometimes qualities like color are apprehended without the substance being apprehended, and sometimes the substance is apprehended without color and such — thus there is no fixed rule regarding the apprehension of substance and quality. And this cognition of substances and such is of two kinds: '<s>savikalpā avikalpā ca pratyakṣā buddhiriṣyate</s>' — 'Perceptual cognition is accepted as both determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>) and indeterminate (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>).' He distinguishes: '<s>ādyā viśiṣṭaviṣayā svarūpaviṣayetarā</s>' — 'The first has a qualified object, the other has bare nature as its object.' For first, the apprehension of mere nature (<s>svarūpamātra</s>) in substances, universals, and qualities is possible. And this is established through self-experience (<s>svānubhava</s>). For one whose mind is concentrated and free from investigation of other objects directly apprehends the thing in contact with the sense-organs — thus self-awareness alone is the proof here. Description of indeterminate perception (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>): Its object is not mere particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) alone, since the appearance of the forms of universal and such is evident. Nor is mere universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) alone its object, since the apprehension of difference is established through experience. And what is said — '<s>labdharūpe kvacit kiñcit</s>' [<s>Bṛhatī</s>] etc. — that refers to mutual absence (<s>itaretarābhāva</s>), not to the difference of real entities (<s>vastubheda</s>). For mutual absence is ascertained after the cognition of the difference of real entities. Having known the pot as having the form of a pot, and the cloth as having the form of a cloth, one ascertains their mutual absence: 'this is not that.' And the cognition of a pot and such does not depend on the apprehension of another entity — so even when another entity is not cognized, the apprehension of that [pot] is not untenable. Therefore, indeterminate perception, cognizing two real entities — universal and particular — first arises as tenable. However, since it is free from the investigation of other entities, it does not cognize them as universal and particular. For what is called universal is that which is common [to many], and particular is that which is distinguished [from others]. And without the investigation of other entities, commonality and distinction cannot be cognized. But even without cognizing them [as such], one can indeed cognize their bare natures — thus indeterminate perception does not have universal and particular as its object [in that specific mode]. Description of determinate perception (<s>savikalpaka</s>): Determinate perception, following upon [indeterminate perception], cognizes those very two entities as having the nature of universal and particular. [Objection:] But the sense-organ is not capable of investigating another entity. And perception arises from the capacity of the sense-organ — so how can what has the nature of universal and particular be the object of perception? It is replied: This would be so if the sense-organs alone were conscious, or if they were cognitions [themselves]. But the self (<s>ātman</s>) is one, the experiencer of all that is to be experienced; through the power of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), investigating another entity, it can indeed cognize the entity through the sense-organ as having the nature of universal and particular. Similarly, even though indeterminate perception cognizes two real entities — universal and particular — it cannot apprehend their difference. For the cognition of difference does not arise from mere difference of entities alone; rather, the apprehension of another attribute (<s>dharmāntara</s>) is also an auxiliary to the cognition of difference. Therefore, since one who does not apprehend commonality and distinction — which are other attributes — does not have the cognition of difference even though the difference between universal and particular exists, at a later time, through the investigation of other entities, those [commonality and distinction] are cognized and difference is ascertained. When difference obtains, the relation of qualifier and qualified (<s>viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva</s>) is ascertained — hence in the stage of indeterminate perception there is no qualified cognition. But in the stage of determinate perception, one does apprehend the qualifier-qualified relation. In the cognition of quality too, indeterminate perception does not delimit the substance as qualified, due to the non-apprehension of the difference between substance and quality. For the difference of quality and universal from substance is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). And since there is no investigation of positive and negative concomitance in indeterminate perception, there is no apprehension of difference; and without apprehending difference, it is unable to grasp the qualified nature — hence qualified cognition belongs to determinate perception alone. In name-attribution (<s>nāmakalpanā</s>) too, the conventional name (<s>saṃjñā</s>), being merely remembered, serves as a qualifier. Action-attribution (<s>karmakalpanā</s>) too is to be explained in the same way. Even when a qualifier is presented by another cognition, a qualified cognition indeed arises. Since the self is the knower, and since determinate perception follows upon indeterminate perception, even though it apprehends what has already been apprehended, its status as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) should be understood by the principle of continuous flow (<s>dhārāvāhikanyāya</s>). Beyond the qualifier-qualified relation, determinate perception also possesses the capacity to apprehend what has not been apprehended. And its having external reality as its object was determined in the <s>Jātinirṇaya</s>. Nor is this cognition non-sense-generated, since its operation depends on the sense-organs. For this determinate perceptual cognition (<s>savikalpaka-pratyaya</s>) is a manifestation of an immediate object (<s>aparokṣārthāvabhāsa</s>).

children.translated_text: Thus they say: "And difference is seen through erroneous cognitions, like the two [moons] in the moon."
[<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 3, verse 389]
And further it has been said: "This apparent division — one part being internal, the other situated externally —
Of cognition, which is in reality non-dual (<s>abhedin</s>), the appearance of difference is an aberration (<s>upaplava</s>)."

Thus. Any cognition whatsoever, of the nature of apprehension or memory regarding objects — in it, the self (<s>ātman</s>) shines directly. For when the self does not appear in a cognition that reveals an object, the objects do not shine forth. All cognition arises in this manner: 'I know this'; there is no cognition of the form 'knows' [without the 'I']. And then, between what is known to oneself and what is known to another, there is no unsurpassable doubt. Nor can the restriction that [the self] is the object of another cognition be maintained. When both [self and object] are the objects of a single cognition, the restriction of co-apprehension is indeed proper. Therefore, all the causes of cognition produce in the self a cognition endowed with direct acquaintance (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>). Determination of the distinction of <s>pramāṇas</s> with respect to the object: But then, is everything perceptual? If with respect to the knower (<s>mātṛ</s>) — this is accepted. If with respect to the knowable (<s>prameya</s>) — no, because there is no invariable rule that the knowable is always directly perceived. In memory, inference, and such, the knowable is not directly perceived. Therefore, it should be understood that the designation of distinct <s>pramāṇas</s> is with respect to the knowable alone. And all cognitions by their nature shine forth as directly perceived. Therefore, their being perceptual with respect to themselves is indeed proper, as is their being <s>pramāṇas</s>. Examination of the self-luminous nature of cognition (<s>svaprakāśatva</s>): What is the distinction in the cognition of the knowable (<s>meya</s>), the knower (<s>mātṛ</s>), and the means of knowing (<s>pramāṇa</s>)? It is said: Regarding the knowable and the knower, the cognition is distinct from them and endowed with direct acquaintance; but regarding the cognition itself (<s>miti</s>), it is non-distinct. 'I apprehend this' or 'I remember this' — only the triad appears. One cognition has the form of appearing solely as the knowable. But another cognition does not shine within that cognition. And does it not appear? If it did not appear, there would be the consequence of nothing appearing at all. Moreover, the knowables are of non-luminous nature, and the knower requires illumination. But illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>), being of the nature of illumination, does not require anything else. For in the waking state, the knowables and the knower are illuminated. In deep sleep, that pair is not illuminated. And yet at that time, that pair does not cease to exist, as is known from recognition upon awakening. But if that pair were of the nature of illumination, even in the state of deep sleep it would be illuminated. Therefore, that pair is accepted as not being of the nature of illumination. But the existence of illumination when it is not illuminating is not accepted. Therefore, the illumination of the knowable and the knower occurs simultaneously with self-illumination alone. Moreover, where something is established from itself, recourse to something else is not proper. The self-illumination of the knowables and the knower is not established from themselves; hence recourse to something else is proper for them. And since there is no impossibility regarding cognition, cognition itself is self-luminous (<s>svayamprakāśa</s>). The <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> according to the <s>Sautrāntika</s> school: There they say: If cognition is accepted as self-luminous, then since something formless (<s>nirākāra</s>) cannot be illuminated, form (<s>ākāra</s>) must necessarily be accepted. And only one form appears; therefore it is proper that the illumination itself has that form. Moreover, if illumination were formless, the determination with respect to each particular object would be impossible, since there would be no distinction regarding all objects. But if it has the form of the object, then 'that cognition is of that which has that form' — thus the determination with respect to each object is possible. Thus they say: 'For it is not proper that the cognition of that object is through the mere existence of awareness, since that awareness being equal everywhere, the consequence of non-distinction would follow; but the conformity in form (<s>sārūpya</s>) entering into it makes it conform to the object and thus effects the specific cognition.' Therefore, it is proper that the conformity in form to the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>) is itself the means of valid knowledge. For the <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of <s>pramāṇas</s> consists in their capacity to determine. And conformity in form to the object is the cause of determination, not the eye and such, since those are common to many objects. Moreover, the co-apprehension of awareness and what is known to awareness is invariably observed; never is the knowable apprehended without awareness, nor awareness without the knowable. And things that appear as mutually distinct do not have the rule of co-apprehension. A pot and a cloth are not invariably co-apprehended. Therefore, since invariable co-apprehension is not pervaded by difference but rather by non-difference, the invariable co-apprehension, being excluded from difference, rests in non-difference alone and establishes non-difference. Thus it has been said: 'Due to the rule of co-apprehension, blue and the cognition of blue are non-different' [<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>]. By this very reasoning, the non-difference of the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness), which has the form 'I,' from awareness should be established. How then do cognitions with the forms of the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and the apprehender (<s>grāhaka</s>) appear as mutually distinct?
And in the error of difference, beginningless latent impressions of difference (<s>bhedavāsanā</s>) are the cause.

children.translated_text: This is to be examined: This cognition which possesses a particular form (<s>ākāra</s>) — does it arise from the external object, or from the immediately preceding cognition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>)?
Thus it has been said: If the cognition has that form, and it possesses a particular form,
Whether it comes from the external object or from something else — this deserves examination.
[<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 2, verse 212]

children.translated_text: 'Inert' (<s>jaḍa</s>) — what is meant? If 'not of the nature of illumination' — then the illumination of what is not of the nature of illumination and is distinct from illumination is established precisely from illumination itself.
Moreover, in the cognition of a variegated painting, since the manifold forms cannot all be of the nature of a single illumination, they are accepted as unreal.
If oneness regarding objects that appear as manifold is not possible,
How then is the cognition itself, which appears as manifold, one?

[<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 3, verse 334]. Thus. There the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> think: The particular form (<s>ākāra</s>) cannot come from the immediately preceding cognition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>) alone, because of the impossibility of spatial and temporal specificity. Even after a cognition of a pot, a cognition of cloth arises. And where and when there is a pot in an external location, if the mere cognition of a pot were the sole cause for the arising of a cloth-cognition, then even when and where there is no cloth, a cloth-cognition would arise. But it is not so. Therefore, there is something beyond the immediately preceding cognition — the object — that is the cause of the particular form of cognition. Moreover, just as in the cognition of water in a mirage, practical efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) is not possible for one desiring water who acts on that cognition, so too it should not be possible even in the case of correct water-cognition. For when there is no distinction in being devoid of an object, the differentiation 'this is correct water-cognition, that is not' cannot be established. Therefore, the external object too should be accepted. Refutation of the <s>Sautrāntika</s> view by the <s>Vijñānavāda</s> school: Others consider that to be mistaken. For thus: First, nowhere is the capacity of an object to produce a particular form directly perceived — that must be postulated. And it is better to postulate it in the immediately preceding cognition, which is directly seen. Let the variety of the immediately preceding cognition be the cause of the variety of cognitions that are its effects. Thus, some particular cognition is the cause of some particular effect at some particular place at some particular time — and the specificity is established. And the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> considers even practical efficacy to be of the nature of cognition. Therefore, some particular water-cognition is capable of producing practical efficacy, and some is not — thus the specificity is established. And necessarily, in the production of cognition with a particular form without an external object, the capacity of the immediately preceding cognition must be relied upon. Otherwise, the specificity of form-appearances in dreams and such would not be possible. And the capacity does not belong to objects existing at another place and another time, since something non-existent cannot have capacity. If one says that the specific form-appearance there is due to <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) produced by prior experience — let it be so. But that experience too is from <s>saṃskāras</s> produced by still earlier experience, and so on — what is the point of accepting objects? And impression from impression — cognition operates in cause-effect sequence preceded by experience alone. Therefore, from a cognition having the form of experiencing an object, whatever subsequent cognition arises has a specific nature; from that too, whatever further cognition arises also has a specific nature. Thus, the very specificity of the nature of cognitions is designated by words like <s>bhāvanā</s> (habitual cultivation), <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression), <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression), and such. And the cognition capable of conforming to practical efficacy is a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), and the other is not — thus the distinction between valid and invalid cognition is also established. Therefore, let cognitions, possessing specific forms, continue in beginningless streams as cause and effect; there is no object whatsoever beyond them. Refutation of the <s>Vijñānavāda</s> view: Here we say: As for what was said to establish that cognition has form (<s>sākāratva</s>) — that without conformity in form to the object (<s>arthasārūpya</s>), the determination with respect to each particular object cannot be established — that is improper. For no <s>sākāra-vijñānavādin</s> has directly experienced the true nature of any object at all, since all cognitions terminate in what is merely the form of cognition. And for that whose true nature is not ascertained, no one can postulate conformity with it. Nor can the object, being determined through the manifestation of the form of cognition, be imagined as having conformity, because even from something non-conforming, the form in the effect can be accounted for. Even without ascertaining the specific state of a seed reddened by lac, the production of a red effect is observed. For there is no valid means of knowledge establishing the principle that the object causing the production of cognition must have the very form that cognition has. Moreover, cognition arises with a gross form, while the object has the form of atoms; cognition has a common form, while the object has an uncommon form — so what conformity could there be? Moreover, if knowability were based on mere conformity, the determination of the known-knower relationship would not be possible, because cognitions of different streams regarding a single object cannot have the known-knower relationship. If the knowable is what produces and imparts its own form — even so, in a flowing stream of cognition, each earlier cognition would be the knowable of each later one. If the knowable is what imparts a specific form — even so, only the immediately preceding cognition turns out to be the knowable, for the immediately preceding cognition has been said to be the cause of the specific form. Moreover, even in formlessness (<s>nirākāratva</s>), the determination with respect to each particular by awareness is not impossible. For that specific property of the person — awareness (<s>saṃvedana</s>) — which conforms to the specific behavioral activity bound to the object, is self-luminous. What shines forth as conforming to behavioral activity bound to the object is determined as the awareness of that object. And the rule of co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>) is possible even when there is difference. For the very cognition of blue is itself the apprehension of blue. How can blue be apprehended without the apprehension of blue? Moreover, by this argument, this undesired consequence follows: that it would be apprehended even without apprehension. For it is not accepted that anything at all is apprehended without apprehension. And apprehension is not itself apprehended by another apprehension. Moreover, the difference between apprehension and the apprehended is not pervaded by the absence of the rule of co-apprehension; rather, the rule, turning away from that, resting in non-difference alone, would be pervaded by that and would indicate it. But for the apprehended and apprehension, the rule is possible even with difference, because apprehension is impossible without the apprehended. Therefore, the rule of co-apprehension observed even with difference is not capable of establishing non-difference. Moreover, since there is also a rule of co-apprehension between awareness and what is known to awareness even with difference, if that too were to become of the nature of awareness, the oneness of awareness would be compromised, and then it would be possible that the rule of co-apprehension exists precisely in difference. Moreover, even one who asserts non-difference of the known from awareness at least does not deny the appearance of the known. This being so, how does the inference arise? For inference does not gain its existence in opposition to direct experience. And as for the inference of non-difference in flames and such — that too does not dislodge the direct experience from its own object; rather, it shows that 'this is the same flame' constitutes two cognitions — apprehension and memory — having established objects. But here, the direct experience of difference would have to be denied by what is to be proved itself — hence no inference arises in opposition to it. 'And difference is seen through erroneous cognitions, like the two moons in the moon' — this too is untenable. For there, difference is not seen; rather, in the case of the single moon, due to the bifurcation of the visual faculty, two cognitions arise. Since those, due to the difference in the activity of the sense-organ, occasion behavior regarding two objects even though the moon is non-different — this has been stated in the respective places. And as for what was said — that if awareness is self-luminous, form (<s>ākāra</s>) such as blue and so forth exists — that too is improper, because the form, appearing as non-different from awareness, cannot logically be of the nature of awareness. If asked: how can formless awareness be luminous? What is meant by 'formless'? If 'without own-nature' — that is wrong, because awareness is accepted as having awareness as its own nature. If 'without forms like blue and such' — what royal decree says that it must be luminous only through blue and such forms, and not otherwise? When there is illumination, whatever is cognized as it truly is — the acceptance of that as being truly so is proper. And what was said — that in dreams the form of cognition appears — that too is improper. For there too, awareness appears as external. And it is not the case that it does not have external objects, because due to the revival of <s>saṃskāras</s> deposited by prior experience, it has objects that are things previously experienced. How then is the prior-experience-ness not recognized, and how is there the determination of being-currently-experienced? It is replied: This is accepted as memory caused by the revival of <s>saṃskāras</s>. And the revival of <s>saṃskāras</s> is caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit), because it causes pleasure and pain, and because pleasure and pain are experienced even in dreams. Therefore, that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> revives <s>saṃskāras</s> only to the extent that pleasure or pain results. And in the remembering of the experienced portion, there is no arising of pleasure or pain; hence there is no revival of <s>saṃskāras</s> there, nor memory. And for this very reason, when the experienced portion is not determined, only bare experience remains — thus the determination of something as experience is also established. And as for what they say — that since what is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>) cannot be illuminated, the form must be of the nature of illumination — that too is not sound.
<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 2, verse 208

children.translated_text: . The more the forms are examined, the more they are found to be untenable — they become empty, they become unreal — this is the meaning. And since those forms, being unreal, are not of the nature of illumination — how then do they appear? Similarly, the difference between the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>), the apprehender (<s>grāhaka</s>), and awareness — being completely unreal and unable to enter into illumination — how would it appear? As for the modes of denying external objects that arise from reflection on the knowable — those have been mostly examined and refuted in the <s>Jātinirṇaya</s> (Determination of Universals) chapter; hence they are not discussed here. And those who, using the example of dream cognitions and the reason 'because they are cognitions,' demonstrate the emptiness of external objects in waking cognitions — their position contradicts the totality of direct experience that has external objects. The defect of the reason being 'opposed' (<s>viruddha</s>) — through establishing that even dream cognitions have external objects as what they apprehend — and the 'deficiency of the example lacking the property to be proved' should be pointed out.

children.translated_text: thus. If the impossibility of something being both agent and object is stated, nothing is lost, for we do not accept the agent-object relation [of the self with respect to cognition]. But if the self-luminosity (<s>svayamprakāśatā</s>) of that whose nature is the manifestation of objects is denied, then there is contradiction with experience. Moreover, how can those who, on the strength of experience, accept that the one self (<s>ātman</s>) has both the status of agent and object deny awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>)? Furthermore, cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is admitted to be inferable. In that inference, mere existence of the object is not the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), due to the absence of an invariable concomitance. If it is said 'object-cognition' is the mark, even that is not the mark by mere arising, since when not manifesting, there is no distinction between what has arisen and what has not. For a mark that does not manifest does not make known the probandum (<s>liṅgin</s>). Nor does the manifestation of object-cognition depend on another cognition. Nor is there apprehension from another cognition — for if apprehension were from another cognition, there would be the unwanted consequence of infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>). Therefore, object-cognition must be accepted as self-luminous. By this, those who say that another cognition — a mental perception (<s>mānasapratyakṣa</s>) like pleasure and such — is the means of knowledge for the existence of cognition, they too are refuted. Since it is tenable through self-luminosity alone, the postulation of dependence on another is untenable — this has been stated. Then what is inferred? Cognition (<s>jñāna</s>). But is it not the case that this is not perceived as different from self-luminous awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>)? True, and that is precisely why it is inferred.
[Objection:] But we do not know what that [cognition] is!
Know that it is the conjunction of self and mind (<s>ātma-manaḥ-sannikarṣa</s>) which is the cause of the arising of awareness — and be satisfied, O long-lived one!

He explains the nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) and fruit: "When awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>) is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the fruit is external [activity] such as avoidance, acquisition, and indifference;
but the fruit of cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is that very [awareness] which is useful for practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>)."

"And the relative instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) is either the mind, or the sense-organ itself,
or the contact of that [sense-organ] with the object — and if [any of these] is the means, the prior [awareness] is the fruit."

Thus. When the derivation '<s>pramitiḥ pramāṇam</s>' (valid cognition is the means) — taking the <s>bhāvasādhana</s> (abstract noun derivation) — is resorted to, then awareness (<s>saṃvid</s>) itself is the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.translated_text: If the relation of words with meanings were only person-made (<s>pauruṣeya</s>), then since people have the power to create conventions only regarding objects accessible to other means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), and since for the Vedic meaning of unprecedented ritual action (<s>apūrvakāryātman</s>) there is no scope for other means of knowledge, convention there would be impossible. Therefore, the inherent (<s>autpattika</s>) relation of words with their meanings is to be established. And when this is established, the authority of Vedic sentences is established, since there is no possibility of defect. For human speech, being person-made in composition, may be suspected of falsity due to the speaker's defects of error, carelessness, incapacity, or deceptive intention. But Vedic sentences, having no author, cannot even be suspected of falsity. And so it has been stated in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> (Path of Reasoning).
The prior position (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>) according to the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view:
There, some assert the word-meaning relation to be person-made (<s>pauruṣeya</s>),
speaking of the Vedas as being created by the Lord of the universe (<s>Jagadīśvara</s>) — the proponents of Vedic authority. [2]
Thus.

children.translated_text: Moreover, when the existence of the Lord (<s>Bhagavat</s>) — who is uniquely skilled in creating the entire universe and who is a direct agent of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — is established by the force of the aforementioned proofs, even through his authorship the authority of the Vedas regarding unprecedented meaning is established. Thus, the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>s' [opposition] is grounded in mere hostility [and not in reason].
The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>):
But the inherent (<s>autpattika</s>) relation of the word with its meaning is the accepted [view];
because the flow of the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddhasaṃvyavahāra</s>) is without beginning. [3]

Thus. For when there exists a beginningless succession of the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddhavyavahāra</s>), the relation of denoted and denoter (<s>vācyavācakabhāva</s>) between word and meaning, established through the usage of the learned, would be established as non-person-made (<s>apauruṣeya</s>). For thus: children, hearing the utterances of the learned who are using [words] in accordance with their meanings, and grasping the connection of the word with the meaning through the method of co-occurrence and non-co-occurrence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), themselves use [words] in that way — and their children too, in the same manner. Thus, even if there is a beginningless flow, since the <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) of each individual is accomplished, what need is there to accept God (<s>Īśvara</s>) as the creator of the word-meaning relation? [Objection:] But the beginninglessness of the succession of the usage of the learned is not established. For since the world has a beginning, due to being an effect, how can its inhabitant, the learned person, be without a beginning? It is replied: This is not so, because the beginninglessness of the world has been shown through reasoning. For it has been demonstrated in the <s>Nayavīthī</s> that atoms are eternal. And their conjunction requires an unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), and <s>adṛṣṭa</s> requires a body, and a body requires previous atoms, and so on — thus, like seed and sprout, the succession of the world is beginningless. [Objection:] But when, at the time of dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>), the world is dissolved, the succession of the usage of the learned is broken. It is replied: Even then, through the persistence of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) in souls, the recollection of the word-meaning relation at the time of creation is accomplished. [Counter-objection:] Then even without God, the word-meaning relation is accomplished through impressions — so why posit God? It is replied: God is needed as the agent of creation who initiates the cycle anew. [Vaiśeṣika position:] Moreover, God's existence is proved as the maker of the world, since the world, being an effect composed of parts, requires an intelligent cause. And this omniscient God, directly knowing <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, created the Vedas — thus through his authorship too, the authority of the Vedas regarding unprecedented meanings (<s>apūrvārtha</s>) is established.
Thus.
