children.translated_text: Thus, when the inference [of convention] is refuted by counter-inference, due to the absence of any [other] <s>pramāṇa</s>, the non-human-authorship (<s>apauruṣeyatva</s>) of the word-meaning relation alone is established.
Hence the following is refuted.
What the outsiders (Buddhists) say: "Whatever is of the same class as that from which it is established, it is from that — like fire and wood.
Even another, whose cause is unseen, is understood to be of that nature."

The relation of word with meaning is held to be non-human-authored (<s>apauruṣeya</s>) by the venerable <s>Jaimini</s>, the foremost among knowers of Vedic meaning, the treasure-house of all logical methods. For he held: although the denotative capacity of words like '<s>Devadatta</s>' and such is based on human convention (<s>saṅketa</s>), nevertheless, for words like 'cow' and such, inference [of convention] cannot be made, because the inference would be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), since the effect — namely, the comprehension of meaning — can be explained otherwise. For even children are seen to comprehend word-meaning based on knowledge of denotative capacity (<s>śakti</s>) grounded in observing the usage of elders (<s>vṛddha-vyavahāra</s>). Therefore, convention alone cannot be exclusively postulated. Moreover, the comprehension of meaning for words like 'cow' is based solely on knowledge of capacity — and this is directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). And when perception is the cause, another cause cannot be inferred. But for words like '<s>Devadatta</s>,' for one whose comprehension of meaning is based on convention, convention alone is the cause. Even in those cases, for those who comprehend meaning by simply observing usage, the cause of meaning-comprehension is knowledge of capacity born from observing usage, not convention. But there, the usage is preceded by convention, and meaning-comprehension likewise; similarly, the knowledge of denotative capacity is also preceded by it. But for words like 'cow,' since usage is possible for everyone from knowledge of capacity alone, the comprehension of meaning [differs] — this is the difference. But since convention is observed for words like '<s>Devadatta</s>,' why not postulate a prior convention for words like 'cow' too? No — because it is swallowed by a counter-inference (<s>pratyanumāna</s>). For the following inference can be envisioned: the earlier people who comprehended meaning from words like 'cow' for objects possessing dewlaps and such, did so through knowledge of capacity established by elder-usage — because they possessed the fitness for meaning-comprehension from words like 'cow' for objects with dewlaps — just like present-day people.

children.translated_text: If production [is meant], then that [production] is from the individual soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>) alone as the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>), and from the conjunction of self and mind as the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>), aided by the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) such as intention and so forth.
If fruit-giving [is meant] —
No; the fruit comes from <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> alone, accompanied by cooperating conditions of place, time, state, and such — it does not require the activity of a conscious being.
Refutation of the God accepted by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>:

[<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 3, verse 243.]
Defense of the beginninglessness of elder-usage:
But this aspiration would succeed if the succession of elder-usage were beginningless; yet that has been denied by earlier logicians. To this we say: granted that everything composite has its existence commenced by the conjunction of parts and is perishable when that conjunction ceases — still, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the claim that everything originates and perishes simultaneously. Rather, in accordance with observation, this alone is proper to maintain: that origination is gradual, and dissolution is gradual.
Moreover, just as present-day people acquire their existence through the union of mother and father, so too earlier people [did the same], since they are people — this can indeed be inferred. And for those born from wombs (<s>jarāyuja</s>) and eggs (<s>aṇḍaja</s>), it does not work that they originate solely through the power of merit (<s>dharma</s>) or demerit (<s>adharma</s>) like sweat-born beings (<s>saṃsvedaja</s>), since such [wombless generation] is not observed for womb-born and egg-born beings. For inference everywhere follows what is observed. Therefore, what is observed with invariable concomitance in sweat-born beings cannot be inferred for the womb-born and egg-born.
Refutation of <s>Īśvara</s> (God):
And the claim that <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> are superintended by a conscious being — that too is unestablished. Let the very <s>kṣetrajña</s> (individual soul) to whom those two belong be the superintendent. If it is said that due to his ignorance, his superintendent-status is not possible — then how is it possible for another either? For that other too cannot have knowledge of the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> residing in another person, due to the absence of a cause. For the senses are not the cause of that, since no capacity of the senses is observed there. Nor the mind alone, since the mind alone does not engage with external things. Nor does <s>Īśvara</s>, who is free from <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, have a connection of senses and mind, since that connection depends on <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. If some other cause of <s>Īśvara</s>'s cognition is posited — that is improper, since the causes of cognition are well-known. For what is observed as the cause of a particular effect is proper as the cause of that — otherwise, since a chisel superintended by a conscious being is observed, how would the superintendence of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> by that [God] follow?
If it is said that <s>Īśvara</s>'s cognition is eternal and uncaused — that too is not good, since the nature of cognition does not admit of eternality. Being eternal, it simply would not be cognition. And superintendence is observed by one who possesses cognition, not by another. If the unseen eternality of cognition is accepted, why not accept the absence of conscious superintendence? If it is said that once superintendence is established, knowledge too is postulated — that is improper. Since, when the cause of superintendence unaccompanied by knowledge and such is absent, and when knowledge is refuted, inference is impossible.
Therefore, the invariable concomitance to be relied upon is: only what is capable of being known by a conscious being possessing knowledge is superintended by a conscious being — as observed. For carpenters and such are seen to superintend chisels and such that are knowable to them, not other things.
Moreover, the nature of superintendence should also be considered. It is not conjunction, since <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, being qualities, lack conjunction. Nor is inherence possible between <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, which inhere in another person, and <s>Īśvara</s>. But in the case of chisels and such, the superintendence of carpenters is through hand-contact and such.
Also, what kind of activity [of God would it be]? Not action (<s>kriyā</s>), since <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, being qualities, lack action.

children.translated_text: <s>Mantras</s> and <s>arthavādas</s> (laudatory passages) are not capable of conveying meaning independently, but only in accordance with the direction of the <s>vidhi</s> (injunction), conveying a meaning conforming to that — therefore they have no validity in establishing accomplished facts (<s>siddhārtha</s>). Thus, the non-human-authorship of the word-meaning relation is established.
To pierce the darkness of bad reasoning that obstructs the vision of students,
this <s>Vimalāñjana</s> (Clear Collyrium) was composed by <s>Śālikanātha</s>.

And what some say — that atoms themselves move by the will of <s>Īśvara</s> — that too is not proper, since such superintendence is not observed anywhere. If it is said that it is observed in the body — no, because the body is governed by the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> of the individual soul. The atoms are not governed by <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. Nor does he act by mere will alone, but by effort (<s>prayatna</s>). And there is no cause even for his will. Nor is the will eternal, since that would entail perpetual activity.
Moreover, just as the superintendence of a conscious being is inferred from the non-conscious nature [of the effect], so too from the absence of purpose, the absence of superintendence is known. Which of these two inferences is stronger — let us consider. Therefore, the invariable concomitance to be relied upon is: only that non-conscious thing where purpose exists is superintended by a conscious being — as observed.
Moreover, inference requires prior apprehension of invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>), and <s>vyāpti</s> is grasped through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). And just as a conscious superintendent is perceived, so too is one possessing a body and such. Therefore, when inference proceeds, it would infer only such a [superintendent]. And neither <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> nor atoms can be superintended by such a [bodiless God] — hence there is no superintendence.
Therefore, the invariable concomitance to be relied upon is: only that non-conscious thing which is fit to be superintended by an embodied being is superintended by a conscious being. But if this [reasoning] were applied, even the well-known inference from smoke and such would be destroyed. For the <s>vyāpti</s> has been grasped with [fire] existing in a kitchen and such; one who is not of that kind cannot be inferred. And regarding that of which kind inference is made — the non-ascertainment of that kind during the apprehension of <s>vyāpti</s> [is sufficient]. That is improper — for the apprehension of the relation is in general, setting aside qualifiers of place, time, and such. Therefore here too, whatever is observed in chisels and such applies to <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> as well. But only that form which is observed as the pervader can be inferred, not another. And here, embodiment and such also enter into the invariable concomitance, and so must be inferred. If that [embodiment] cannot be inferred [of God] — better to abandon the inference of a conscious [superintendent] altogether than to infer one without that [embodiment].
Therefore, due to the absence of a logical reason for the inference of <s>Īśvara</s>'s omniscience, there is certainty of the absence of [such] knowledge. Hence the beginningless succession of elder-usage alone is the cause of the comprehension of word-meaning. And there is no convention made by <s>Īśvara</s> at the beginning of creation, since he is simply incapable of making a convention. For present-day people, not understanding the meaning of the convention-sentence, do not grasp the convention. Therefore, a beginningless succession of elder-usage must be accepted.
Thus, since for a person there is no means other than words for the cognition of <s>dharma</s>, and since the validity of the Veda regarding its object — which is unprecedented and action-natured — would not hold if it were human-authored, the non-human-authorship of the Veda must be accepted.
Determination of the non-human-authorship of the Vedas:
How is the non-human-authorship of the Vedas [established]? We reply: because no author is remembered. And even inference of an author is not possible. For one who has not cognized the meaning through another <s>pramāṇa</s> is incapable of composing a sentence [about it]. And even the designation '<s>Kāṭhaka</s>' and such does not suffice to establish the existence of an author,

Statement of the subject-matter of the chapter.
Regarding the reality of the <s>ātman</s> (self), there are many-sided disputes among philosophers.
We, the <s>Prābhākaras</s>, endeavor for the determination of that reality. [1]

children.translated_text: Here, to determine the truth of the matter, this discussion is commenced.
The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>):
The self (<s>ātman</s>), different from intellect, senses, and body, is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>) and permanent (<s>dhruva</s>);
It is manifold, different in each body, and appears in the cognitions of objects. // 2 //

Thus. Some consider the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) itself to be the self (<s>ātman</s>); others the sense-organs alone; still others the body alone. Similarly, some say the self is inferable and different from intellect, senses, and body; some say it is known through mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>); some that it is self-luminous; and others think it is established through all cognitions. Some say it is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>); others that it is immutably eternal (<s>kūṭastha-nitya</s>). Those with various views dispute — that it is of atomic size, of the size of the body, all-pervading, and so on. Similarly, some hold one self in all bodies, and others that it is manifold, different in each body.

children.translated_text: Because [difference] is sublated by the perception of what is opposed to what pervades it.
Thus they say:
"For the non-dual reality of intellect and self, through perceptions that have been distorted,
Is perceived as if having the distinctions of apprehended, apprehender, and awareness."

Thus. Objection according to the <s>Vijñānavāda</s> school: But we do not perceive any difference between the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) and the knower (<s>boddhṛ</s>). How so? Because in 'I know the pot,' people understand the self as different from the intellect, as the knower. True, but this is an error, like the cognition of two moons and such, or like the cognition of an image and its reflection — so say the epistemologists (<s>prāmāṇikas</s>). And through the rule of co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>), the difference between the intellect and the knower is refuted, since difference is not pervaded by invariable co-apprehension.

[<s>Pramāṇavārttika</s>, Chapter 2, verse 354]. Similarly, even those who accept a knower other than the intellect say that his knower-hood exists only when the intellect exists regarding that object. And thus, let the intellect itself be the supreme knower; there is no need for another knower. And since the knower is the self (<s>ātman</s>), the intellect alone is the self. And that intellect is self-luminous, flowing in a beginningless stream through cause and effect; in sleep, intoxication, fainting, and such states, being overpowered, it does not again enter the path of recognition (<s>anusandhāna</s>).

children.translated_text: It is said: The whiteness is mostly of the nature of fire, being in mist or frost; for upon its removal, that whiteness is not perceived.
And as for the blue color that is observed at night, that does not belong to space.
To what then? To nothing.
But how can a quality belong to nothing? True.

Thus. And for the <s>Deśikas</s> (Mahāyāna teachers), the purified stream of consciousness of those endowed with great compassion (<s>mahākaruṇā</s>) pervading the entire world from <s>Brahmā</s> to a blade of grass, acquired through practice across many births, is infinite. Refutation of that: This is without substance, because the difference between the intellect and the knower, established through direct experience, is not fit to be refuted. As for the rule of co-apprehension — how it is possible even with difference, we shall state right here. And this has been refuted in the <s>Ṛjuvimalā</s> on the establishment of external objects. As for what was said — that the intellect alone suffices, there is no need for a knower — that is proper to say regarding a postulated knower, but regarding one established through direct experience, there is no room for this empty talk. And what was said — that the intellect continues even in sleep and such — that too is without substance due to lack of evidence. The cause of intellect in waking and other states we shall state right here. Presentation and refutation of the sense-organ-is-the-self view: Then let the sense-organs themselves be conscious — thus the appearance of difference between the intellect and the knower will be explained. This would be so if there were no recognition of a single object through sight and touch. In 'what I saw, that I now touch,' a single recognizer is apprehended. And the memory of objects of the respective senses, even when those senses cease to function, which is observed — that is impossible if consciousness belonged to the senses. Objection and refutation of the body-is-the-self view: Then let the body itself be the self; these two defects would not apply. Not so. For the self is a knower, and the body cannot be a knower. For thus: the body is a specific material substance (<s>dravya</s>) of the earth element. But if it is earthen, would there not be the consequence of not perceiving qualities of other elements? No, we say. We say that the combined elements do not produce further effects as separate elements; but we do not say that the elements do not combine with each other at all. Therefore, the perception of qualities of combined elements is not impossible. But how is the impossibility of being a producing cause established? It is said: First, the combined production from five or four elements is not possible, because of the consequence that what is produced from visible and invisible substances, and what inheres in it, would be invisible. For what is produced from visible and invisible substances and what inheres in it is not visible — like the combination of air and a tree. And the body is visible. Therefore, it is not produced from five or four elements, since space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and air (<s>anila</s>) are invisible. Demonstration of the invisibility of space: But how is space invisible? And whether the existence of what is invisible is even valid — this too must be considered. It is said: Space is invisible because, being a substance, it has no color — like the self (<s>ātman</s>). But space is not colorless — for it is perceived as white, or as dark like a blue lotus petal.

children.translated_text: For by having color, darkness would be a substance, and that substance produced from multiple substances would be visible — but those substances do not exist.
If they do exist, they should produce darkness even during the day.
Therefore, just as for blind persons, this appearance of blue color regarding space is merely a false impression — this is proper.
Refutation of darkness as a substance.

Therefore, this is an error of cognition on the part of the dull-witted, when in fact there is no cognition. Hence, its non-perception during the day. Otherwise, the eye, aided by solar rays, would reveal the blue color in space even more clearly. And since color is accompanied by touch, space would have touch. And then there would be the consequence of obstruction of all corporeal substances. Some, however, say that the darkness has a blue color that is perceived as belonging to space. That is wrong, say some, because the production of darkness cannot be established.

children.translated_text: But if the ground-surface itself is the shadow, how can there be reference to another substance in 'this is his shadow'?
It is said: We have stated that the ground-surface from which light has been removed is itself the shadow.
There, the reference is proper with respect to that by which the removal of light is caused.
And thus, the usage of the authors of <s>smṛti</s> — 'One should not deliberately step on a shadow' and such — is also well-established.

As for what is said — that shadow (<s>chāyā</s>) itself is darkness, and shadow, possessing qualities such as movability, immovability, largeness, smallness, distance, nearness, and so on, is a real entity — that too is without substance, because its production cannot be established. And what was mentioned about movability, immovability, and such — that too is due to superficial observation. For thus: When light is removed, shadow is expected; but upon removing the light, no shadow is seen as distinct from the ground-surface and other things in the area where light has been removed. Therefore, we think: the ground-surface and other things from which light has been removed are themselves the shadow. By this, movability, immovability, largeness, smallness, distance, nearness, and such are explained. For whichever substance obstructs light, as it moves here and there, light is accordingly released and obstructed — and thus shadow appears as if moving. Otherwise, when the body moves, why should the shadow also move? Because there is no cause of movement for the shadow itself. By this, the immovability when the body is stationary is explained. Largeness requires number and size — without that, how would this shadow come about? Enough of this discussion by the superficial thinker, which lacks coherence.

children.translated_text: Because it is established through inference from its characteristic quality of sound (<s>śabda</s>).
But even the quality-ness of sound is not established, since it is accepted as a substance by the proponents [of that view].
Thus they say: "And those sounds that are of the nature of phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>), eternal and all-pervading —

children.text: pṛthagdravyatayā te tu na guṇāḥ kasyacinmatāḥ" //
children.translated_text: They are held by some not to be qualities of anything, but to be separate substances."

And the usage of the <s>śāstra</s> authors — 'The effect of shade is the same for an umbrella, house, and such' — is to be explained with reference to the removal of light. But would not the non-perception of the ground-surface follow from the removal of light? Not so. Conjunction with the most abundant light-particles is prevented there, but small particles of light, moving about from all directions, do conjoin. But where there is total absence of their conjunction, that is great darkness — and this is faultless. And as for what is said — that one with wide-open eyes sees water in the middle of a well, or a hole in the middle — there too, the answer is that particles of light, having obtained delimitation by the rim of the well, are perceived in that way. Doubt about the establishment of space: And even so, space is not thereby unestablished.

children.translated_text: A substance composed of these three would acquire a touch different from all three, like a variegated cloth.
Just as a cloth composed of white, black, and other threads has a color different from the thread-colors, so too the body would have a touch different from the touches of its constituent substances.
And this [body] is perceived as having neither-hot-nor-cold (<s>anuṣṇāśīta</s>) touch.
By this, the two-natured theory (<s>dvyātmakatā</s>) is also refuted.

[Reference: <s>Sāṃkhya Darśana Kaumudī</s> p. 92] Thus. Its refutation: This is premature. For the quality-nature [of sound] is established by being perceptible to one sense-organ alone, just like color and such. Nor is there the fallacy of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>) with respect to wind (<s>vāyu</s>), because wind is accepted as beyond the senses (<s>atīndriya</s>). And even for those who accept wind as sense-perceptible, there is no fault, due to the inclusion of the qualifying condition 'in the absence of touch.' Thus, sound (<s>śabda</s>), whose quality-nature is established, will infer its substrate (<s>guṇin</s>). Since there is no cause for knowing it to be of the nature of earth, water, etc., it is established as a different substance entirely. The difference is known through the difference of qualities whose co-location (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) has not been perceived. [Objection:] But sound is perceived as residing in the mouth etc. It is replied: No. The organ of hearing (<s>śrotra</s>) operates by reaching its object, being an external sense-organ like the sense of touch. Now, the ear does not go to the location of the mouth, for the ear-conch (<s>karṇaśaṣkulī</s>) is directly perceived as staying in its own location. Nor does the mouth approach the location of the ear, for it too is perceived only in its own location. Therefore, sound is apprehended as residing in the ear itself. The notion that sound is in the mouth is an error. And since the proximity of sound, being a quality, cannot be conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) — its proximity is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) alone. And thus, since the ear possesses the quality of sound, that substance which has sound as its quality and is denoted by the word <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — that alone is the organ of hearing. This is established. [Objection:] But let the earthy ear-conch be the organ of hearing, and let it apprehend the sound residing in space through conjunction-inherence (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>). This is not so. For when direct proximity is possible, taking recourse to a channel (<s>praṇālī</s>) is improper. Nor is the body three-natured (<s>tryātmaka</s>), because of the unwanted consequence of the manifestation of additional qualities. For earth, water, and fire have respectively neither-hot-nor-cold, cold, and hot touch.

children.translated_text: And since they [pleasure and such] are causes of bodily modifications, all the more are they qualities of the body — for a quality not belonging to a substance cannot modify that substance.

Moreover, since a single odor (<s>gandha</s>) inhering in an earthy substance is incapable of producing another odor by itself, the body would be without odor [if not earthy]. If [the body] is produced by earth and fire, or by water and fire, it would be without odor, and similarly without taste — this should be understood. Therefore, the body, possessing color, taste, odor, and touch, is earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>) alone. And cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> quality. And in a composite substance, a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> quality is produced by qualities of the same type in the causal substances. Therefore, if cognition were a quality of the body, it should arise from cognitions in the constituent atoms — but those are absent. Nor can cognition be the specific quality (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) produced from a specific configuration, because specific qualities arise from specific causes, and no such specific cause is available in the body's atoms. Furthermore, if cognition were a quality of the body, it should perish when the body perishes — but the fruitfulness of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> in another birth would be impossible. And if the body alone were the self, then 'my body' — this usage in the genitive case indicating a relation of possessor and possessed — would be impossible, since self-relation is contradictory. [Objection:] But this genitive can be explained as in 'the body of <s>Devadatta</s>,' where <s>Devadatta</s> is merely the name of the body.

children.translated_text: a plant-body (<s>udbhijja</s>) is not a body at all,
because no experience (<s>bhoga</s>) is observed [in plants] — for a body is motivated by the need for a locus of experience, and there is no proof that trees and such serve as loci of sense-organs.
And further —
"A tree is born in the cremation ground, frequented by herons and vultures."

For the body is modified by the dilation of the eyes, the beaming of the face, the bristling of hair, and such [when pleasure arises]. When pleasure and such arise in that body — which, as the effect, is the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) [of the modifications] — it is proper that the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) too should be proximate to it. And it cannot be said that the conjunction of a pleasure-possessing self alone is the non-inherent cause of the modifications inhering in the body, because there is no proof [for such a self]. [Refutation of the materialist (Cārvāka) view:] But this [Cārvāka position] is untenable. For cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> quality, and a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> quality in a composite substance arises from qualities of the same type in the causal substances — but there is no cognition in the atoms constituting the body. [Regarding the Cārvāka objection about the genitive:] The genitive usage 'my body' (<s>mama śarīram</s>) indeed indicates the relation of possessor and possessed. And the [Cārvāka] example 'the body of a stone-child' is inapplicable, since it is a mere figurative expression where no real possessor-possessed relation is intended. As for the objection that 'my self' too would entail another self — this does not follow, since the genitive there is employed in the sense of the referent itself, not in the sense of possession. And pleasure and such, being apprehended as objects of self-consciousness, are not thereby established as mere bodily qualities — for self-consciousness (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) itself indicates a substrate beyond the body. And the causal relation of pleasure to bodily modifications does not entail that pleasure is a quality of the body — for even the conjunction of a self possessing pleasure with the body can serve as the non-inherent cause of bodily modifications. And the existence of such a self is proved by the fact that cognition cannot be a quality of the body, as shown above, and by the fruitfulness of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> in another birth, and by the experience 'I who saw the pot yesterday now see the cloth' — which indicates the continuity of a single experiencer across different cognitions. And regarding the four types of bodies — born from a womb (<s>jarāyuja</s>), born from an egg (<s>aṇḍaja</s>), born from moisture (<s>svedaja</s>), and born from the earth (<s>udbhijja</s>) —

children.translated_text: And substance (<s>dravya</s>) is of two kinds: a composite substance (<s>anekadravya</s>), and a non-substance-substance (<s>adravyadravya</s>).
In the case of mind being a composite substance, there would be explanatory heaviness (unnecessary complexity), because of the consequence of having to accept produced and producer-substances.
Even in the case of being a non-substance-substance, accepting supreme magnitude, there is the impossibility of conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) with the self (<s>ātman</s>).
For conjunction is not possible between what is supremely great and what is without motion, and between what is without parts.

Thus, from the recollection that a plant-born body (<s>udbhijja śarīra</s>) is the result of prohibited conduct, it appears [to be established]. But that too is untenable, because there is no means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for that particular aspect. Because the memory [of such a result] being baseless, its primary meaning cannot be established. Nor can the <s>Veda</s> itself serve as the basis, since [the prohibitive injunction] does not have an effect as its purpose. Because in the meaning 'transgression results from performing what is prohibited' — from the negative injunction (<s>nañvidhi</s>) — there is no capacity to indicate [a plant-body as the result]. Although, upon reflection on the <s>siddhānta</s> position in the <s>Śaṃyvadhikaraṇa</s> (<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 3.4.10), some adverse consequence does arise even from prohibited acts, nevertheless it cannot be concluded that the result is a body in the form of a tree and so on, since such a result is unfit for logical connection (<s>anvaya</s>). For that whose fitness for logical connection has been ascertained enters into the meaning of the sentence, but that whose fitness for connection is impossible does not enter into the sentence-meaning either — like the expression 'sprinkle with fire.' And whatever usage of such meaning occurs in the <s>Veda</s>, that should be explained as secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>) or figurative (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>); here too, it should be explained through secondary or figurative usage. Therefore the body is of only three kinds. As for the non-earthy, non-womb-born body that some accept as based solely on the predominance of <s>dharma</s> — that cannot be inferred, since there is no exception to the earthiness of all bodies. Examination of the mind (<s>manas</s>): In all bodies there is mind (<s>manas</s>); along with skin, these are a pair of sense-organs that are undistinguished [across body types]. And mind is internal to the body and of atomic dimension (<s>paramāṇu-parimāṇa</s>). It, being a substance (<s>dravya</s>), is regarded as possessing the quality of conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>).

children.translated_text: For in negative statements, nothing is absolutely negated; rather, something specific is negated in some specific context.
But you, who maintain the non-duality of <s>Brahman</s>, desire an absolute negation.

children.translated_text: And thus, this arrow of your own strikes you back: 'Something of a certain nature is negated somewhere in something that has obtained a form;
therefore, without a positive establishment (<s>vidhāna</s>), negation is impossible.'

Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is of three kinds only: produced by the action of one party (<s>anyatarakarma-ja</s>), produced by the action of both parties (<s>ubhayakarma-ja</s>), and produced by [another] conjunction (<s>saṃyoga-ja</s>).
Therefore, the mind (<s>manas</s>) is of atomic dimension (<s>paramāṇu-paribhāṇa</s>).
And it is eternal, because it has an existent cause [that is itself uncaused, i.e. it has no cause for its destruction].
It moves with the greatest speed, because we observe the sense-organs being superintended with the greatest swiftness.
For a sense-organ not superintended by it [the mind] is not capable of making its own object determinate, since one whose mind is engaged elsewhere does not perceive another object.
The conjunction of that mind with the individual soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>) is beginningless and depends on merit (<s>dharma</s>) and demerit (<s>adharma</s>); and the conjunction with another body [in the next life arises] through the grace of action (<s>karman</s>) born from the contact of the self and mind, which depends on unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).
This self (<s>ātman</s>) is the enjoyer (<s>bhoktṛ</s>); the body is the seat of enjoyment (<s>bhogāyatana</s>); the sense-organs are the instruments of enjoyment (<s>bhogasādhana</s>); the objects of enjoyment (<s>bhogya</s>) are internal — pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) etc. — and external — earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>) etc.; and enjoyment (<s>bhukti</s>), that is, experience (<s>vitti</s>), is the experience of pleasure and pain. Thus all reality is comprehended in these five categories.

Determination of the means of knowledge regarding the self (<s>ātman</s>):
By what means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) then is the self known? And if it is not known, the acceptance of its existence is groundless.
Thereupon some say: mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>), as in the case of pleasure etc., is the means of knowledge regarding the self.
The <s>Prābhākaras</s> say this is improper. For it is impossible for the same entity to be both agent (<s>kartṛ</s>) and object (<s>karman</s>) with respect to itself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon its own self.
Nor is there non-contradiction on account of the 'I'-awareness (<s>aham-iti-saṃvid</s>), since that [I-awareness] is accounted for either through self-luminosity (<s>svayam-prakāśatva</s>) or through being within the range of object-cognition.
And in this case, the rule of invariable co-perception (<s>sahopalambha-niyama</s>) with objects is established.
Others think: a means of knowledge is needed for objects whose nature is non-luminous; but for what is naturally luminous, the need for illumination regarding its own self is futile — like consciousness (<s>saṃvitti</s>) itself.

Investigation of the self-luminosity of consciousness:
For consciousness (<s>saṃvitti</s>), which is the result (<s>phala</s>) of the means of knowledge, must necessarily be accepted as self-luminous.
Otherwise, even though [consciousness] has arisen, if it remains unmanifested, the practical usage of 'the objects have been known' — which conveys the knownness of objects — would not occur. Nor should it be said that the person's awareness of objects is merely fitness for practical activity, and that [awareness] is inferred by its result when the activity arises.
For it is agreed by all people that the knownness of objects is ascertained even prior to the onset of practical activity.
Nor is consciousness to be apprehended through mental perception (<s>mānasa-pratyakṣa</s>).
Since self-luminosity itself sufficiently accounts for it, there is no evidence for positing that [mental perception].
For if objects, being enduring, were accepted as self-luminous, then states like sleep etc. of persons would become impossible [since objects would always manifest themselves].
But regarding consciousness, which is self-luminous, this fault does not arise, since in sleep etc. it itself does not exist [at that time].
Objects, however, whose stability is established by the force of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), cannot be said not to exist for persons even in states of sleep etc.
Therefore they are of dependent luminosity.
But consciousness is self-luminous — thus a proven example [is available].
The acceptance of the existence of what is self-luminous does not depend on another means of knowledge.
And thus, even in the fourth state (<s>turīya</s>), luminosity does not cease.
And for this very reason, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) would not be desired by persons.
Even this the foremost experts in valid knowledge do not approve.
[They reason:] if luminosity were natural to the person, then just as in waking, dreaming, and the fourth state, luminosity would also arise in deep sleep — and sleep would not differ from those [other states].
For what is natural (<s>svārasika</s>) cannot be destroyed or obstructed.
As for what someone prattles — that 'even the natural blackness of earthy atoms is removed by conjunction with fire, which is to be perceived at the stage of baking' —
That is wrong. Whatever is uncreated (<s>akṛtaka</s>) is all indestructible, like space (<s>dik</s>) etc.
And the blackness of earthy atoms is uncreated — since this is grasped by inference, it should not be disregarded.
Moreover, the naturalness of blackness to earthy atoms is not established, since redness too is admitted to be produced by baking, [so the original blackness could also be produced].
Eternality is precisely being without a cause [of destruction].
If even what is without a cause were non-eternal, then no definition of 'eternal' could be framed.

Statement of our own view:
But the knowers of reality declare: the self (<s>ātman</s>) does not appear without being pervaded by objects, and objects do not appear without the knower appearing — this much is established.
Now, that which is the means of knowledge regarding objects — the consciousness (<s>saṃvit</s>) generated by it — arises taking as its object both the person and its own objects.
Even though the person is in the position of the result-portion of that consciousness, [the person] is not an object (<s>karman</s>) but rather an agent (<s>kartṛ</s>), like a walker.
Just as a walker, even though connected with the result of walking (the conjunction [with the destination]), is not an object but an agent — so too should it be understood for the knower.
For the experts on action define as 'object' (<s>karman</s>) that which is connected with the result of an action that inheres in another.
And for this very reason, the rule of co-perception of object, knower, and consciousness is also established.
And thus, since the self is within the range of object-cognition, upon the cessation of the means of knowing objects, the non-manifestation [of the self] in sleep etc. is perfectly reasonable.
Even in the fourth state (<s>turīya</s>), the self, with all means of apprehension having ceased, merely remains in the state of bare existence.

Description of liberation as cessation of suffering — our own view:
Nor is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) without human purpose, since liberation has the nature of the cessation of the manifold sufferings of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
For the cessation of suffering is desired by persons.
Nor is this reasoning valid: 'Just as [liberation] is the supreme human goal because it has the form of cessation of all suffering, so too it is not a human goal because it has the form of the destruction of all pleasure.'
For the discriminating person, worldly pleasure, being characterized by dependence on means and by being perishable, is considered as swallowed up by suffering — indeed, it is suffering itself — and therefore [such persons] do not greatly prize it.
For this very reason they strive toward liberation.
And thus even the acceptance of supreme bliss (<s>paramānanda</s>) is of meager fruit.
Nor does any means of knowledge operate to establish that [bliss], since the scriptures do not have the capacity to make known an already established entity, and there is contradiction with direct perception.
Those who are transmigrating do not experience such bliss.
Nor is non-experience due to being overpowered [by ignorance].
For the overpowering of bliss that is naturally self-luminous is impossible.
Nor is the proof of the self's bliss-nature established from its being the supreme object of love, since love for the self is not established.
For from the arising of suffering that harms the body, all seek to avert that harm — thus there is the presumption of love for the self.
Moreover, since the natural supreme bliss of transmigrating beings has never been previously experienced, how can there be love based on it for the self?
Therefore, bliss is only that which is born from the enjoyment of specific objects — this is the correct view.
And liberation is a human goal on account of the cessation of worldly suffering — this is the complete [view].

Summary of <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>'s view:
What then is this liberation? 'The cessation of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)' — say some.
That one and only non-dual, uncontaminated, purified of all limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) — the reality of <s>Brahman</s>: that, through the force of beginningless ignorance, appearing as though accompanied by body etc., as though contaminated by limiting adjuncts, having obtained the designation 'individual soul' (<s>jīva</s>), appears as though bound.
Therefore beginningless ignorance itself is <s>saṃsāra</s>, and from the dawn of pure knowledge that transcends all conceptual construction, the cessation of that [ignorance] alone is liberation — so they say.

Refutation of that [Advaita view]:
This is merely the flourishing of faith, say those who rely on valid means of knowledge.
This would be so if non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) were the object of some means of knowledge.
But this is not so — non-duality is not the object of any means of knowledge.
One might think: direct perception itself, whose operation is exhausted in mere positive determination and which does not touch mutual difference, directly apprehends a single non-dual reality.
That is wrong. True, direct perception is indeed positive-determining. But even while determining, it determines form as form and taste as taste — it does not reduce everything to unity.
If the continuous cognition that operates regarding form were of the same nature regarding taste as well, then non-duality would indeed be directly apprehended by perception. But this is not so — and this is known to all perceivers through their own experience.
As for [the argument] that, by establishing through the classification of objects of knowledge that reality is only the general (<s>sāmānya</s>), and since being (<s>sattā</s>) has the form of the highest universal, only that much is real —
That too is like trying to swallow the sky.
Reality is not mere generality in all cases, since the universal — which is to be known through the invariable recurring appearance — cannot be denied.
Nor is reality a single entity consisting of both universal and particular, because of the contradiction of two natures in one thing. Rather, the universal and particular, as two mutually connected entities, are apprehended by perception — so how is the non-duality of being established?
And the principle that there is no 'this'-cognition (<s>iha-pratyaya</s>) regarding universal and particular, individual and class — this has been determined in the section on universals in this very work.
Nor does scripture (<s>āgama</s>) serve to establish non-duality.
Not so — because validity cannot be established for scripture regarding an already accomplished entity, since scripture has action (<s>kārya</s>) alone as its domain.
Moreover, scripture is accepted as a means of knowledge in the form of sentences. And a sentence, being constituted of multiple words, generating a cognition of the sentence-meaning which consists of multiple word-meanings — how could it manifest non-duality?
If this is said: 'This is the teaching: "not thus, not thus" (<s>neti neti</s>)' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.6] — by negating all limiting adjuncts and eliminating diverse realities, non-duality is established through scripture —
That too is without substance. For the entity that has been recognized in the form 'this is such' — as having the nature of being — is unfit to be connected with the meaning of the negative particle that imputes non-existence, just as 'exists' and 'does not exist' [cannot both apply].
And when two word-meanings are unfit for syntactic connection, they cannot form a sentence-meaning.
'But then all negative statements whatsoever would be rejected!' —
<s>Brahmasūtra</s>, <s>Kāṇḍa</s> verse 2.

children.translated_text:
Therefore, since the scripture (<s>āmnāya</s>) that teaches non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) has a meaning contradicted by perception and other [means of knowledge], it is not proper to expound it in its literal sense. What has been elaborated at length — that even when contradicting perception and such, scripture alone is stronger, and by its force the erroneousness of perception and such must be imagined — that too is mere wishful thinking. When there is contradiction with perception and such, since the semantic fitness (<s>anvaya-yogyatā</s>) of word-meanings is absent, the very comprehension of meaning from scripture does not arise in the case of that contradiction. Therefore, when there is contradiction with perception and such, a secondary (<s>gauṇī</s>) or figurative (<s>lākṣaṇikī</s>) interpretation must be resorted to in scripture.

Interpretation of the <s>ānanda</s>-śrutis and such according to our own view:
There, the <s>ānanda</s>-śrutis (scriptures about bliss) are to be explained as having the purport of the absence of suffering that is natural — since worldly bliss is meager and accompanied by suffering. The oneness-śrutis have the purport that in one abode (<s>āyatana</s>) there is ownership by one alone. '<s>Indra</s> appears in many forms through <s>māyā</s>' — the meaning is that through the identification of self with the body, he appears as if different in each birth. The purport of the denial of multiplicity is that even though embodied in many bodies, the <s>ātman</s> is one alone.
'He is <s>neti neti</s> (not this, not this)' — this is the denial of the self-nature of the body and such, aimed at establishing the cognition of what is different from them.
The consciousness-śrutis are aimed at stating the distinction [of <s>ātman</s>] from space and such, since it possesses the power of consciousness (<s>cicchakti</s>).
The 'self of all'-śrutis are figurative due to the purposive relation (<s>tādarthya</s>), since everything exists for the sake of the <s>ātman</s>.
What is stated — 'When the <s>ātman</s> is known, all this becomes known' [<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s> 4; <s>Maitrāyaṇī Brāhmaṇa</s>] — that is because the knowledge of <s>ātman</s> has as its fruit the supreme human goal, <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation); when that is known, all other knowledge becomes fruitless — this is the purport.

If it is said: the illumination of what is different from consciousness and is of non-luminous nature is simply impossible. Whatever is illuminated is non-different from illumination, and <s>Brahman</s> is of the nature of illumination. Therefore the world is of the nature of <s>Brahman</s> — thus non-duality is established.
This contradicts their own position. How do intelligent people say such things? For if the diverse forms are non-different from illumination, then illumination itself would become manifold — and non-duality would be far removed.
If it is said: this varied phenomenal diversity appears due to the superimposition of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — this too contradicts their own statement. Illumination is of the nature of being (<s>sat</s>); that the forms, being of the nature of non-being (<s>asat</s>), are non-different from it does not work. And being of the nature of non-illumination, how could they possibly be illuminated?
Moreover, it has been stated in the [section on] establishing external objects that illumination is possible only for what is of non-luminous nature. Therefore, this too is merely the delusion of the <s>Brahmavādins</s> (Advaitins), since it amounts to entering the Mahāyāna Buddhist position.
Moreover, how can <s>avidyā</s> be capable of illuminating a phenomenal world that is absolutely non-existent? For <s>avidyā</s> is not the cognition of the non-existent (<s>asatkhyāti</s>), but is rather of the nature of non-apprehension (<s>agrahaṇa</s>) — this has been established in the <s>Nayavīthī</s>. Therefore, <s>mokṣa</s> is not the cessation of <s>avidyā</s>.

Determination of <s>mokṣa</s> and its means according to our own view:
Rather, the absolute cessation of the body (<s>dehoccheda</s>), which is based on the complete exhaustion of all <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, is <s>mokṣa</s>. This is proper. For the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>), controlled by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, transmigrates through various wombs. When those two are completely destroyed, being freed from the connection with body and senses, with all worldly suffering and its train completely uprooted, he is called 'liberated' (<s>mukta</s>).
But how is the complete exhaustion of all <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> [achieved]? Not merely by experiencing their fruits — for the <s>karmāśayas</s> (latent impressions of action) accumulated through the beginningless series of bodies, being infinite, and being accumulated even at the time of fruition, cannot be exhausted.
We reply: One who is distressed by worldly sufferings and has become free from desire even for pleasures that are contaminated by their association with suffering, and who rises toward <s>mokṣa</s> — such a one, turning away from prohibited acts that cause punishment (<s>pratyavāya</s>) and from desire-prompted acts that are means to prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>), causing the previously ungenerated <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> to be exhausted through experiencing [their fruits], and through knowledge of <s>ātman</s> strengthened by the auxiliaries of tranquility (<s>śama</s>), self-control (<s>dama</s>), celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), and such — as enjoined for the purpose of non-return by 'He does not return again' [<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 8] — destroying all residual <s>karmāśayas</s>, he is liberated.
Nor can the [statement about] non-return be explained as mere <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage), since the knowledge of <s>ātman</s> does not serve another purpose (<s>aparārthatva</s>).
For if it served another purpose, then by the <s>parṇamayī</s>-principle,
the mention of fruit would be explained as <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage).

But when the injunction of knowledge does not serve another purpose, that very [fruit-statement] becomes a qualifier of the eligible person (<s>adhikārin</s>), as in the <s>Rātrisatra</s> (night-long sacrifice).

children.translated_text: The body and senses that are acquired through the particular <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> belonging to a given [soul] — those are the instruments of experience for that soul alone.
If it is asked: what determines the arrangement of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> themselves? — that depends on the connection with the ritual actions (<s>karman</s>) that are the means for them.

And the arrangement of the connection with ritual action is based on the connection with body and senses that serve as its inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) — thus, due to the beginninglessness of the series of body, senses, <s>dharma</s>, and <s>adharma</s>, everything is accounted for.
Refutation of the doubt regarding the oneness of <s>ātman</s>.

Nor is the knowledge of <s>ātman</s> a subsidiary (<s>śeṣa</s>) of ritual injunctions (<s>karmavidhi</s>), since it does not serve another purpose; and since there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for its serving another purpose; and since the subsidiary-status characterized by usefulness (<s>upakāra</s>) has been refuted — enough of excessive elaboration.

Determination of the measure of <s>ātman</s> according to our own view:
But what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the bare existence of the liberated <s>ātman</s>, which has transcended all perception? We reply: What exists (<s>sat</s>) and is uncaused (<s>akāraṇa</s>) is imperishable, like space (<s>gagana</s>). And this <s>ātman</s> exists and is uncaused — hence its permanence (<s>dhruvatva</s>) is established from its imperishability.
And the supreme magnitude (<s>paramamahattva</s>) is the measure of <s>ātman</s>, like space. Wherever a quality of <s>ātman</s> is observed, there the <s>ātman</s> is present — this is established by <s>pramāṇa</s>. For a quality cannot exist without its possessor.
Here the doubt arises: Does it go [to various places] and become present, or is it present without movement? If dependence on movement is accepted, then movement must be postulated, and its non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) must be postulated. And there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for that. Since presence is possible even without going, like space.
If it is said: if the <s>ātman</s> is present even where no body is, then its qualities would be perceived there too, as in the body — that is not so. For the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind is the non-inherent cause of all qualities of <s>ātman</s>. And that conjunction, being in two loci, does not exist elsewhere in the absence of mind. And the mind resides within the body — as stated. And the effect exists only where the non-inherent cause exists — hence there is no perception of qualities of <s>ātman</s> outside [the body].
But then, the postulation of movement for the body too would be without <s>pramāṇa</s>. No — because if the body existed in one place, there would be the unwanted consequence of its being seen elsewhere. But for the <s>ātman</s>, even though existing [everywhere], since the unwanted consequence of perception by those who have transcended all instruments of cognition cannot be produced, perforce the <s>ātman</s> is conjoined with all locations. And that is not possible without supreme magnitude — hence it is not of atomic measure or body-measure.
And being of body-measure without being composite is impossible. For such magnitude depends on one of these: multiplicity of parts, magnitude of parts, or a special type of accumulation. And there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for postulating parts.
But if the person is all-pervading, there would be the unwanted consequence of experience in another body too. Not so. For whichever body belongs to whichever [soul], that is the seat of experience for that one; and whichever senses belong to whichever [soul], those are the instruments of experience for that one — hence there is no unwanted consequence of experience in another seat.

Resolution of the doubt about confusion of experience given the all-pervading nature of <s>ātman</s>:
But what is the basis of the determinate connection with body and senses? We reply: It is based on the connection with <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — let the wise understand.

children.translated_text: And the Vedic passages about a single <s>puruṣa</s> have already been explained [otherwise]; thus it is established that persons are distinct in each body.
Dispelling the mass of darkness of manifold controversies,
this <s>Tattvāloka</s> (Light of Reality) has been set forth by <s>Śālikanātha</s>.

An objection: If the self (<s>ātman</s>) is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>), then let there be one self in all bodies, like space (<s>gagana</s>). Just as space, being one, is related to various things such as pots, gems, and so on, why should the self not also be accepted thus? What is the point of accepting multiplicity? We reply: One who cognizes the owner of another body infers him, through the observation of effort-preceded action identical to one's own bodily action, as possessing effort (<s>prayatna</s>). But he does not cognize that other as identical with the subject [himself], but rather as belonging to the category of the object-known, as a non-self. Therefore, since difference is established through cognition, the statement 'enough of accepting difference' is futile. For the inference 'mine' cannot properly arise with respect to the owner of another body. Because it contradicts direct perception to say 'just as in my body there is action preceded by my effort, so too in another's body the action is based on my effort alone.' For effort is directly perceived as inhering in one's own self. And since the effort corresponding to the actions of another's body does not become directly perceptible in one's own self, it is inferred that another is the agent of effort in another's body. Objection: If the other self is known through inference, how then is it said 'the ungraspable is indeed not grasped' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s> 4.2.4)? We reply: The meaning of that is 'it is not grasped by another as identical with the subject' — therefore there is no contradiction. Moreover, persons are distinct in each body, having distinct arrangements, as seen from the distinct arrangement of <s>dharma</s> (merit), <s>adharma</s> (demerit), pleasure, pain, and so on. Otherwise, the merit, demerit, etc. of one would belong to all. A doubt based on the view of the author of the <s>Brahmasiddhi</s>: Here a certain self-styled scholar says — the arrangement of pleasure and pain will be merely conventional. Just as in one body the arrangement of sensations in the foot and so on is not interchanged, so too it will not be interchanged across different bodies. For the sensation located in the foot is not in the head, nor is the sensation in the head in the foot. Nor can it be said that sensations inhere in the feet and so on themselves, since they are non-conscious. For the knower alone is connected with sensations, since they are of the nature of specific forms of suffering. Refutation of this: This is merely a deception of the naive, say the wise elders. 'There is pain in my foot,' 'there is pain in my head' — in all sensations, one sufferer is manifest. In the feet and other [parts], however, what inheres is heat and the like. There, heat is conjunction with fire, and piercing pain is conjunction with wind — this should be understood in all disorders born from the disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm. And the conjunction of bile and so on with even non-conscious things like the feet is not contradicted. The pain born from that inheres in the self alone. If it be said: 'Just as reflections of a single original appear in gems, swords, mirrors and the like due to their conditioning adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), and qualities like darkness are determined [by those adjuncts], so too pleasure and so on of a single self are determined by the conditioning adjuncts of various bodies' — that is wrong. Because properties that are merely adjunct-dependent, being governed by the adjunct, lack real connection with the original. Such arrangement is possible for properties belonging to a single substratum. But pleasure and so on are not merely adjunct-dependent; rather, they inhere in the self itself — therefore, if belonging to a single self, the distinct arrangement is impossible.

If sound (<s>śabda</s>) were to perish as soon as it is uttered, then its natural capacity to denote its own meaning could not be determined through the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddha</s>). For it is through observing repeated usage, by excluding non-proper meanings in each case, that the capacity to denote the proper meaning is ascertained. And for a sound that ceases as soon as it is uttered, repeated observation of its usage is not possible. And if the capacity to denote its own meaning is not ascertained, the sound, as if heard for the first time, cannot convey meaning. And validity is not appropriate for what does not convey meaning — therefore, for one who desires the validity of words, it is proper to establish the eternality of the designating [word]; and this has a purpose. Objection: Even if phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>) are momentary, the determination of the connection [between word and meaning] is possible through the usage of the learned regarding objects like cows and the like. What need is there for the effort to establish eternality? We reply: It is not possible to postulate cowhood (<s>gotva</s>) and the like in phonemes that are different in each utterance, since even without grasping their difference, the cognition of non-difference can be explained — like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl — through non-apprehension of difference. For where non-difference is ascertained despite actual difference, there, through the impossibility of any other explanation, recourse to a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is appropriate. And even those who hold phonemes to be non-eternal do not accept a direct determination of difference in phonemes at each utterance. Objection: It is proper that in mother-of-pearl and silver, the practical activity of non-difference arises from non-apprehension of difference, and universals are impossible — since a sublating cognition arises: 'this is not silver.' But here, since universals are possible, the postulation of error is without evidence, since there is no sublating cognition 'this is not the letter ga.' We reply: The postulation of error does not depend merely on sublating cognition, but also on defects in the causal conditions. And it is observed that error occurs from non-apprehension of difference due to extreme similarity; so even when a sublating cognition has not directly arisen, it is proper to determine error. Therefore, cowhood and the like are not possible there [in momentary phonemes]. 'If manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) [of sound] is impossible due to the dissimilarity of the manifesting agents, then if [sound] is also not caused by effort (<s>prayatna</s>), its perception dependent on that [effort] would not be possible.' Therefore this inference should be employed: Sound is produced by human effort (<s>puruṣaprayatna</s>), because, given that it is not manifested by that [effort], it is perceived immediately after it — whatever is not manifested by something yet perceived immediately after it is produced by it, like a pot by the potter's wheel. Moreover, after human effort, the hearing of sound can be conceived in two ways: either [the sound], being previously non-existent, comes into being through effort, or it is manifested, being previously unmanifested. Of these, the manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) of sound by effort is not possible. For something is manifested either by the removal of an obstruction (<s>āvaraṇa</s>) or by proximity (<s>sannidhāna</s>). But obstruction of sound is not possible. For obstruction is established through the blocking of sense-organ contact, as a pot is obstructed by a wall. But the sense-organ contact of sound cannot be blocked, since it is eternal. For obstruction consists of the prevention of origination and cessation, and that is not possible for what is eternal. For space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is the organ of hearing, since it possesses sound; and possessing sound means being the instrument for perceiving sound, like the eye [which possesses color]. Just as the eye, perceiving color, possesses color, so too the ear possesses sound. And since space possesses sound, it itself is the ear-organ, and sound, being its quality, eternally inheres in it — so obstruction is not possible. Therefore, manifestation through removal of obstruction is not possible. For this very reason, manifestation through proximity is also impossible, since that which is to be manifested is always in proximity. Moreover, manifesting agents manifest all things in the same location simultaneously, like a lamp manifesting colors and so on. Color, dimension, number — all are manifested by a lamp and the like at once. Therefore, the perception of all sounds [simultaneously] would be unavoidable. Moreover, since sound is a specific quality of space, and space is one, a sound manifested by someone in <s>Srughna</s> would also be perceived by someone in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>. And the cessation of perception at any time would not occur.

children.translated_text: Others, however, say: The first sound is produced from conjunction or disjunction.

children.text: yathā tālvādivāyusaṃyogānugṛhītādvāyvākāśasaṃyogādākaśe śabdassañjāyate, tathā tālvādivāyuvibhāgopakṛtādvāyvākāśavibhāgādākāśa eva śabdaśśabdāntaramārabhate, tadapi śabdāntaramiti karṇaśaṣkulīmaṇḍalāvacchinne nabhasi śrotrabhāvamāpanne niṣpannaśśabdaśśrūyata iti /
children.translated_text: Just as from the conjunction of air and space, assisted by the conjunction of air with the palate and other articulatory organs, sound is born in space; so too from the disjunction of air and space, assisted by the disjunction of air from the palate and other organs, sound gives rise to further sound in space. And the sound produced in the space delimited by the region of the ear-cavity, which has assumed the nature of the ear-organ, is heard.
From the diversity of effort, the diversity [of sound] is observed;
and from the dissimilarity of sound, the effect [i.e., meaning-cognition] arises through dissimilarity. [3]

Thus, since manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) is untenable, if [sound] were also not caused by effort (<s>prayatna</s>), its effort-dependent perception would not be possible. Therefore this inference should be employed: Sound is produced by human effort, because, given that it is not manifested by that effort, it is perceived immediately after it — whatever is not manifested by something yet perceived immediately after it is produced by it, like a pot by the potter's operation. By what process, then, is sound produced by effort? Regarding this, some say: By the parts of air set in motion by human effort, modified by the specific dispositions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of particular locations [of articulation such as the palate], moving in all directions, and assisted by the non-inherent cause called conjunction — sound is produced as inhering in them. And since air possesses motion, the sound produced from it also possesses motion, and is perceived when conjoined with the space delimited by the region of the ear-cavity, which has assumed the nature of the ear-organ. And the motion of air is based on the disposition called velocity (<s>vega</s>); upon its cessation, due to the interruption of motion, the sound is not heard by a distant ear, since [the sound] does not reach its proximity. But this is not tenable: if sound were of the nature of air, it would be perceived by the sense of touch by the deaf. One might think: 'It is not perceived by the sense of touch because it is overpowered [by other tactile qualities].' That is wrong, because it deserves to be perceived through direct perception. For if it were overpowered, it would not be perceived by the ear either. Nor should one say that air is not perceivable by the sense of touch — since air is known through its conformity to [touch]. If one thinks that only touch is perceived by the sense of touch, not the substance air — that is wrong, since the substance is recognized even apart from touch.

children.translated_text: But sound, being perceived as soft when the effort is gentle and as loud when the effort is strong, does not relinquish its status as the effect of effort.
The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>):
When the sound and the cognition of it are clear, through the postulation of multiple manifesters,
the regularity of perception will be properly explained. [4]

Moreover, if sound were merely manifested (<s>abhivyaṅgya</s>) by effort, it would not be perceived as different with each different effort. For even when the manifesting lamp (<s>abhivyañjaka</s>) differs, objects are not perceived as having different natures. But difference of the causal agent is well-known as the cause of difference in the effect. Therefore, it is ascertained that effort produces (<s>janayati</s>) sound. Just as the difference in effect that follows the difference in causal agent is unimpeded, so too, even in the case of difference [of the manifester], the manifester cannot [produce] a difference in the manifested.

children.translated_text: Because the velocity of the chest-air, assisted by the push of external wind, has the capacity to travel far.
But in the theory of one sound producing another sound, the favorable wind (<s>anuvāta</s>) has no use whatsoever.
Due to the multiplicity of manifesters, sound is perceived as if multiple,
like the moon [perceived as multiple] by those with an eye-disease (<s>taimirika</s>), due to the difference in the activity of the eye. [5]

If we can demonstrate clear recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) of sound, then, with the productive capacity of effort being refuted and its manifesting capacity being established, we shall explain the regularity of perception through the multiplicity of manifesters. It is the organ of hearing (<s>śrotra</s>) itself that is refined; and the capacity to refine it is the capacity to manifest [sound]. For the air in the chest (<s>koṣṭhyavāyu</s>) rises up due to the conjunction of the self possessing effort. That air, striking at eight places beginning from the navel and the chest, being refined, rushing with whatever velocity it has, reaching the organ of hearing, initiates a refinement (<s>saṃskāra</s>) conducive to the apprehension of sound. That very conjunction [of air with the ear] is the refinement of the organ of hearing. And due to the velocity of the air, when, at the arising of action, through the disjunction from the ear and the cessation of conjunction, the apprehension of sound immediately ceases. And due to the difference of effort, the difference of the action of air, and the variation of the conjunction at places beginning from the chest — the hearing of different sounds is explained. Even the proponent of the production theory accepts a difference in producers, for otherwise the difference of effects would be impossible. And what was brought up — that just as the eye refined by opening does not establish regularity through things located in the same place — that is improper, because there the manifester (opening) is one alone. For one single opening alone initiates the refinement of the eye conducive to all apprehensions — so how could apprehension be regulated? But here, the oneness of the refinements is not established. [Objection:] But if what is manifested is graspable by a single sense-organ, the manifester too should be one alone. [Reply:] Those that are graspable by the same sense-organ — for them, the first manifester alone is the manifester of all that is grasped simultaneously.
When the apprehension of that [sound] is clear, the perception of multiplicity in sound is indeed unestablished.

children.translated_text: Rather, the mutually independent manifesters — the chest-airs arising from different speakers, being multiple, initiating different refinements of the ear-organ and generating cognitions of different sounds — [cause] sound to be cognized as if multiple, like the moon [seen as multiple] by one with a splitting of the timira defect in the eye.
For regarding perception in different locations, there is universal agreement that it is an error,
since sound is heard only as residing in the aperture of the ear. [6]
