children.translated_text: The difference in the nature of phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>) is not, moreover, the accepted view;
because the error of [perceiving] such [difference] can arise from the softness and loudness of the tone (<s>nāda</s>). [7]

What is said — that if sound is a product (<s>kārya</s>), the perception in different locations follows from the difference of causal locations — that is improper. For even if sound is produced, since there would be the unwanted consequence of simultaneous perception by those near and far, and since there would be no distinction between favorable and adverse wind, [the production theory has difficulties too]. Those who can discriminate the locations [of sound] understand through reasoning that the ear-residing sound is grasped [there], while the apparent location [of the speaker] is an error due to the association with the place of utterance. But the error of location-attribution is something experienced even in perception. For when the eye, being long and thin, touches an object, the object appears to be at the tip [of the eye's ray] rather than at the eye itself. Similarly, the ear grasps sound in itself, but attributes it to the place of utterance.

children.text:
spaṣṭe tadgrahe prayatnastāvadvarṇānāṃ janako neti sthite, tadanantaropalambhaniyamena991 cābhivyañjakatve nirṇīte, abhivyañjakavṛddhihvāsayoścābhivyaṅgyavṛddhihvāsahetutvābhāvānna śabdo vardhate, hvasate vā /
kintu balavati prayatne mahān vāyurutpadyate, 992tasyāvayavā bhūyāṃsaḥ karṇaśaṣkulīmaṇḍalasya nemibhāgairbahubhissambadhyante /
tataścābhivyajjakasaṃyogabahutvāt, yugapadupalambhakabahutvāt, teṣāñca vicchedāgrahaṇānmahāniva śabdo 'vabhāti, tarūṇāmantarālāgrahaṇādiva mahadvanam /
yadā te vāyvavayavāssahasā, vilambena vā saṃyujyante, tadopalambho 'pi drutaḥ, vilambito vā /
yadā tveṣāmuccāraṇe tālvādīnāṃ saṃvṛtatvaṃ bhavati, tadā tadanurodhena varṇopalabdhirapi ekamātrākālaiva bhavatīti, hvasvavarṇavyavahārasiddhiḥ /
yadā 993vivṛtataratvam, asaṃvṛtatvaṃ vā tālvādīnāmeva sampadyate, tadā varṇapratīterapi mātrākālavṛddhyā dīrghavarṇavyavahārasiddhiḥ, vṛddhavyavahāre tadanurodhenāpyarthābhidhānadarśanāt, tathaiva pratipādakatvamapyāśrīyate /
na caivamabhidhānasyānityatvadoṣa, tadupādhiviśiṣṭasya varṇasya vācakasyānityatvāt1 ato varṇānupūrvyanityatve na kaściddoṣaḥ /
ānupūrvīviśeṣabhājāṃ varṇānāṃvācakabhūtānāṃ nityatvāt /
nanu 994kṣaṇikā śabdasyābhivyaktiriti, kathaṃ tadgrahaṇasambhavaḥ /
upalabdhe hi ghaṭādibhāve tadvaśena pūrvānubhavāhitasaṃskāraprabodhena "sa evāyami"ti pratyabhijñodīyate /
children.translated_text: For when an object such as a pot is perceived, the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) deposited by the prior experience is awakened by the force of that [perception], and the recognition 'this is that very same one' arises.

children.text: śabde punaruccarita-tirohite, punaruttarakāle kathaṃ pratyabhijñodaya iti /
children.translated_text: But regarding sound, when it is uttered and then disappears, how can recognition arise at a later time?
To this he says: It is not necessarily the case that the awakening of an impression requires the apprehension of that very same [object];
from an impression awakened by another cause, the apprehension of that [recognized object] arises. [8]

When the apprehension of that [sound] is clear — once it is established that effort is not the producer of phonemes, and once its manifesting capacity is determined through the invariable rule of perception immediately following [effort], and since the increase and decrease of the manifester do not cause the increase and decrease of the manifested — sound does not increase or decrease. Softness and loudness are qualities of the tone (<s>nāda</s>), which is produced. And softness and loudness of the tone, by being mistakenly attributed to the phoneme manifested along with the tone, create the false appearance of difference in the phonemes. And just as a face reflected in mirrors of different sizes appears large or small due to the size of the mirror without the face itself being large or small, similarly the phoneme, reflected as it were in the tone of different intensities, appears soft or loud without itself being different. Therefore, the phoneme is eternal, and its recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) across different utterances is established.

children.text:
yadi hyayaṃ niyamaḥ--tadupalambha eva tatsaṃskārodbodhaheturiti, tato nopapadyate śabde pratyabhijñā /
saṃskārāstvaniyatodbodhahetava iti, kāraṇāntaravaśenodbuddhāt saṃskārāt prathamasamāgamasamaya eva śabde pratyabhijñā bhaviṣyati /
nanu"sa evāyaṃ gakāraḥ" iti 995pratītistadgrahaḥ, na punarbhedāgrahaṇāditi, kathameṣa nirṇayaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But the cognition 'this is that very same <s>ga</s>-sound' is an apprehension of that [same sound] — it is not [merely] the non-apprehension of difference. So how is this determination made?

children.text: dṛṣṭo hi śuktikāyāṃ bhedāgrahāt"tadevedaṃ rajatami"ti pratyayaḥ---iti /
children.translated_text: For it is observed that in the case of a shell, from non-apprehension of difference, the cognition 'this is that very silver' arises.
To this he says: When there is no means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for difference, as in the case of shell and silver,
the apprehension of that [same object], established through experience, by what can it be prevented? [9]

For if there were the fixed rule that the apprehension of something is the only cause of the awakening of the impression of that same thing, then recognition of sound would be impossible. But since impressions have non-fixed causes of awakening, from an impression awakened by another cause, recognition arises at the very first moment of encounter.

children.text:
spaṣṭe hi śuktikā-rajatayorbhedāvasāyini pramāṇe, sādṛśyādbhedānavabādhādabhedapratītiriti kalpyate /
śabde tu na pratyakṣasiddhaḥ pratyuccāraṇaṃ bhedaḥ /
kathaṃ na siddhaḥ /
nanu mahattvā-lpatvābhyāṃ vibhinno varṇa upalabhyate /

children.translated_text: This is not so.

children.text: mahattvā-lpatve pratiyato 'pi, varṇapratīte mahattvā-lpatve eva bhinne avabhātaḥ, na varṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: Even though loudness and softness are perceived with each [utterance], what appears as different is the loudness and softness in the perception of the phoneme, not the phonemes themselves.

children.text: na vā'numānenāpi bhedo 'vagantuṃ śakyata iti prāgeva niveditam /
children.translated_text: Nor can difference be ascertained even through inference — this has been explained earlier.

children.text: ato bhede pramāṇābhāvāt, abhinna evāyaṃ bhinnāvabhāsa iti, sākṣātpratītibalanaivāvasthāpitam // 9 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, in the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for difference, this [sound] is indeed non-different though appearing different — this is established by the very force of direct experience. [9]

For when a <s>pramāṇa</s> determining the difference between shell and silver is clearly available, the cognition of non-difference is postulated [to arise] from the non-comprehension of difference due to similarity. But in the case of sound, there is no perceptually established difference with each utterance. [Objection:] How is it not established? Is there not [difference] through loudness and softness?
[Objection:] But it is precisely by the force of the apprehension of that [recognition] that inference was refuted.
And when inference is refuted, 'the apprehension of that [same sound]' [depends on the refutation] — so this is mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>)!
To this he says: By the refutation of inference, the apprehension of that [same sound] is established;
But the suspicion of error is warded off because the cognition of identity is established through direct experience itself. // 10 //
The doubt that this is an error based on non-apprehension of difference is removed by the refutation of pure inference.

children.text: pratītibalasiddhastu tadgraho na kāraṇāntaramapekṣata iti, kathamitaretarāśrayatā /
children.translated_text: But the apprehension of identity, established by the force of direct experience, does not require another cause — so how can there be mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>)?

children.text: nanu kimiti tadgrahabalājjvālāyāmapi bhedānumānaṃ na nirākriyataityata āha--- jvālābhedaṃ vinā 998bhāsāṃ vitatirnopapadyate /
children.translated_text: But why does the inference of difference in the flame not get refuted by the force of the apprehension of identity? To this he says: Without the difference of flames, the spread of light (<s>bhāsa</s>) is not possible;
But recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) is proper due to the non-cognition of difference and due to similarity. // 11 //

children.text:
avayavī-jvālā /
sarvaścāvayavī svāvayavasaṃyogena jātaḥ, tadvināśena vinaśyati /
tantuvyatiṣaṅgajanito hi paṭastantuvibhāge vināśī dṛśyate /
999prabhā ca gṛhodarādivartinī taijasaṃ rūpam /
na ca dravyāśritā rūpādayo dravyaṃ virahayya vartante /
tena taijasāḥ paramāṇavo nityamabhibhūtatvādanupalambhamāna api, pratyakṣato yāvatprabhāvitati sannidhīyanta ityaṅgīkaraṇīyam /
teṣu ca deśāntaramanuprāpteṣvetadāśrayaṇīyam-eteṣāṃ saṃyogā vighaṭanta iti /
vighaṭiteṣu teṣu, tadārabdhe dravye 'pi nāśamupeyuṣi, 1000jvālādarśanaṃ jvālāntaradarśanamantareṇa nopapadyate /
children.translated_text: When those conjunctions are broken, and the substance produced from them also perishes, the perception of a flame is not possible without the perception of another flame.
But recognition based on non-apprehension of difference is an error — this is established since such error is observed in the shell-silver and similar cases.
But without difference, nothing whatsoever is impossible regarding sound.
The apprehension of identity is therefore accepted here by the method of reasoning (<s>nītimārga</s>) stated. // 12 //

The flame is a composite entity (<s>avayavī</s>). And every composite entity, born from the conjunction of its parts, perishes upon their destruction. For a cloth, produced from the intertwining of threads, is observed to perish upon the separation of threads. And the light (<s>prabhā</s>) present in the interior of a house and such is a luminous form (<s>taijasa rūpa</s>). And color and such, residing in a substance, do not exist without a substance. Therefore, although luminous atoms, being eternally overpowered, are not perceived, it must be accepted that they are present to the extent that light spreads. And when those move to another location, this must be relied upon — that their conjunctions break apart.

children.text: pratyuccāraṇaṃ bhedavyatirekeṇāpi prayatnānantaropalabhyamānatvaṃ yathopapadyate, tathoktameveti, apratipakṣā pratyabhijñā /
children.translated_text: The fact that sound is perceived immediately after each utterance — even without difference — how that is possible has already been stated; thus the recognition of identity is unopposed.
Therefore, because of being the type of entity for which there is both a cause of existence and no cause of destruction, sound (<s>śabda</s>) is eternal;
For this alone is what is accepted as eternality in space (<s>vyoma</s>) and such. // 13 //
For sound, effort (<s>prayatna</s>) alone is considered as the probable cause.

And that effort, by the force of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), has been shown to be a manifester (<s>abhivyañjaka</s>) in the second and subsequent perceptions; therefore, in the first perception too, it is a manifester alone.
Therefore, sound is eternal because it exists while being without a producing cause — like space and such.
Hence it is not non-eternal.
This establishment of the eternality of sound has been composed by <s>Śālikanātha</s>;
Following the view of Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>, the <s>Nyāyaśuddhi</s> (Purification of Reasoning) is proclaimed. // 14 //

children.text: iti mahāmahopādhyāyaśrīśālikanāthamiśrapraṇītāyāṃ prakaraṇapañcikāyāṃ nyāyaśuddhirnāma navamaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam1006 //
children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, the ninth chapter named <s>Nyāyaśuddhi</s> (Purification of Reasoning) is concluded.
The tenth chapter named <s>Mīmāṃsā-jīvarakṣā</s> (Protection of the Life of Mīmāṃsā).
Having reflected upon the view of Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>, this is stated:
This <s>Mīmāṃsā-jīvarakṣā</s> is the refutation of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>). // 1 //

children.translated_text: Just as a thing undivided in space and time shines forth as one, so too even what is divided in space and time shines forth as one alone; and the arising of such a cognition is not possible without a single cognition — therefore, this single cognition must be accepted.

children.translated_text: To establish the reality of the effect, even an un-perceived cause must be postulated; but one should not, by looking at the face of the cause, contemplate the reversal of a clearly observed effect.

children.text: tena yadyapi kavalādindriyāt, kevalāt pūrvānubhavasamāsāditajanmano bhāvanābhidhānāt saṃskārādvā naivaṃvighamidaṃ vijñānumudetumarhati /
children.translated_text: Therefore, although from the sense-organ alone, or from the <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression) — called <s>bhāvanā</s> (habitual cultivation) — whose birth is acquired from prior experience, this cognition of such a kind cannot properly arise,

Nevertheless, the <s>ācāryas</s> (teachers) considered that this is the effect of those two [sense-organ and impression] when they have mutually attained an intermediate state through their coming together.

Here, the followers of the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha) declare all entities without exception to be momentary (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅgin</s>).
What, then, is their means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for this? Direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), at any rate, is not capable of perceiving momentariness, since one who examines most carefully an entity such as a pillar has no determination of its momentariness.
One might have this thought: momentariness is not something external to the essential nature of an entity; therefore, through the very experience of the entity, direct perception also directly apprehends momentariness.
The wise consider this to be mere wishful thinking.
For thus: 'The determinations of objects are grounded in cognition' — this position is undisputed among all philosophers.
So this momentariness too, being the essential nature of the entity, while ascending into cognition, would be established as non-different from it — not otherwise.
But we do not observe any cognition arising in that manner; so whence is its inclusion in the essential nature of the entity? And even more so, whence is its being cognized through the cognition of that [entity]?
If one were to think: 'Even though momentariness is observed by perception, it does not enter the path of determination, and therefore appears as if not grasped — yet perception is still the means of knowledge for it' —
The <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) [say]: where the operation of perception, which by nature ranges into the domain of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), is followed by a subsequent conceptual cognition (<s>savikalpaka-pratyaya</s>), there perception is a means of knowledge. But where the cognition 'this has been seen' does not arise, that is not apprehended by perception — this is merely verbal play of those whose minds are darkened by the gloom of [their own] doctrine.
As for what some have said — 'Perceptual knowledge, being momentary, makes known momentariness by having as its object things associated with its own moment' —
That too is childish talk. For momentariness means existing for only a single moment.
Perception does not determine 'this very thing exists just now,' since perception is indifferent with respect to other times.
On the contrary, perception itself, in the form of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), completely casts away momentariness, since it construes the entity as associated with both prior and subsequent times.
Inference (<s>anumāna</s>) too, which depends on the investigation of a relation, is not capable of taking momentariness as its thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), since there is no awareness of the relation of any logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) with it [momentariness].
For the awareness of a relation with a relatum does not arise regarding what has not been perceived.
And the followers of the <s>Sugata</s> do not accept any means of knowledge beyond these two [perception and inference].
'This is sky-delusion!' — the <s>Saugatas</s> dismiss [our objection].
For they declare momentariness to be ascertainable through inference using the essential-nature reason (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>).
What then is that inference?
'Whatever exists is momentary; all entities exist' — thus, for a property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>) that is invariably connected with the mere existence of the entity, the essential-nature reason applies.
Just as: <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness [entails] tree-ness. For tree-ness is invariably connected with mere <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness.
So here too, momentariness is invariably connected with mere existence (<s>sattā</s>).
But how is the invariable connection with mere existence established? Through the operation of a sublating means of knowledge (<s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>) in the counter-positive (<s>vipakṣa</s>).
For in the case of non-momentariness, the non-perception of the pervader (<s>vyāpaka-anupalabdhi</s>) sublates existence (<s>sattā</s>).
For existence is causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritā</s>); there is no other [form of existence].
And that [causal efficacy] is pervaded by [either] sequence (<s>krama</s>) or simultaneity (<s>yaugapadya</s>), since there is no third alternative.
Since these two are mutually opposed, the negation of one entails the positive establishment of the other.
But sequence and simultaneity are not possible in non-momentary entities.
And their removal also removes existence, just as [removing] <s>śiṃśapā</s>-ness [removes] tree-ness.
How is there absence of causal efficacy in non-momentary entities through sequence and simultaneity? Here they say:
A non-momentary entity would either be of the nature of being capable of generating causal efficacy, or not of that nature — there is no third alternative.
In the first option: since all causal activities would be accomplished in a single moment, and since what has been done cannot be done again, in the next moment there would be an emptiness of causal capacity, leading to the consequence of having the mark of non-existence — hence the loss of non-momentariness.
In the second option: causal activity would never arise from it — leading again to the consequence of having the mark of non-existence.
One might think: 'An entity, though capable by nature, sometimes acts through the assistance of cooperative conditions (<s>sahakārin</s>), and at other times does not, due to their absence.'
That too does not withstand scrutiny. For does that cooperative condition produce something, or not? If it produces something, one must consider: is what it produces part of the nature of the entity held to be capable of causal efficacy, or not?
In the case of non-production, one must state what purpose the cooperative condition serves. For no expectation of what provides no assistance is meaningful.
If what is produced is part of the nature of the entity held to be the means of causal efficacy, then the consequence of the entity's [new] origination arises. For something that has not arisen does not possess the nature of what is arising, since the superimposition of contradictory properties leads to differentiation.
And if the origination of the entity is accepted, then the thesis of non-momentariness is destroyed.
If one accepts the production of something that is not of the entity's nature — since the entity was previously incapable, causal efficacy cannot be achieved sequentially from a non-momentary entity.
Therefore, causal efficacy must come from an external, adventitious [factor]; since it exists when that exists, and is absent when that is absent.
And besides the positive and negative concomitance, there is no other method.
Since there is no perception of the co-existence of mutually contradictory [properties] in one locus.
'But a momentary entity too — is it of the nature of being capable of generating causal efficacy, or not?' — this does not go beyond the earlier reasoning.
For one whose nature is the capacity for generating causal efficacy, there should be no dependence on cooperative conditions. For causal efficacy does not arise from what is incapable.
Hear the supreme secret of the <s>Saugatas</s>: an entity whose nature is the capacity for generating causal efficacy, having reached the final moment, produces even a single effect.
'Why then does it not produce without cooperative conditions?' —
When something is a generator without dependence, then what would the cooperative condition of that [entity] look like? — this must be stated.
Here we say: as for the statement 'why does it not produce even without cooperative conditions?' — that is the yawning of one who lacks skill in the <s>Saugata</s> doctrine.
For a momentary entity does not exist without cooperative conditions. How can what does not exist produce anything?
But what exists [at that moment] is precisely that [entity together with its conditions] — nothing has been diminished.
To the question 'why does it not come into being even without cooperative conditions?' — the answer must be given in terms of the nature of causes: they are such [as to require cooperation], and they produce accordingly.
The cooperative condition of entities existing at the final moment is their joint production of a single effect.
'But those [cooperative conditions] too, being generators independent of anything else, why do they not produce another effect?' —
Here too we are unable [to explain further]: entities produce what they produce — we are only able to accept this.
And these producers, being existent, produce just that [specific effect] — for us observers, our acceptance extends only that far.
'But if one has already done [the work], what does the other do?' —
This would be so in the case of sequential causal efficacy; but in joint production, there is simply no 'already done.'
'But if it is achieved from even one [cause], what do the others do?' —
This is not so. They are not deliberate agents who might reason thus: 'Another is also capable of doing this without us; we are not up to the task.'
Rather, their presence depends on [their own] causes, and they are not able not to exist — so what impossibility is there?
'But how does a single effect arise from multiple [causes]?' —
Difference in causes is the reason for difference in effect; otherwise the consequence of producing everything [from anything] would follow.
We reply: the difference in the effect is not due to difference in cooperative causes, but due to difference in the aggregate (<s>sāmagrī</s>) — this is easily understood by those who have labored over the <s>Hetubindu</s>.
Therefore, even in the doctrine of momentariness, there is no room for the same objections as in the non-momentariness thesis.
For through the transformation of the successive moments of seeds etc., such a moment arises from which, immediately upon the activation of a cause requiring no further cause, the sprout manifests.
'But even so, the recognition "this is the very same" regarding successive moments of the seed etc. is untenable.' —
Moreover, one should not say 'how can inference establish itself when contradicted by the direct perception of recognition?' —
Or if it does establish itself, there would be the consequence of inferring coldness even in fire [since perception would be overridable].
The resolution is stated: those moments, though utterly different, being extremely similar — for one who is unable to distinguish their difference even when seen — the practical usage of non-difference operates, based on the non-grasping of difference, just as the practical usage of silver operates regarding a mother-of-pearl shell.
Nor is there a contradiction with the arising of inference, because causal efficacy is otherwise inexplicable.
Recognition, however, is accounted for even by the non-grasping of difference — so there is nothing objectionable.
For this very reason the elders say: 'Inference is even more powerful than direct perception.'
And we see that this is reasonable.
Since there is no cause for the arising of a single cognition of the form 'this is that very same thing' — the sense-organ operates only with respect to what is present, and does not touch the relation with a prior time; and the dispositional trace (<s>bhāvanā</s>) cultivated by prior experience does not [touch] the connection with a subsequent time.
This has been illustrated by the example of recognition regarding [successive] flames.
Moreover, the destruction of produced entities is observed to be inevitable.
From this too, momentariness can be inferred.
For thus: if destruction is inevitable for them, then they do not require any other cause for it.
And destruction is inevitable for produced things — thus, an inference having a mark characterized by the perception of a concomitance contradicting the opposite (<s>viruddha-vyāpti-upalabdhi</s>) repels the dependence of destruction on another cause.
For inevitability, being perceived as concomitant with the independence that contradicts the dependence on another cause being negated, presents the non-dependence of destruction on another cause.
And this [inevitability] removes the dependence on another cause, which contradicts it.
For those that depend on another cause are not inevitable in their occurrence.
Just as: coloring etc. of cloth [are not inevitable but depend on external causes].
Therefore, the perception of inevitability — which is concomitant with independence that contradicts dependence on another cause — is itself the non-perception of non-inevitability.
Since non-inevitability is not perceived, destruction does not depend on another cause.
Similarly, if entities too depended on a cause other than their own cause for destruction, then since there would be no evidence for the necessary presence of that other cause, some produced thing would never perish.
But for what is destructible, immediately upon arising from its own cause, there is cessation — thus momentariness is established.
Furthermore, this must be considered: do produced entities, arising from their own causes, arise with a destructible nature, or with an indestructible nature?
If of destructible nature, they dissolve immediately upon arising — hence they are momentary.
If of indestructible nature, they would never perish.
Nor could their destruction come from another cause, since this alternative cannot withstand analysis.
For the destruction that arises — is it non-different from the entity, or different?
It is certainly not non-different, since the causes are different.
But if different, the consequence arises that the entity would be perceived etc. as before.
Even if one posits that it is concealed by [the destruction], this very analysis regarding concealment must be stated — but enough of excessive digression.

Refutation of the momentariness doctrine by a partial view (<s>ekadeśin</s>):
Here some resolve the matter thus: the single perceptual cognition called recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), in the form 'this is that very same thing,' which comprehends the two [temporal referents] as mutually combined, blocks the inference of momentariness.
This is not correct. These two cognitions — grasping and remembering — each operating only with respect to 'that-ness' and 'this-ness' respectively, are not capable of manifesting the object as present at the time of both experiences, because of the contradiction in perception.

children.translated_text: Here too, they apply the same procedure.

children.text: nedamasmanmatamekāntatobhinnanyeva sarvavastūni, abhinnāni 1052veti, kintu sarvabhāveṣu bhedā-bhedau saṅgirāmahe /
children.translated_text: It is not our view that all things are absolutely different or absolutely non-different; rather, we acknowledge both difference and non-difference in all entities.

children.text: tatra bhedamātravikalpasambhavīni1053 dūṣaṇānyabhedāśrayaṇena parihṛtāni, abhedamātrāśritāni cabhedāvalambaneneti /
children.translated_text: There, the refutations that pertain to the option of difference alone are answered by resorting to non-difference, and those pertaining to non-difference alone are answered by resorting to difference.
But how can these contradictory — difference and non-difference — co-exist in one thing?

But this too is not proper. That this is not perception cannot be maintained, because even though the <s>saṃskāra</s> is contributory, since its birth depends on the operation of the sense-organ, there is no distinction from what is accepted as perception by all schools for what arises at the time of first contact, where there is no dispute. Nor is there any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that this is a pseudo-<s>pramāṇa</s> (mere semblance of valid knowledge), because there is no sublation, no causal defect, and no other contradicting cognition regarding its object. Nor does the mind find satisfaction in the claim that this very inference is the sublating cognition, because of the fault of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). For as long as this cognition is unsublated, the inference itself is unable to arise; and once the inference arises, this becomes sublated — thus the mutual dependence is quite clear. And the unsublated-ness of the object is itself the cause for the arising of the inference; otherwise, why would coldness not be inferred in fire? But then, how is the difference of flames and such, which are determined as one, established through inference? Presentation of the dual nature of things (<s>dvyātmakatā</s>) according to the <s>Bhāṭṭa</s> school: Here they state the essence of the <s>siddhānta</s>: All things have a dual nature of universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) and particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>). In the case of flames and such, perception has the universal as its object, while inference has the particular as its object — since perception and inference, operating in different domains, are not in conflict, perception does not contradict the arising of inference. But how does a non-momentary thing produce practical efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>)? Gradually, they say. That entity, endowed with specific attributes acquired through the combination of auxiliary factors, produces the respective practical efficacies gradually. But a dilemma has been posed: do the auxiliary factors impart a distinction that is different from the entity, or a non-different one? And the refutations for both horns of this dilemma have been previously stated.

children.translated_text: Therefore, since the cause of that [cognition] exists, that very [cognition] must occur.

children.text: anupalabdhirapitasya saivetyanupalabdhireva tasya nopalabdhiḥ, tannibandhanaścābhāvavyavahāro 'pīti sarvamanākulam /
children.translated_text: And the non-apprehension of what has passed is that very [new apprehension]; therefore, there is non-apprehension of it, not apprehension — and the usage of non-existence based on that is also [consistent] — thus everything is without confusion.
The life-protection (<s>jīvarakṣā</s>) of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, which strikes at the vital points, has been administered
Against <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> bitten by the poison-fire of momentary destruction — the venom of the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha). // 1 //

There they say: These two are not contradictory, because they are observed together. For contradiction consists in the inability to co-exist, and inability to co-exist is based on non-observation [of co-existence]. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Refutation of that: This is beautiful only when unexamined — and hence is not approved by Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>. For he saw: Difference and non-difference simply cannot co-exist in one thing, because of contradiction. For their co-observation is not possible. A cognition of a single form is itself the observation of non-difference, and a cognition of dissimilar forms is the observation of difference. There, if the cognition is of a single form, then the cognition of dissimilar forms does not exist. And when dissimilar forms are cognized, the cognition of a single form simply does not exist. Therefore, the justification of practical efficacy by resorting to difference-and-non-difference together does not work. Nor does recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) contradict inference, because recognition itself is to be examined. It is observed that in the case of a shell, there arises the cognition 'this very thing is that silver.' And that is based on non-apprehension of difference due to similarity — thus examination is proper here too. There, when upon examination, momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) is determined through the impossibility of practical efficacy [from a permanent thing], it is concluded that this is a deception of the production of similar and dissimilar [momentary entities]. And even for one who reflects, in cases of directional confusion and such, there is the reversal of a cognition that has arisen through the force of inference. But in the case of fire and such, the cognition of heat that has arisen, even when examined, is not explained otherwise — hence the inference of reversal does not arise. Therefore, enough of this excessive insistence on the evidence of deception. The <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion): Now the one who has seen across the deep ocean of the profound teacher's vision states the resolution: When things like pillars and such, first experienced and then with interrupted perception due to concealment and such, are experienced again, the cognition arises: 'this is that very same thing.' There, if practical efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) is somehow possible even from a permanent thing, then why should it be postulated that this usage of non-difference is based merely on non-apprehension of difference? And practical efficacy is indeed possible even from a permanent entity, because it gradually acquires adventitious specific modifications (<s>āgantukakriyādi-rūpa-viśeṣa</s>) through the influence of auxiliary factors. And that specific modification is indeed different from the entity that produces practical efficacy. And it is not the case that the modification alone produces practical efficacy while the entity stands idle — that is sound reasoning. Rather, the entity's capacity as a means consists precisely in being affected by such specific modifications — practical efficacy arises consequent upon that, and it is through possessing such specific modifications that ordinary people attribute to entities the status of being means. But how is that specific modification said to belong to that entity? Through inference from its being the substrate of that [modification]. But how is it established as the substrate? If you say 'through the force of its own causes' — then please desist, sir; we have been followed far enough. Now, why is the entity's non-difference rather than difference inferred? Because it accords with recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), we say. And inference that follows what is observed is proper, because it has its source in observed logical connection. And just as practical efficacy is observed, so too the entity is observed as permanent — and inference in accordance with that is proper. Therefore, even in the permanent, since the non-occurrence of simultaneous activity pervading practical efficacy is not established, the non-perception of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalambha</s>) is unproven; and when that is unproven, since there is no sublating cognition for the contrary, existence (<s>sattā</s>) is unable to establish momentariness that depends on that unproven premise alone, because of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>). Nor is existence merely the production of practical efficacy; rather, it is fitness for connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For intrinsic existence is fitness for connection with a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, even without producing practical efficacy, something can exist — and there is nothing wrong with that. And as for what was said — that entities are independent with respect to destruction — that too, when examined, dissolves like an ornament of lac being burned. What indeed do you consider destruction to be? If 'posterior absence' (<s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s>) is destruction — what then is posterior absence? If it is said that cognitions such as 'in the curd, milk does not exist' are about existing entities — then the principle stated in the <s>Amṛtakalā</s> should be cited here. For there is no cognition 'does not exist.' Rather, the mere experience of the form of curd alone, being self-luminous, is the mere application of the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>). That alone is the non-existence of milk — namely, the apprehension of nothing but the form of curd even when looking. And with respect to that, it is not proper that milk alone is the independent cause, when no other cause has presented itself, and milk itself is still perceived. Nor can it be said that milk is no longer perceived — because recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) establishes non-difference. But if dependence on another cause is accepted, then permanence is not established! But from what is permanence known? If from observation — then let it also be known from observation that there must be another cause. And we are not children to be frightened by such arguments. And as for the objection that even regarding perishable things arising from their own causes, if destruction is dependent on another cause, even when the separate [destroying cause] has arisen, there would be the consequence of the continued perception of the entity as before — to this we reply: We have stated that the mere apprehension of that [new] form alone is destruction.

children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, the tenth chapter named <s>Mīmāṃsā-jīvarakṣā</s> (Protection of the Life of Mīmāṃsā) is concluded.
Section 1.

children.translated_text: To refute those, he declares:
The cognition of sentence-meaning arises from the words alone — in the manner
We set forth according to the view of Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>. // 1 //

There, those who maintain the <s>kāryavākyārtha</s> (action as sentence-meaning) propose <s>bhāva</s> (being), <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force), and <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented result) as the sentence-meanings. Among these, <s>apūrva</s> alone being the sentence-meaning is to be established. Its root is the theory that words denote connected meanings (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>); therefore, that is first purified. Here, those who say that the sentence itself, with the distinction of individual words having disappeared, is the expresser of sentence-meaning; and those who say it is only the last phoneme of the sentence; and those who say that word-meanings, denoted by words without being connected, make known their mutual connection from themselves —

children.text: padebhya eva, na vākyāt, nāpyantyavarṇāt, nāpi padārthebhya ityarthaḥ // 1 //
children.translated_text: From words alone — not from the sentence [as a whole], nor from the last phoneme, nor from the word-meanings [independently] — this is the meaning. // 1 //
He begins to state that manner:
If by words whose capacity is exhausted in merely denoting their own connected meaning,
The own meanings are made known, then the sentence-meaning too [is known] in that case. // 2 //

children.text: vākyārthapratipattau hi padānāmanupāyatve tadanyathānupapattyā, vākyamekaṃ tadupāyabhūtaṃ kalpyate /

children.translated_text: Although meaning is not understood from a word without recourse to convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>),

children.text: yadyapi cā'nantyādvākyānām, tadarthānāñca, vaidikasya cār'thasyānanyopāyatvāt vyutpattiraśakyā /
children.translated_text: And although convention is impossible due to the infinity of sentences, their meanings, and the fact that Vedic meaning has no other means [of being known],
Nevertheless, it is accepted that one comprehends sentence-meaning from a sentence that has been processed through postulated word-and-word-meaning conventions.

children.text: yadi kālpanikatve pada-padārthānāṃ pramāṇābhāvādekaikavarṇoccāraṇer'thānavabodhāt, krameṇoccāritānāñca yugapacchavaṇāsambhavāt, pūrvapūrvavarṇānubhavajanitasaṃskārasahito 'ntyo varṇaḥ pratyāyakaḥ, tasya ca pāramārthikapada-padārthavyutpattissahakāriṇīti pakṣassvīkriyate, yadi vā padaissukaravyutpattayo 'nanvitā eva svārthā abhihitā vākyārthamavabodhayantītyaṅgīkriyata, yadi tu padānyevānvitānsvārthānabhidadhatīti śakyate sādhayitum, tadā vākyārthasyāvabuddhatvānnaitāḥ kalpanā ātmānaṃ labhante // 2 //
children.translated_text: If the position is accepted that, due to the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for the fictitious nature of words and word-meanings, since meaning is not comprehended from the utterance of each individual phoneme, and since phonemes uttered sequentially cannot be heard simultaneously, the last phoneme together with the dispositional impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by the experience of preceding phonemes is the conveyer, and that the conventional understanding (<s>vyutpatti</s>) of real words and word-meanings serves as its cooperating cause — or if it is accepted that words, having easily learnable conventional understandings, designate their own meanings without syntactic connection, and those meanings then produce the sentence-meaning — but if it can be established that words themselves designate their own meanings as syntactically connected (<s>anvita</s>), then, since the sentence-meaning is already comprehended [by that], these speculative constructions find no place for themselves. [2]
For in the cognition of sentence-meaning, if words are not the means, then, since it is otherwise inexplicable, a single sentence is postulated as the means for that.
But how is the comprehension of sentence-meaning achieved when words convey only their own meanings as syntactically connected? To this he says:
Having obtained mutual syntactic connection through the relation of principal (<s>pradhāna</s>) and subordinate (<s>guṇa</s>),
the learned declare that word-meanings themselves are sentence-meanings. [3]

children.text: nanu teṣāṃ bhūyastvād bhūyāṃso vākyārthāḥ, vākyāni ca syurityatrā'ha---
children.translated_text: But since those [word-meanings] are many, the sentence-meanings would be many, and the sentences too [would be many] — to this he says:

children.text: bhūyāṃso yadyapi svārthāḥ padānāṃ te pṛthakpṛthak /
children.translated_text: Although the own-meanings of words are indeed many, separately,
by virtue of serving a single purpose, they indicate one sentence-meaning. [4]
And because of being a single effect producing that cognition, the sentence too is called one.
But how is there a single purpose? To this he says:
For the presentation of the subordinate elements has the single purpose of the principal. [5]

children.text:
yaddhi pradhānabhūtaṃ, tadeva kathannāma viśiṣṭaṃ pratīyatāmityevamarthaṃ guṇānāṃ pratipādanam, tena tatraiva tātparyam, tadeva prameyam, tātparyaviṣaya eva śabdasya prāmāṇyābhyupagamāt, tasya tathābhūtasya pratipattirnaikapadanibandhaneti, vākyameva tatra pramāṇam /

pṛthagbhūtāśca padārthāḥ, na prameyāssantītyarthaḥ /
etacca tatraiva spaṣṭamuktam // 5 // 1076 //
children.translated_text: For the presentation of the subordinate elements is for the purpose that the principal element itself be cognized as qualified — thus the purport (<s>tātparya</s>) is directed toward that alone, and that alone is the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>), since the validity of words is accepted only with respect to what is the object of purport. And the cognition of that, being of such a nature, does not depend on a single word — therefore the sentence alone is the <s>pramāṇa</s> there. For this very reason it has been said: 'In the sixth [<s>adhyāya</s>] and the first [<s>pāda</s>], there is no such thing as a word in the sentence, nor are there such things as word-meanings in the sentence-meaning' [<s>Bṛhatī</s> commentary 6.1.1]. A word taken in isolation is no <s>pramāṇa</s> at all. And word-meanings taken in isolation are not objects of knowledge — this is the meaning. And this has been clearly stated there itself. [5]

children.translated_text: To refute that, he says:
In the usages of the elders, which are accompanied by hearing sentences,
the denotative capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of words is ascertained through the method of agreement (<s>āvāpa</s>) and difference (<s>uddhāra</s>). [6]
Now, those who say that the sentence alone is the designator of sentence-meaning, and those who say that the final phoneme of the sentence alone [is the designator] —

children.translated_text: It is not without an object, since the relation of cause and effect is accepted.
What is this causal relation of the non-designator? This is no fault.

children.text: vākyāddhi yatpadaprayoge1081 sati, yatpadārthānvito vākyārthaḥ pratīyate, tatpadaṃ tasyār'thasyāvācakamapi bhavati nimittam /
children.translated_text: For in a sentence, when a particular word is employed and the sentence-meaning is cognized as connected with that word-meaning, that word, even though not the designator of that meaning, is its cause.
But in their view too, the over-postulation of capacities (<s>śakti</s>) is exactly the same, by the previously stated reasoning.

Although all linguistic convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>) is preceded by the usage of elders, and usage is conducted through sentences only, nevertheless, when a particular word is included (<s>āvāpa</s>) and the meaning is included, and when it is excluded (<s>uddhāra</s>) and the meaning is excluded, the denotative capacity of that word is ascertained with respect to precisely that meaning. And this being so, it is not the case that the comprehension of sentence-meaning would not be possible, since the principle will be stated hereafter. [There is nothing] by whose compulsive force a sentence should be postulated as one, concealing the distinction of phonemes and words that is directly perceived.
Moreover, in eight sentences such as 'Boy! bring the cow,' 'Boy! tie the cow,' 'Child! bring the cow,' 'Child! tie the cow,' 'Lad! bring the cow,' 'Lad! tie the cow,' 'Youngster! bring the cow,' 'Youngster! tie the cow' — eight denotative capacities would have to be postulated [by the sentence-theorist]. But for the word-theorist, only seven capacities for seven words — this is parsimony of postulation. By this very direction, when the word '<s>śuklā</s>' (white [cow]) is inserted, the sentence-theorist must postulate eight more [capacities], whereas the word-theorist needs only one.
And when the division into words and word-meanings is not ultimately real, what does the conventional understanding rest upon? — this too should be considered. But for those who maintain the denotative capacity of the final phoneme of the sentence, in their view too, since the division of word-meanings is ultimately real, conventional understanding is indeed possible.
But it is said: conventional understanding is precisely the grasping of the signifier-signified relation. And for those who maintain the denotative capacity of the final phoneme, the word is not the designator of the word-meaning. Therefore, in their view too, the conventional understanding is without an object.
We reply:

children.translated_text: To this the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>) says:
'For words, having designated their own respective meanings, have their function completed.
Then those [meanings], being understood, produce the comprehension of sentence-meaning.' [<s>Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā</s> 1.1.25]

Those who say that the sentence itself, having been grasped by memory, conveys the sentence-meaning — for them too, the previously stated fault of over-postulation of capacities is insurmountable.
And the statement of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>) — 'The last phoneme together with the dispositional impressions generated by prior phonemes is the conveyer' [<s>Śābara-bhāṣya</s> p. 46] — is without a real object.
And the simultaneous remembrance of a great sentence (<s>mahāvākya</s>) is impossible.
Therefore, the denotative capacity of words alone must be accepted.

Here some raise an objection: The ascertainment of the denotative capacity of words within a sentence employed in the usage of elders is itself not possible. For the validity of human sentences as <s>pramāṇa</s> with respect to meaning is accepted only in the mode of being an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>). For from the sentence, which is an effect, the prior cognition of the speaker regarding that meaning is inferred as the cause. And since that cognition is non-deviant from its object, there is certainty about the object — thus there is no ascertainment of denotative capacity.

We reply: Surely you have not properly grasped the meaning stated in the <s>Nītipatha</s>. For it has been explained there: A child learning language perceives, immediately following the hearing of the words of the elder directing him, a cognition of meaning inferred from the elder's specific action — and understands it as caused by the words. Having thus learned language, he sometime encounters a sentence composed of words with unconnected meanings by some speaker; and while thus observing, a reflection arises: 'This sentence, which appears to consist of words with unconnected meanings, how did it produce a determinate cognition of meaning in the directing elder? Even in the elder's case, the suspicion of an arrangement of words with unconnected meanings in a humanly produced sentence is possible, as it is for me.'
When such doubt arises, this determination then arises: 'Surely this speaker has been ascertained by [the elder] thus — that he employs words with connected meanings only.' And the regularity of this speaker's employment of such words is not possible without the perception of syntactic connection — thus, by inferring the perception of syntactic connection, the connection is ascertained. And when the connection is ascertained, this sentence is a restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) of that meaning.
And thus, since by being a restatement, that sentence is indeed a designator of that meaning — he thinks that the prior knowledge of denotative capacity was not erroneous. 'Only I had not previously understood that his ascertainment of meaning was preceded by inference.'
And this inference of the specific cognition of the speaker, when the syntactic connection of the meaning is not ascertained, is not possible merely from grasping the bare form of words, but rather from grasping a specific character. And no specific character of words other than their capacity (<s>śakti</s>) is grasped. Therefore, by him too the denotative capacity of words has been ascertained — thus, from the speaker's employment of words designating specific syntactic connections, the prior cognition of the speaker regarding that object has been inferred. This is the profound great ocean of logic.

The doubt regarding the impossibility of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (designation-of-the-related):
Here some say: Granted that there is knowledge of the capacity of words in word-meanings; even so, <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> cannot be established. For: since the correlates are infinite, the syntactic connections are infinite; and when those are infinite, even the things syntactically connected are infinite — hence the grasping of the relation is difficult. And if a word whose relation has not been grasped has denotative capacity, then from one word, the cognition of all meanings would follow.
Nor should designation of general syntactic connection be suspected, since specific syntactic connection is comprehended from sentences.
And since the comprehension of sentence-meaning is possible even through the designation of mere form (<s>svarūpamātra</s>), in accepting <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> there is over-postulation of capacities.
Also, when a word designates its own meaning as syntactically connected — is it designated as connected with the meaning designated by another word, or with one not so designated? This dilemma must be considered. If with one not designated — then the employment of the other word is purposeless. And from one [word] the cognition of all connections would follow. If with one designated — then that word too, as designating the syntactically connected, would require the meaning supplied by another word for its designation — and thus mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>) would result.
Therefore, words designate only the bare form of meanings, without dependence on the designation by other words. And those word-meanings, thus designated by words, possessing expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), proximity (<s>sannidhi</s>), and fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>), produce the comprehension of sentence-meaning. The requirement of grasping their relation should not be suspected — for this is a property of words, not of meanings.
He begins to refute this:
Words' own meanings, possessing syntactic connection, are included (<s>āvāpa</s>) and excluded (<s>uddhāra</s>) [in sentences];
therefore it is understood that the capacity (<s>sāmarthya</s>) of words is in [their meanings as] syntactically connected. [7]

children.translated_text: To this the followers of the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> (<s>Kumārila</s>) say:
'Words do not abandon their capacity even with respect to sentence-meaning;
from those word-meanings, which are settled merely as such, it [the sentence-meaning] is understood.'

An objection from the standpoint of the <s>Vārtika</s> (of <s>Kumārila</s>):
To this one says: Granted that <s>āvāpa</s> and <s>uddhāra</s> have syntactically connected word-meanings as their objects; even so, <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> is impossible — since that can be explained indirectly (<s>pāramparyeṇa</s>) as well. For thus: even though the meaning designated by words without syntactic connection serves as the cause for the cognition of syntactically connected meaning — thus words have a causal role even with respect to the syntactically connected, indirectly.
<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Adhikaraṇa</s> 7, verse 229.

children.text: padārthapratipādanañca vākyārthapratipattaye prayuktānāṃ padānāmavāntaravyāpāra iti ca, teṣāmeva vyavahāraḥ---
children.translated_text: And the designation of word-meaning is an intermediate function (<s>avāntara-vyāpāra</s>) of words employed for the purpose of comprehending sentence-meaning — and their usage is thus:
'When those [words] are directed toward [comprehending] sentence-meaning, it is indispensable —
the designation of word-meaning, like flames for the wood in cooking.'
<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Adhikaraṇa</s> 7, verse 343.
Setting aside this objection itself, he resolves another fault:
When words are said to designate their own meanings as connected with other [eligible] meanings possessing expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), proximity (<s>sannidhi</s>), and fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) —
when this is the accepted conventional understanding — [8]

children.translated_text: Therefore —
Whatever is expected, fit, and present in proximity,
with that connected, the word conveys its own meaning.

then there is no fault from either infinitude or deviation. As for what was said — that due to infinitude, the ascertainment of word-capacity is impossible, and that if the capacity is not grasped, there would be the unwanted consequence of deviation in designation — that is untenable. The comprehension of the relation is possible even through resort to a characterizing mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>); the conventional understanding is accepted that a word conveys its own meaning as syntactically connected with what is expected, fit, and proximate.

children.translated_text: Therefore, here too, expectancy is only for the sake of establishing connected denotation (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>).

children.text: yadi paramayaṃ viśeṣaḥ, "dvārami"tyādau tasyaiva padasyānvitābhidhānāyā'kāṅkṣā, "gāmānaya śuklāmi"tyādau tu 1119padāntarasyeti /
children.translated_text: If, however, this distinction [is to be made]: in '<s>dvāram</s>' ('the door') and such, the expectancy is of that very word's connected denotation; while in '<s>gāmānaya śuklām</s>' ('Bring the white cow') and such, the expectancy is of another word —
The desire to know the correlative, for the sake of connected denotation
or for the sake of assembling the stated meanings — that is called <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy).

Thus the summary verse. The reasoning regarding the topic of <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) — its presentation and refutation [of objections]. What then is this <s>ākāṅkṣā</s>? It is the desire to know on the part of the cognizer. What is its basis? Some say it is based on invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>): since an action is invariably concomitant with its causal factors (<s>kāraka</s>), having cognized the action, one desires to know the causal factor, and similarly having known the causal factor, one desires to know the action. We consider this improper, because the desire to know would never cease. For thus: when there is a desire to know a causal factor, there would also arise a desire to know its producer, its qualities, its actions, its other causal factors, and so on. If, due to the absence of purpose, nothing beyond the causal factor is desired to be known, then even where there is mere cognition of an action but no purpose in knowing the causal factor, there should be no desire to know. For when an action to be performed is understood, since its performance is impossible without the causal factor, the knowledge of the causal factor does not have a purpose [beyond that]. But in present-tense descriptions and such, since the action is not to be performed, there is no purpose in knowing the causal factor. And yet, even where they consider the sentence incomplete, it is because it conveys a meaning that has expectancy, and that is what makes it incomplete. Hence they even supply an ellipsis (<s>adhyāhāra</s>) there. And even where there is cognition of an action to be performed, there should be a desire to know all the causal factors exhaustively. For example, in 'O <s>Devadatta</s>! Bring the cow' — since the instrument is not mentioned, there would be incompleteness. If, however, the performance is possible even with the knowledge of just one causal factor so that there is no desire to know another, then even when in 'O <s>Devadatta</s>! Bring the cow with a stick' the word 'stick' is employed, there should be no expectancy for it. And hence, since it is not expected, its connection in the sentence-meaning would not obtain. If, however, expectancy is postulated due to the utterance of the word 'stick,' because otherwise the utterance of the word 'stick' would be purposeless since its meaning would have no connection — even so, in the Vedic sentence '<s>aruṇayā ekahayanā piṅgākṣyā somaṃ krīṇāti</s>' ('One purchases <s>Soma</s> with a reddish one-year-old cow with tawny eyes') [<s>Taittirīya Saṃhitā</s> 6.1.9], there would be the same unwanted consequence of non-connection. For there is no proof that Vedic word-utterance must not be purposeless, so there is no cause for expectancy arising there, and what is beyond '<s>somaṃ krīṇāti</s>' (one purchases Soma) would be unconnected. Moreover, since action and causal factor are worldly [concepts], even with any mention of action and causal factor their establishment is unimpeded, so intense desire to know specifics is not tenable. For the desire to know arises regarding what is unknown, not regarding what is already known. Statement of <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> according to his own view: It is replied: The incompleteness of denotation and the incompleteness of the denotable are the bases for the arising of the desire to know. For when a single word is employed, as in '<s>dvāram</s>' ('the door'), the denotation itself does not reach completion — for without the utterance of a word that brings the correlative into proximity, connected denotation (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>) cannot be spoken of. Since it is ascertained through the usage of the learned that words are directed toward conveying connected meaning, the desire to know the correlative for that purpose is indeed proper. Even for one whose established conclusion is <s>abhihitānvaya</s> (post-denotation connection), in that view too, since the meaning of a word is incapable of connection without another word-meaning, the desire to know the correlative is proper for the sake of establishing that. And when this [expectancy] obtains, since it is known in ordinary usage that ellipsis (<s>adhyāhāra</s>) completes an incomplete sentence, the ellipsis of a suitable correlative is made based on context and such. In sentences like '<s>amāvāsyāyām aparāhṇe piṇḍapitṛyajñena carantī</s>' ('performing the <s>Piṇḍapitṛyajña</s> on the new-moon afternoon') [<s>Āpastamba Śrautasūtra</s> 1.3.7, <s>sūtra</s> 1.2] — even though multiple words are employed and connected denotation obtains, since the effect of <s>abhihitānvaya</s> — namely the unprecedented ritual (<s>apūrva</s>) — cannot be a proper effect without performance, and since performance is impossible without an agent, and since agency is impossible without eligibility (<s>adhikāra</s>), and since eligibility cannot be postulated without a person to be enjoined (<s>niyojya</s>), the desire to know a person fit for connection who is to be enjoined is indeed proper. And when this obtains, from the understanding of incompleteness, when ellipsis is to be made as in ordinary usage, since life (<s>jīvana</s>) is necessary and intrinsic (<s>antaraṅga</s>), no suspension of the performance of the injunction can be postulated [due to it]; hence, setting that aside, when [the focus] rests on the qualifier of the person enjoined in a desire-dependent (<s>kāmya</s>) rite — since heaven (<s>svarga</s>), desired by all persons of desire, alone is fit to be the qualifier of the person enjoined — '<s>svargakāmaḥ</s>' (one who desires heaven) is supplied as the person enjoined. Similarly, in the injunction of study (<s>adhyayanavidhi</s>), since the effect is accomplished by the performance prompted by another, no person enjoined is supplied. And in the case of an unprecedented effect (<s>apūrvakārya</s>), which is supra-mundane (<s>alaukika</s>), the expectancy does not cease without the supply of the person enjoined. And precisely because of its supra-mundane nature, in sentences such as '<s>sauryaṃ caruṃ nirvapet ghṛte śuklānāṃ vrīhīṇāṃ brahmavarcasakāmaḥ</s>' ('One desiring Vedic splendor should cook an offering to <s>Sūrya</s> of white rice-grains in ghee') [<s>Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā</s> 2.2.2], since the injunction cannot be accomplished without the instrumental aid (<s>karaṇopakāra</s>), there is a desire to know it, and a desire to know the word-meaning that generates it. Hence, in its absence, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>), suspecting the deficiency of the sentences, resolved [it]. [Objection:] But if so, in ordinary usage too, three words are employed — '<s>gāmānaya śuklām</s>' ('Bring the white cow') — and there, since the impossibility of two causal factors does not hold, there is no expectancy, so how is connected denotation established, since the sentence is complete with just '<s>gāmānaya</s>' ('Bring the cow')? True. [This is the case] when the additional word is not uttered. But when that [word] is uttered, since it too is in proximity with '<s>ānayati</s>' (brings), and since the understanding of single-sentence-ness arises from that proximity, and since its own meaning is denoted as connected with '<s>ānayati</s>', and since this is impossible without expectancy, expectancy of '<s>ānayati</s>' is postulated. And thus said the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>): 'There is indeed [expectancy] when what is colored is expected' [<s>Śābarabhāṣya</s> p. 117].
Thus the summary verse.

children.translated_text: It is replied: Since the cognition of sentence-meaning from a sentence depends on reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>), the king is connected only with 'son' which perpetually requires [a correlative], and when the expectancy is satisfied by that connection, the connection with 'man' is not experienced. Thus <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> too is resorted to as an indicative mark of <s>vyutpatti</s>.
Even when a fit [word] is proximate, it is not connected if [the sentence] is [already] complete;
therefore, <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> too is an indicative mark in the <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) of words.

And this <s>ākāṅkṣā</s>, when it occurs, is resorted to as an indicative mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) of <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding). Why then is proximity (<s>sannidhi</s>) and fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) alone not resorted to, since connected denotation is not observed in the absence of expectancy? In '<s>ayameti putro rājñaḥ, puruṣo 'yamapanīyatām</s>' ('This son of the king is coming; let this man be removed'), the king, whose expectancy is satisfied by the word 'son,' is not connected with 'man.'
Thus the summary verse.

children.text:
sā ceyamākāṅkṣā pratiyogiṣu sarveṣu na sahasaivopajāyate, kintu kāraṇopanipātakrameṇa /
tathāhi---viṣayamantareṇāpūrvaṃ kāryaṃ pratyetumeva na śakyata iti, pratipattyanubandhabhūtaviṣayāpekṣā prathamaṃ vidheḥ /
atha pratipanne viṣayasambandhini vidhyarthe, niyojyamantareṇa tatsiddhyasambhavānniyojyākāṅkṣā /
tathā viṣayībhūte bhāvārthe karaṇe labdhe, vaikṛtāpūrvāṇāṃ karaṇopakārākāṅkṣā, labdhe ca tasmin, tajjanakapadārthākāṅkṣeti /

children.translated_text: And thus they say:
"The expectancy regarding all correlatives does not arise at that very moment;
but rather in order, following the sequence of the presentation of causes."

And this <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> does not arise simultaneously with respect to all correlatives, but rather in the order of the presentation of causes. For thus: since an unprecedented effect (<s>apūrva kārya</s>) cannot be cognized without an object, the expectation of an object, which is bound up with cognition, belongs to the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) first. Then, when the injunctive meaning involving the object-relation is cognized, since its accomplishment is impossible without a person enjoined, there arises the expectancy for the person enjoined (<s>niyojya</s>). Similarly, when the objective meaning (<s>bhāvārtha</s>) with its instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) has been obtained, the expectancy for the instrumental aid (<s>karaṇopakāra</s>) of modified unprecedented [rites] arises; and when that is obtained, the expectancy for the word-meaning that generates it.
Thus.
And here there is a verse:
As the desire to know the related [correlatives] arises in the cognizer in a certain order,
just so is the capacity of words to denote connected meaning.
And following that sequence, connected denotation (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>) too proceeds in sequence.

children.translated_text: Therefore, in the <s>Viśvajit</s> and such [sacrifices], connected denotation is accomplished through the person enjoined; everywhere through instrumental aid (<s>karaṇopakāra</s>); and in modified rites (<s>vikṛti</s>) through the meanings of the model-rite (<s>prakṛti</s>) words, even though they are not presented through words.

children.text: ākāṅkṣāvacca sannidhāvapi sannidhāpakakrameṇaiva kramo veditavyaḥ, tadanusāreṇa cānvitābhidhānamapitathaiva---iti /
children.translated_text: And just as in <s>ākāṅkṣā</s>, so too in <s>sannidhi</s> the order follows the sequence of what brings about proximity — and connected denotation follows that order accordingly.
In <s>vyutpatti</s>, <s>sannidhi</s> (proximity) is the very arising of the word, not an indicative mark [in the strict sense];
because connection is observed in ordinary usage even with a meaning supplied [by ellipsis, without a word].

Examination of <s>sannidhi</s> (proximity): Now, what is <s>sannidhi</s>? The turning of the cognition toward another meaning, immediately upon hearing, by virtue of <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) and <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness). And it is not based on word alone; it is merely an indicative mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) in the <s>vyutpatti</s> of connected denotation, since connected denotation is observed in ordinary usage even with a supplied [elliptical] element. Nor should it be said that what is supplied is a word, and that word presents the meaning — because that is useless and unsupported by any <s>pramāṇa</s>. Even though ellipsis (<s>adhyāhāra</s>) is warranted by the <s>pramāṇa</s> of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), still the postulation of a word is untenable. For only that without which there would be impossibility is the object of <s>arthāpatti</s>. And there is no impossibility of meanings without a word. One might think: <s>arthāpatti</s>, operating for the postulation of a meaning, terminates in a word as prior, since that meaning is knowable through determinate cognition (<s>savikalpaka-jñāna</s>), and since determinate cognitions are preceded by words. That is wrong. Just as in determinate cognition preceded by a word, the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the sense-organs in the indeterminate stage have their capacity ascertained only in the object [not in the word] — so in observed <s>arthāpatti</s>, since the <s>pramāṇa</s>-status of <s>arthāpatti</s> is accepted with respect to the directly establishing object alone, in heard <s>arthāpatti</s> too, its <s>pramāṇa</s>-status is proper only with respect to the object, not the word — since the word is incapable of directly resolving the impossibility. Moreover, in all determinate cognitions, the word, being involved in recollection, does not deserve <s>prameya</s>-status (being an object of valid knowledge). And the prior-perception of the word in determinate cognitions is not strongly supported by a <s>pramāṇa</s>; rather, it is established through experience that the recollection of the word occurs simultaneously with the cognition of the meaning. Therefore, heard <s>arthāpatti</s> does not have a word as its object. And since the impossibility is not of the word, the postulation should not be of a word. But the postulation, proceeding from the impossibility of connected denotation, rests only in the meaning of a suitable correlative — since that alone is expected — and by the principle of the tenth man and such, even the word, though previously perceived like the word-meaning, is to be disregarded. And in cases like '<s>dvāram</s>' ('the door'), where ellipsis is made, <s>arthāpatti</s> is not capable of postulating [specifically] '<s>āvriyatām</s>' (let it be closed) or '<s>saṃvriyatām</s>' (let it be shut), since it is a cause only of general postulation. Therefore, the legitimacy of ellipsis is from ordinary usage alone, as completing what is incomplete. And there, the determination of the specific [supplied meaning] is through fitness and through the force of context and such — it is only the meaning that completes, so the supply of a word is useless.
The proximity of all correlatives does not [arise] at once;
it follows a sequence, in accordance with the sequence of the aggregate of causes that bring about proximity.
As the proximity of the correlatives arises in order,
Thus, gradually, through words alone, the cognition of connected meaning [arises].

children.translated_text: We reply: The determination of fitness through a general [category] serves as a means for the cognition of the particular — so there is no fault.

children.text: yadapi tadapūrvam, tadapi kāryameveti dṛṣṭacarakāryasambandhaṃ yat, tadyogyamityavasīyate /
children.translated_text: Even though that [Vedic result] is unprecedented, it is indeed an effect; therefore, that which has an observed connection with effects of the same kind is determined to be fit.
Fitness that has been determined in ordinary experience through a general [category] alone
serves as the distinguishing criterion (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) in the acquisition of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (denotation of connected meaning).

These are the summary verses. Therefore, the expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>) as described: the meaning is that [a word-meaning] that is proximate, expected, present, and fit (<s>yogya</s>) is [understood as] connected with the other word-meaning obtained through proximity (<s>sannidhi</s>). Examination of fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>): What, first, is this fitness? We reply: That which is fit for a relation (<s>sambandhārha</s>). How is it known that 'this is fit for a relation'? Because it has been observed in a relation. Objection: If so, then how can <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (denotation of connected meaning) operate with respect to an unprecedented effect in the <s>Veda</s>, since no relation of anything with that [unprecedented effect] has been observed?

children.translated_text: Just as one cannot determine the fitness of anything with respect to an object not knowable through any other means of knowledge, so too one cannot determine unfitness — [and then] everything would be connected with everything in every way, even with what has not been cognized.

children.translated_text: Since the connection is only with the meaning of the verbal action as the object, and since only the one qualified by an unacceptable qualifier — such as 'one desiring heaven' — is connected as the one to be enjoined, the restriction is not established — enough of over-extension. [8]
This is the summary verse. Presentation and refutation of an alternative view regarding fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>): Others, however, [say]: That which has not been determined as unfit is fit.
This same [reliance] applies equally to the cognition of connection even with respect to word-meanings [in the rival view]. [9]
Objection: In the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> view, the very reliance on a distinguishing criterion (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) in the acquisition [of word-meaning] is a complexity. To this he says:

children.text: yasyāpi mate padārthā evānyonyānvayamavagamayanti, tenāpi pratiniyatānvayabodhasiddhyarthamidamāśrayaṇīyameva--ākāṅkṣā--sannidhi--yogyatāvanta eva padārthā 1133vākayārtha bodhayanti, nānya iti, etadeva kathamiti paryanuyuktena vṛddhavyavahāre tathādarśanāditi parihāro vācyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Even according to one whose view is that word-meanings themselves convey mutual connection, this must be relied upon for the establishment of the cognition of a specifically determined connection: only word-meanings possessing expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), proximity (<s>sannidhi</s>), and fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) convey the sentence-meaning (<s>vākyārtha</s>), and not others. When asked 'How is this so?', the answer must be given: 'Because it is so observed in the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddha</s>).'
Therefore, since this [reliance on criteria] is common to both views, it is not a valid objection. [9]
To this he says:
But for those [word-meanings], this unobserved capacity [to convey connected meaning] must be postulated through another means of knowledge,
a capacity that is brought about through contact with other words directed toward a qualified meaning. [10]
Objection: Even so, on what specific grounds is the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> (connection of what has been denoted) view abandoned in favor of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (denotation of connected meaning)?

children.translated_text: Thus say the <s>Vārttikakāra Miśra</s>s:
"For one seeing an indistinct form and hearing the neighing sound,
and [hearing] the sound of hoof-beats — the cognition 'a white horse runs' [arises].

For word-meanings, being cognized from sources of knowledge other than words (<s>śabda</s>), are not observed to have the capacity of conveying mutual connection — therefore, the capacity for such understanding must be postulated for what is denoted by words. And it must be relied upon that contact with words is the very cause for the origination of that capacity. For words are observed to be employed in worldly transactions with the aim of conveying qualified meaning. And since a word is not directly capable of conveying sentence-meaning, it makes word-meanings into intermediate instruments. And if those [word-meanings] were capable of conveying mutual connection by themselves, then their serving as intermediate instruments would be [explained]; otherwise not — therefore, it is from the very contact with words directed toward the understanding of qualified meaning that this capacity of theirs arises. Thus, for words too, the capacity of implanting the capacity for connection-understanding in word-meanings must be relied upon. [Objection:] This would be the case if word-meanings ascertained through other means of knowledge did not have the capacity to convey mutual connection. But they do have it — as seen in the case of whiteness whose specific locus has not been determined (perceived directly), a horse whose specific qualities are not known (inferred from the neighing sound and hoof-beats), and a running whose specific agent is unknown — the capacity to produce the connected cognition 'a white horse runs' is observed. To this, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> (<s>Kumārila</s> <s>Miśra</s>) says:
