children.translated_text: And thus it has been said:
"The affix is always employed with respect to a qualified meaning,
because [the meaning] is qualified by the stem-meaning that was known earlier."

This is observed without any sentence." (<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Vākya</s> section, verse 358.) 'Indistinct form' means: a form not clearly discerned — the meaning is that the specific quality is not determined by direct perception. Here we reply: Is this cognition 'a white horse runs' had by the very person who has apprehended the neighing-sound and hoof-beat-sound as belonging to the same locus as whiteness? Or even by one who has not determined the source of those sounds? What of it? If it is said [to apply to one] who has not identified the source of the neighing, walking-sound, and hoof-steps — then there is a contradiction with experience. For such a person would cognize: 'There must be a horse in this area, and something must be running.' But if, through the force of habitual expertise, he apprehends the neighing as belonging specifically to a horse, then he infers only the vigorous motion belonging specifically to a horse — he does not first apprehend [the running] in isolation and then, through the capacity of word-meanings, understand the connection. And one who, having determined 'there is nothing other than a horse in this area,' ascertains through elimination that the horseness is co-located with whiteness even without determining the source of the neighing — for him too, the means of knowledge is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), like inferring outdoor location from not seeing someone at home: 'That which is white — that is a horse.' And for one who ascertains that the neighing and hoof-clatter are co-located with whiteness — for him too, the inference is of horseness and vigorous movement as belonging to what is white, not [cognized] independently. Therefore, apart from inference and presumption (<s>anumāna</s> and <s>arthāpatti</s>), the capacity of word-meanings apprehended as unconnected through other means of knowledge to convey mutual connection is never observed. Moreover, if the understanding of mutual connection arises from the mere apprehension of word-meanings, then it must be stated under which means of valid knowledge this falls. Not under verbal testimony (<s>śābda</s>), since there are no words. For your established doctrine is that the knowledge of connection arising from words through the intermediate operation of denoting word-meanings is verbal. Therefore, this does not fall under verbal testimony. And if another means of knowledge is accepted [for this], verbal testimony would be destroyed, since that [other means] would also have validity regarding objects apprehended through words. Therefore, for word-meanings denoted by words, the unobserved capacity to convey sentence-meaning must be postulated elsewhere [i.e., in words themselves]. And the capacity of words to implant this capacity — by parsimony of postulation, it is proper to postulate for words merely the capacity to convey their own meaning as connected [with other word-meanings]. Therefore, the [claim] that words have the capacity [to convey connection] indirectly through word-meanings is refuted. Objection: Infinite capacities of words would have to be postulated, directed toward infinite relata in the understanding of one's own meaning as connected. But in the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> doctrine, there is only one capacity of each word for one meaning. Reply: That is wrong — because, through a single capacity to denote one's own meaning as connected with what is expected, proximate, and fit, the difference of effects [i.e., different connected meanings] is explained through the difference of relata — just as with the eye and other sense organs. Just as the eye, with a single capacity of seeing, generates different cognitions due to the difference of relata such as pots and so on, so too should words be understood. Moreover, this [same issue] applies equally to [the rival view regarding] word-meanings — so this is no objection at all. Others say: Word-meanings possessing expectancy, proximity, and fitness become the sentence-meaning; they do not, however, convey the sentence-meaning [actively]. This is exceedingly foolish — since there would be the consequence of there being no cause for the understanding of sentence-meaning. If words are not the means, then even word-meanings are not the cause of the cognition of connection — and it would arise without any cause. One might think: When a verb-stem or a case-affix denotes a meaning that has expectancy, the word-meaning of another word, being a fit relatum, is brought into proximity and thereby stands as its relatum. True. But the basis of understanding that relation must be stated. Rather: when the first word-meaning, having expectancy, has been denoted, the next word that is uttered brings its own meaning forward as related to that [first meaning], just like an affix (<s>pratyaya</s>). Just as, when the stem-meaning has been previously understood, the affix being uttered denotes its own meaning as qualified by that [stem-meaning], so too does another word. As it has been said: 'The stem and the affix together denote the affix-meaning' (<s>Mahābhāṣya</s>). This means that the stem brings its own meaning forward as a qualifier of the affix-meaning — and thereby 'speaks' that meaning along with the affix.

children.translated_text: The view of <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> (<s>Kumārila</s>) regarding sentence-meaning.
The <s>Vārttikakāra Miśra</s>s, wishing all sentence-meanings to be figurative (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>), refute the postulation that word-meanings have the capacity to convey [mutual] connection.
For the word-meaning, having been denoted in an unconnected state, figuratively indicates its own state of being connected.
For since there is a relation between a state and the thing possessing that state, when the state-possessor is denoted, the state too becomes present in the mind.

He says. Moreover, if the affix is a denotter of connected meaning (<s>anvitābhidhāyin</s>), then, there being no difference, why should it not be accepted that words too denote connected meanings? Why this half-heartedness? If <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> applies to both stem and affix, then let the word <s>dvāram</s> ('door') be examined: does the expectancy that necessitates <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> [apply here], or should [a verb like] 'let it be opened or closed' be supplied? We reply: The word <s>dvāram</s>, being a <s>prātipadika</s> (nominal stem), primarily denotes no meaning beyond its stem-meaning. So with what would its denoting of connected meaning operate? The verbal completion (such as 'let it be entered') in [cases like] the affix <s>praviśati</s> and so on, in which the meaning is separate — that is a supplementation required by the impossibility of the denoted meaning alone, just as in [the <s>Vedic</s> rites like] <s>Viśvajit</s> and so on — so there is no fault.

children.translated_text: Here it is said:
How then is this secondary indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) [to be defined]?
When the denoted meaning of a word cannot be syntactically connected in the sentence-meaning,
the syntactic connection of [another meaning] obtained through the relation with that [denoted meaning] is called secondary indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>).

And it is already established that whenever one relatum is seen, a cognition of the other relatum arises.
Therefore there is no need to posit a capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of words for conveying connected meaning (<s>anvita-bodhana</s>).
Thus they say:
'The sentence-meaning, being indicated (<s>lakṣyamāṇa</s>), is [obtained] everywhere — this is not our position.'
Here others say: this is not secondary indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), because there is no abandonment of the primary meaning.
For secondary indication is seen in [expressions like] 'the <s>Gaṅgā</s>' [meaning 'the bank of the Gaṅgā'] through the abandonment of the primary meaning — so they say.
But they say this only due to deficiency in their grasp of the inner workings of the <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> system.
For depending on what is to be indicated, sometimes there is abandonment of the primary meaning, and sometimes inclusion.
In '<s>sṛṣṭīr ūpa dadhāti</s>' ('he bestows beauties'), secondary indication is accepted, since the qualified entities listed in that group are indicated even without the word '<s>sṛṣṭi</s>,' and because the meaning of '<s>sṛṣṭi</s>' is included within them.
Similarly, in '<s>paurṇamāsīṃ yajate</s>' ('he sacrifices on the full moon'), the word '<s>paurṇamāsī</s>,' denoting a sacrifice, indicates the aggregate of sacrifices through secondary indication, since the singular number is otherwise untenable.
And in grasping the aggregate there is no abandonment of the aggregate, since [the singular] depends on it.
Similarly, in a <s>dvandva</s> compound denoting reciprocal association, the state of being accompanied by another entity is resorted to through secondary indication because the dual or plural number is otherwise untenable — yet there is no abandonment of the entity possessing that state.
Similarly, in the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> of the <s>Niṣāda-sthapati</s> topic [MS 6.1-10], it is said that there would be secondary indication of the genitive meaning — yet no abandonment of the stem-meaning occurs there.
Similarly, in '<s>ratha-ghoṣeṇa</s>' ('by the sound of the chariot'), there is no abandonment of the chariot.
Similarly, the singular-ending <s>mantra</s> '<s>medhāpataye medhām</s>' ('intelligence to the lord of intelligence') is placed in the ritual context through secondary indication, yet there is no loss of the two qualified deities <s>Agni</s> and <s>Soma</s>.
Thus, secondary indication is proper even without the abandonment of the primary meaning.

children.translated_text: Let there be purposelessness if you wish.
But something known only through general observation (<s>sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa</s>) does not have the power to determine specific connection.

If [it is said that] the devotion of words to things that are desired, proximate, and fit is understood from the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddha-vyavahāra</s>), and specific connection is understood by following that convention —

children.text: tanna tatra vṛddhavyavahāra eva tatparatā padānām, padārthānāṃ vā upāyābhāvena kathaṃ nāma nirvahati ?me cintā sā hi padānām, padārthānāṃ vā śaktikalpanāṃ vinānupapanneti manyāmahe // 10 //
children.translated_text: That is not so. How can the devotion of words, or of word-meanings, to that [specific connection] be sustained in the usage of the learned alone, without a means [for establishing it]? For we consider that this [devotion] is untenable without positing a capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of words or of word-meanings.

Thus is the summary verse.
In [expressions like] '<s>gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ</s>' ('the hamlet on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>') etc., since the scriptural meaning of the word '<s>gaṅgā</s>' (the river itself) cannot be syntactically connected in the sentence-meaning, that [primary meaning] is abandoned, and through its relation [with the river], the meaning 'bank' etc. — which has attained cognitive proximity — is determined to be syntactically connected in the sentence-meaning.
Thus they say: 'Secondary indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) operates through impossibility [of the primary meaning] and through relation [with it].'
Here, however, in [expressions like] '<s>gām ānaya</s>' ('bring the cow') etc., there is no unfitness of the scriptural meaning for syntactic connection, nor is the connected state unfit for the relation of bringing.
Because of the impossibility of another syntactic connection for the meaning already connected.
If it be said: 'Let this not be secondary indication; rather, the word conveys its own state as being connected with the action-related factor (<s>kāraka</s>) apprehended through the verb, due to invariable concomitance' —
We reply: the verbal nature (<s>śābdatva</s>) of the apprehension of [syntactic] connection has thus been denied; rather, it would have to be accepted as falling within the domain of inference from general observation (<s>sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa</s>).
And then the apprehension of a specific connection, being unexplained, becomes groundless.
If one says: 'Without specific connection, practical activity cannot be constructed, so word-utterance would be purposeless — therefore [specific connection] is resorted to' — even so, the understanding of specific connection [would come] from the utterance of purposive speakers who use only meaningful sentences.
But in the <s>Veda</s>, since purposelessness cannot obtain [yet] there is no evidence for knowing specific connection — [the argument fails].
And merely because purposelessness would also arise in worldly [usage], it is not reasonable to determine specific connection without a [proper] means.
For just because the use of water by one who wishes to burn would be purposeless, the burning capacity of water does not manifest.
And that [capacity] belongs to words alone, as is stated:
Because of primacy, because of being denoters, and from the ascertainment of purport (<s>tātparya</s>) —
it is better to accept that very capacity (<s>śakti</s>) as belonging to words alone.

children.translated_text: For the awakening of the dispositional trace that produces the remembrance of the related meaning must necessarily be accepted for the purpose of establishing the remembrance of the relation.

Therefore, the denotative character of words consists precisely in the acceptance of conveying connected meaning not apprehended at the time of grasping the relation — and one who accepts this must resort to the doctrine that words denote connected meanings (<s>anvita-abhidhāyakatā</s>).
But [some say] —
'A word, because of the absence of anything additional, is not distinguished from a mere reminder (<s>smāraka</s>).'

It is not proper to attribute the capacity for conveying sentence-meaning to the [word-]meanings, bypassing words which are primary.
Moreover, that words are denoters (<s>abhidhāyaka</s>) is undisputed. Therefore their denotative capacity is already accepted; it is easy to extend that very capacity to the culmination of [conveying] syntactic connection.
But for word-meanings, even the capacity for generating cognition would have to be posited [anew].
Therefore, 'rather than positing a property of the property-bearer, it is more economical to posit a property' — hence the capacity for conveying connected meaning (<s>anvita-abhidhāna-śakti</s>) is properly attributed to words alone.
Moreover, words are accepted as denoters; if they were to produce only a cognition of the bare form of the word-meaning, even then their denotative character would be undermined, since that cognition is born from the awakening of the dispositional trace (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that produces word-meaning cognition at the time of grasping the relation.
<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, chapter 6, verse 107
And similarly —
'The word denoting the productive activity (<s>bhāvanā</s>) merely reminds of it, as in ordinary usage.'
<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, chapter 7, verse 248

'Also from the ascertainment of purport (<s>tātparya</s>).'
For even the philosopher who accepts that words have merely a reminding function with respect to word-meanings also admits that words are devoted to conveying the sentence-meaning; otherwise, the consequence would be that the sentence-meaning is non-verbal.
If so, then let words themselves have the direct capacity for conveying sentence-meaning — what need is there for resorting to intermediaries?

children.translated_text: Therefore, those who assert that words have a denotative character with respect to word-meanings beyond mere reminding must posit three capacities.

One is the denotative capacity of words [with respect to individual meanings]; another is the capacity to bestow upon word-meanings the capacity for conveying syntactic connection; and the third is the capacity of word-meanings for making known the [syntactic] connection.

children.text: smārakatvavādinastvabhidhānaśaktiṃ hitvā śaktidvayakalpanālāghavāt, uktenaiva nyāyena padānāmeva śaktikalpanāyā 1162ucitatvāt, anvitābhidhāyīni padānīti sthāpitam // 11 //
children.translated_text: But proponents of the reminding theory, by abandoning the denotative capacity [as something separate], achieve the economy of positing only two capacities; and by the reasoning already stated — that it is proper to attribute the capacity to words alone — it is established that words denote connected meanings (<s>anvita-abhidhāyin</s>).

children.translated_text: Now, to resolve the previously stated fault of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>), he shows how sentence-meaning is understood from words:
All the words that have been heard, having reminded [the hearer] of their unconnected meanings,
subsequently convey the sentence-meaning, the specific referent being established through reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>).

children.translated_text: Thus say the Vārttikakāra's [i.e. <s>Kumārila</s>'s] words:
'Since even those [words], when not remembered, do not convey the sentence-meaning to us,
therefore, validity [as a means of knowledge] resides in their remembrances when combined.'

One who has not grasped the [word-meaning] relation, or one in whom the dispositional trace from grasping the relation has not arisen or has been destroyed — such a person is not qualified for understanding the sentence-meaning.
But one whose dispositional trace from grasping the relation is unimpaired, upon hearing a word, surely remembers this: 'This [word] denotes that which is connected with its desired, proximate, and fit counterpart.'
And thus, while remembering, what is remembered is the bare form, unconnected — [this is the lot] of those not partaking of [syntactic] connection.
And no one thinks that the sentence-meaning is understood from hearing a single word.
Even according to the proponents of the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> (expressed-then-connected) theory, as long as another word has not presented another meaning, there is no understanding of the [syntactic] connection.
Because the word-meaning that makes known the connection requires another word-meaning, since connection requires a counterpart.
Therefore, even in their theory, what is denoted must always be the individual meaning in its unconnected state.
Only afterwards, from all those [meanings] having ascended into memory, should the understanding of the sentence-meaning be accepted.
<s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>.

children.translated_text:
For this very reason, the definition of sentence given by the revered teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>] is: 'A sentence is words that collectively designate a meaning' [<s>Śābara-bhāṣya</s>, <s>Balākādhyāya-pāda</s> 824].
But how is the comprehension of sentence-meaning achieved by the proponents of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s>? For the meaning that was not conveyed by the word while it was being heard — how could it appear when the word has disappeared?
We reply: Even for the proponent of <s>abhihitānvaya</s>, this rule does not hold — that the last phoneme together with the dispositional impressions generated by prior phonemes is the conveyer of word-meaning only while being heard. For it is observed that meaning is understood even from the Veda, studied in childhood and recalled later, whose meaning was not grasped at the time of study, through the dispositional impression of knowledge of the ancillary parts remembered later. Therefore, the capacity of what has been grasped by memory to convey meaning is not a fault.
For the word being heard, since <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> requires the correlate, the meaning was not designated earlier due to the absence of the cooperating cause; it is designated later — what is impossible in this?
Some disputants say: Let a single word alone be the designator of syntactically connected meaning, while the other words are operative merely in bringing the correlates into proximity. Nor is there non-apprehension of the distinguishing feature, since the distinguishing feature is grasped through primacy or through being the principal word. For this very reason it has been said: 'The first word is the sentence, or the principal word is the sentence' [<s>Vākyapadīya</s> 2.2].
To them he responds with 'all [words].' If only the first word were the sentence, then all word-meanings would be syntactically connected with the first word-meaning. But this is not a rule. [For example,] in '<s>aruṇayā ekahāyanyā piṅgākṣyā somaṃ krīṇāti</s>' (He buys <s>Soma</s> with a reddish, one-year-old, tawny-eyed [cow]) [<s>Taittirīya Saṃhitā</s> 6.1.9], redness and such are connected only with the buying.
Moreover, since there is no fixed order of words in a sentence, sometimes that very word would be first and thus the designator of syntactic connection, and at other times not — this is not reasonable.
Similarly, the sentence-status of the principal word too is improper, since not all [word-meanings] are syntactically connected with the meaning of the word '<s>soma</s>.' Although all [qualities] like redness have the relation of serving <s>Soma</s> — still, in this sentence, the syntactic connection of redness and such with <s>Soma</s> is only through buying, in the mode of action-instrument relation (<s>kriyā-kāraka</s>). But with <s>Soma</s>, there is only the relation of serving through the medium of buying.
If it is said: the word whose presentation the sentence aims at is the principal — then here, it is buying alone that is presented as delimited by all objects and instruments. Therefore '<s>krīṇāti</s>' (buys) alone is the principal word, and the syntactic connection of all [meanings] like redness is with it.
To this we say: The purport (<s>tātparya</s>) of a sentence is not fixed. Sometimes it is aimed at the verb — as in '<s>agnihotraṃ juhoti</s>' (he offers the <s>Agnihotra</s>). Sometimes it aims at the injunction of a qualifier — as in '<s>dadhnā juhoti</s>' (he offers with curds). Therefore, since the principal-word status can belong to all words, the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> capacity of all words must be accepted. And being so, even where the capacity has been established, its being a designator of syntactic connection is not contradictory. And this is equally the case for word-meanings.
But then, in '<s>gām ānaya</s>' (bring the cow) and such, all words would be synonymous with each other — just as '<s>gām</s>' designates as syntactically connected with bringing, so too '<s>ānaya</s>' would designate as connected with cow.
We reply: There are just two meanings here — cow-ness connected with bringing, and bringing connected with cow. Since each [word] designates one meaning each, whence the unwanted consequence of synonymy? And this is the same for word-meanings too.
But since the meaning of '<s>krīṇāti</s>' designates syntactic connection with multiple meanings like redness and such, there would be sentence-division through repetition of the verbal form.
No — because of consolidated utterance (<s>tantroccāraṇa</s>). And since consolidation is impossible when there is difference of form, sentence-division would follow.
'Processed through principles to manifest individual sentence-structure' — what this means is: unless the individual sentence-structure is processed through principles, the class of words does not function as conveying sentence-meaning. By the principles operative in worldly usage — such as 'this is the injunction, this is the restatement,' 'this is the principal, this is the subordinate,' 'this is intended, this is not intended' and so forth — unless these are duly ascertained, the meaning of no Vedic sentence is comprehended.
To this the <s>Vārtikakāra Miśra</s> (<s>Kumārila</s>) has said:
'For doubt remains regarding a Vedic sentence that is heard,
only so long as the individual sentence-structure is not clearly ascertained.
But upon knowing the individual sentence-structure, the experts in <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> principles —
all doubts regarding the meaning of Vedic sentences are resolved.'
To this they themselves have said:
'For when <s>dharma</s> is being ascertained through the Veda as an instrument,
<s>Mīmāṃsā</s> will fulfil the procedural component (<s>itikartavyatā-bhāga</s>).'
For this very reason, <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> has the status of a procedural requirement (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) in the comprehension of Vedic sentence-meaning.
<s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>.

iti /
nanu loke drāgeva vākyārthāvagatirneyatīṃ sāmagrīmapekṣate /
ucyate---atyantābhyasteṣu vākyeṣu syādevam, adṛṣṭārtheṣu smṛtyādivākyeṣu, loke 'pi nānāvidhavivādotthānāt kuto drāgevār'thaniścayaḥ /
api ca kāraṇābhāvenāpi lokasyāyaṃviveko nāsti /
children.translated_text: But in ordinary life, the comprehension of sentence-meaning is quick and does not require this elaborate apparatus. We reply: That may be so for extremely well-practiced sentences; but for sentences of <s>smṛti</s> and such with unfamiliar meanings, even in ordinary life, since various kinds of disputes arise, whence could there be quick certainty of meaning? Moreover, even without a cause, ordinary people do not have this discernment.
To this it has been said:
'Regarding cognitions that arise suddenly, depending on distinctions of multiple universals (<s>jāti</s>), qualities (<s>guṇa</s>), substances (<s>dravya</s>), and actions (<s>karman</s>),
which are of the nature of Vedic or figurative [meaning] —
ordinary people, due to the absence of a cause, are unable to determine [them].
But the experts in sentence-analysis investigate [them] for the purpose of establishing the stronger and weaker [interpretations].'
<s>Tantravārttika</s>.

children.text:
iti /
yaccedaṃ sarvapadānāmanvitābhidhāyitvamucyate, tat sarveṣu śrautārtheṣu padeṣu /
lākṣaṇika-gauṇārthapadaprayoge tu yadeva tatra śrautārtha padam tadevānvitābhidhāyakam, itarattu padaṃ pratiyogisannidhāpanaparameva /
children.translated_text: This assertion that all words have the capacity for <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (designation-of-the-connected) — that applies to all words with primary (<s>śrauta</s>) meanings. But when words with figurative (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>) or secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>) meanings are employed, only that word which has a primary meaning there is the <s>anvitābhidhāyaka</s> (designator of the connected); the other word serves merely to bring the correlate into proximity.
There, since the denotative capacity [of the figurative word] has not been ascertained, it is a non-designator of its own meaning at that time, due to the unfitness for syntactic connection.

children.text: kintu tadarthena smṛtena yat svasambandhi, svasadṛśaṃ vā svayamanvayayogyamupasthāpyate, tenānvitaṃ śrautārthameva padaṃ svārthamabhidhatta iti darśanarahasyamidam /
children.translated_text: But through the meaning remembered from that [figurative word], which presents something related to itself, or similar to itself, that is itself fit for syntactic connection — with that, the word with primary meaning alone designates its own meaning as connected. This is the secret of the doctrine.

children.text: na ca sarvapadānyeva lākṣaṇikāni, gauṇāni vā vākye sambhavantīti niravadyam /
children.translated_text: And since it is not the case that all words in a sentence are figurative or secondary, [the theory is] faultless.

children.text: kvacidabhidhānaṃ nimittam, kvacidabhihitor'tha iti ca yaduktam, tacchabdopasthāpitatāṃ darśayituṃ gauṇamabhihitatvagrahaṇam // 12 //
children.translated_text: And what was said — that sometimes designation is the cause, sometimes the designated meaning — that, to show the word-presented character, the term 'designated' (<s>abhihita</s>) is used in a secondary sense. [12]

children.text: kathaṃ punaranvitābhidhāyināṃ padena svarūpamātraṃ smārayituṃ śakyamityāha---
children.translated_text: But how can a word in the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> view merely remind [one] of the bare form? To this he says:
Even in the designation of the connected, the bare form is always present;
therefore, even regarding mere form, the word produces recollection. [13]
Now, that even the recollection of mere form is not impossible from the word — to this he says:
Just as by a meaning that is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, its own word is sometimes recalled,
so too by a word that is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, its meaning will be recalled. [14]
Thus first the recollection of bare form as included within the grasping of the relation has been stated.

children.text:
na hi yatpramāṇaṃ, tadeva smaraṇakāraṇam, apramāṇameva hi tat /
yasya tu yena saha kadācitpratyāsattiḥ pratītapūrvā, sa tatra saṃskārodbodhaddhāreṇa śaknotyeva smṛtiṃ janayitum /
asti ca svarūpasyāpi tadabhidheyāntargatyā śabdena pratyāsattiriti, śāknoti tatrāpi śabdassmṛtiṃ janayitum, arthavat /
yathā nirvikalpakadaśāpratītamarthasvarūpamātramanabhidhemapi śabdaṃ smārayati, tathā śabdo 'pyarthamiti, kimanupapannam /
etena---padoccāraṇānantaraṃ padārthasvarūpapratītissamarthitā /
abhihitānvayavādino 'pi sā na pramāṇam, abhyadhikārthaparicchedābhāvāt /
"anadhigatārthagantṛ pramāṇami"ti siddhāntābhyupagamāt /

children.translated_text: To this it has been said:

children.text: "sarvasyānupalabdher'the prāmāṇyaṃ smṛtiranyathā" [ślo. vā. au. sū ślo. 11.] iti /
children.translated_text: 'When there is non-apprehension of everything in the meaning, there is validity; otherwise it is memory' [<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Autpattika-sūtra</s> verse 11].

children.text: ata eva smṛtiriyam, yadi punassmṛtireṣā nābhyupeyeta, tadā pramāṇa-smṛti-saṃśaya-viparyayebhyaḥ pratipattyantarānabhyupagamāt padāt padārthapratītiḥ kvāntarbhāvyatāmiti vācyam /
children.translated_text: For this very reason this is memory. But if this were not accepted as memory, then — since no mode of cognition other than <s>pramāṇa</s>, memory, doubt, and error is accepted — one would have to say where the cognition of word-meaning from the word should be classified.
For this very reason, even in the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> view, the function of mere reminding is what pleases us. [14]

For it is not the case that only what is a <s>pramāṇa</s> is a cause of recollection — rather, it is precisely what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. But that which has had some prior association (<s>pratyāsatti</s>) with something at some time — it is capable of producing recollection through the arousal of dispositional impressions. And even bare form, by virtue of being included within what is designated by the word, has an association with the word — hence the word is capable of producing recollection of it too, just as with the meaning [designated].
Just as the bare form of a meaning, perceived in the non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) stage, causes the recollection of the word even though not designated [by it], so too the word [causes recollection] of the meaning — what is impossible in this?
By this, the cognition of the bare form of word-meaning immediately following the utterance of the word has been justified. For even the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> proponent [admits that] it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, due to the absence of ascertaining any additional meaning. Since by the established principle '<s>pramāṇa</s> is that which grasps a meaning not previously grasped' [this bare-form cognition is not pramāṇa].
Now he resolves the [objection of] mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>):
With meanings brought into proximity by memory, each word thus states
its own meaning as connected — therefore there is no mutual dependence. [15]

children.translated_text: If there is the objection that double designation would result — let it result; there is no fault.

children.text: pūrvaṃ kevalaṃ padamananvitaṃ svārthamabhidhatte, pratiyogipadāntarābhihitavastvantarasahāyaprāptyā tu tattadanvitamarthamāha, iti na kaściddoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: First, the bare word designates its own meaning without connection; then, upon obtaining the aid of another entity designated by a correlative word, it states the connected meaning — thus there is no fault.
And even in this manner, in our view there is parsimony of postulation of capacity, because the postulation of a capacity for word-meanings to produce the knowledge of connection is abandoned.

children.text: tulyāyāmapi śaktikalpanāyām, padānāmevānvitabodhanaśaktirāśrayitumucitā,1198na padārthānām, prathamāvagatatvāt, vākyārthe ca 1199 tātparyasyopagamāditi // 15 //
children.translated_text: Even when the postulation of capacity is equal, it is more proper to accept the capacity for producing the knowledge of connection as belonging to words themselves, not to word-meanings — because words are first apprehended, and because purport (<s>tātparya</s>) is accepted with respect to sentence-meaning. // 15 //

For in merely remembering the bare form of its own meaning, a word does not require another word. And what is memory-presented (<s>smṛti-sannihita</s>) is indeed present. Therefore, there is no mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). But the convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>) is from the usage of the elders, and the usage is based on the cognition of connected meaning — therefore, from observing that, only the cognition of connected meaning can be inferred, not the mere remembering of unconnected word-meaning. We reply: The otherwise-inexplicability of the connected cognition inferred from the usage is itself the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the possibility of the remembering of one's own unconnected meaning. For it has been shown that connected cognition is not possible without unconnected cognition. Here someone says: If <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (designation-of-the-connected) is maintained by others relying on the memory-presented, then since memory is based on proximity (<s>pratyāsatti</s>), and since proximity is possible for many meanings, and since there is no apprehended distinction among those memory-presented meanings, in '<s>urvāyāṃ pacati</s>' (he cooks on the thigh), cooking would be designated only as connected with the thigh. For since cooking connected with a potter and such has also been cognized, from the memory of that, it would be designated as connected with the thigh too. Similarly, the meaning of 'cooks' has been understood with the instrument of rice-flour and such, so from the memory of that, it would be designated as connected not with rice but [with rice-flour]. But in the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> (designation-then-connection) view, this defect does not arise, since each meaning is separately designated. We reply: First, the cognition of word-meaning from a word cannot be said to be different from memory. Therefore, it must be accepted that it is the remembered meanings themselves that produce the knowledge of connection. And thus the defect is equal [in both views]. If the objection is that words remind meanings, and the reminder-capacity for connection is found in the usage of elders — this defect is equally [applicable] in the other view. And this is not absolute, because — as stated — in the usage of elders, <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> is observed with a supplemented (<s>adhyāhṛta</s>) meaning of fitness (<s>upanaya</s>). If the objection is that words remind many meanings, but we do not know by which one the connection is produced — and in the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> view, the connection-producing capacity naturally belongs to what has been designated — that is wrong. What denotative capacity (<s>abhidhāyakatā</s>) is there beyond reminder-capacity (<s>smārakatva</s>) that would serve as the basis for the determination? If it is said that reminder-capacity is based on proximity, and therefore a denotative capacity distinct from reminder-capacity — characterized by proximity — must be accepted — that is not so, because reminder-capacity itself is observed in the usage of elders, and reminder-capacity is logically established. For the relation of 'making-known-and-what-is-made-known' (<s>pratyāyya-pratyāyakatā</s>) is the relation of 'signified-and-signifier' (<s>vācya-vācakatā</s>); and although for fire-and-smoke and such it is observed as preceded by another relation, for words it is not accepted in that way — rather, the designator-capacity is understood from the very understanding of designator-capacity. Similarly, the reminder-capacity is understood from the very understanding of reminder-capacity — so what need is there of resorting to another proximity? Moreover, this determinate connection (<s>pratiniyatānvayitva</s>) is established only for those who hold the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> view — because what is reminded as having denotative capacity for a meaning connected with another word-meaning is observed in the usage of elders as having that connected meaning alone as its signified. And where supplementation (<s>adhyāhāra</s>) occurs, there too the attainment of designation-of-a-specific-connection through the force of the supplement is known from ordinary experience itself — so there is no fault. Moreover, this much is known: by this word, this meaning is to be designated as connected. There, if it were designated as connected with something else as well, there would be sentence-splitting. And that is not proper when sentence-unity (<s>ekavākyatva</s>) is possible. Thus it has been said: 'When sentence-unity is possible, sentence-splitting is not accepted' [<s>Ślokavārttika</s>, <s>Prakaraṇa Sūtra</s>, verse 9]. Therefore, whenever sentence-unity can somehow be maintained, sentence-splitting is improper. And in ordinary usage, secondary usage (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) and figurative usage (<s>gauṇī vṛtti</s>) are resorted to precisely out of fear of sentence-splitting. Otherwise, why, splitting the sentence and supplementing a suitable alternative meaning, are not all words taken in their primary meanings? Even in the Veda, it is by the force of sentence-unity alone that in <s>arthavādas</s> (laudatory passages), recourse is taken to <s>guṇavāda</s> (treating as a subordinate statement) and such; in the <s>Sammārgādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.1.4], the description of interchange of case-endings; in the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> of the <s>Audumbarādhikaraṇa</s>, somehow resorting to animal-fruit-ness; in the <s>Citrādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 1.4.2], abandoning the established meaning and somehow resorting to name-ness in '<s>pañcadaśānyājyāni bhavanti</s>' (<s>Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa</s> 20.1.1); in the <s>Vājapeyādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 1.4.5], resorting to name-ness precisely out of fear of sentence-splitting; in the <s>Paurṇamāsyādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.2.3], establishing the re-statement-ness of the aggregate when multiple quality-injunctions would lead to sentence-splitting; in the <s>Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.3.11], describing the figurative nature of the word <s>Agnihotra</s> precisely due to the fault of sentence-splitting; in the <s>Grahādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 1.3.7], treating oneness as not intended; in '<s>ardham antarvedi minoti, ardhaṃ bahirvedī</s>' [<s>Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā</s> 3.9.4], resorting to location-based secondary meaning [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 3.7.6]; in the <s>Kṣaumādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 6.1.5], abandoning the injunction of two garments; in the <s>Havirārtyādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 6.4.6], not intending both words; in '<s>vāruṇyā niṣkāsena tuṣaiścāvabhṛthaṃ yanti</s>' [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 7.3.5], abandoning independence; and in the <s>Paryudāsādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 10.8.7], treating the meaning of the negative particle as secondary — and much more is seen. There, if the word being co-expressed, abandoning its own designated meaning, is observed as connected with another — then its sentence-unity would be compromised. It is for this very purpose that it was said: 'The particular meaning to be established by reasoning' — for sentence-unity is the principle (<s>nyāya</s>). In accordance with that, whatever meaning [is proper], that should be accepted for the sentence. In the understanding of word-meaning regulated by convention acquired from the usage of elders, whatever principles are known from the usage of elders as causes for the comprehension of sentence-meaning — without abandoning those, sentence-meanings are to be understood — thus there is no room for any of these objections. Then let there be designation of connection with another word-meaning by the force of sentence-unity through that which is memory-presented; but why would there not also be designation of connection with another meaning that is also self-remembered and consistent with sentence-unity? We reply: Because when <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> is accomplished through just two words, the expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>) is satisfied. If the expectancy is not satisfied, then who indeed would prevent <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> there? For this very reason, when a single word is uttered, among the many meanings that are memory-presented through the connection of word-meaning, the designation of connection is with that meaning alone whose specific distinction is grasped in some way — and when no distinction is grasped, there is simply indetermination (<s>anadhyavasāya</s>) and hence non-cognition. For this very reason, in modified rituals (<s>vikṛti</s>), what is remembered through similarity with the original and reminds one of its own helpful element — it is through that very helpfulness that completion [of the ritual] occurs. Therefore, where the similarity based on the commonality of many properties is most prominent, there alone, because memory is quickly established, is the acceptance of that helpfulness alone. But in <s>darvihomas</s> (ladle-oblations), since there is no distinction among all the original elements due to non-distinction, the distinction cannot be grasped — hence there is simply indetermination regarding the helpfulness of the original, and therefore the postulation of helpfulness is for that alone. Moreover, the comprehension of sentence-meaning is in accordance with the understanding from the usage of elders. There, through the word itself, only that meaning is invariably reminded for a person whose impression of grasping the relation is uncorrupted — and through that alone, the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> of the other word is observed, not through another meaning. For every word invariably reminds its own meaning through the grasping of the relation, not another meaning. And therefore, [the word] produces the knowledge of its own meaning as connected with that — and there is no fault. Moreover, if the acceptance that words produce the knowledge of their own meaning as connected is the very thing through which the knowledge of determinate connection is accomplished, and not otherwise — then let the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> capacity of words also be postulated.

children.translated_text: Here is the reply to that:
A word that designates the connected is itself a designator of the connection.
Otherwise, the meaning would be connected but not designated — therefore, through the meaning in its connected form, the connection is accepted.

children.text: taṃ vinā tadasambhavāditi, nāparā tadviṣayā padānāṃ śaktiḥ kalpanīyā // 16 //
children.translated_text: Since without that [connection], it [the connected meaning] is not possible — therefore, no separate capacity of words regarding that [connection] needs to be postulated. // 16 //

Since the connection has been grasped along with the meaning, no other capacity is required. // 16 // This <s>Bhāṣya</s> was stated in anticipation of an objection. What was the anticipated objection? If words designate connected meanings, then they should not designate the connection itself. To establish that, another capacity of words would have to be postulated.
But how is that connection grasped along with the meaning? To this he says:
Since the connection, being cognized, enables one to cognize what is connected,
It is said to be like a <s>jāti</s> (universal) or a <s>vyakti</s> (particular) within the meaning. // 17 //

children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>) uses the word '<s>vākyārtha</s>' (sentence-meaning) to refer to the connection.
But in the Veda, we shall say that the sentence-meaning is the connected [meaning] whose nature is the unprecedented [ritual effect] (<s>apūrva</s>).
And since its own nature is not otherwise known, it is this alone that has the status of sentence-meaning.
By the reasoning thus stated, connected denotation (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>) has been specifically established. [17]

For what is connected (<s>anvita</s>) is that which possesses connection (<s>anvaya</s>). Without the cognition of connection, it would not be cognized at all — only its bare nature would be [known]. And that is not called 'connected.' Therefore, one who cognizes the connection itself cognizes the connected. Just as one who cognizes the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) cognizes the universal (<s>jāti</s>). But here is the distinction: since only what possesses connection is called 'connected,' the connection too enters into the denotation. [But] the universal is not the very nature of the individual; rather, the universal, being a different form (<s>ākārāntara</s>) of the individual, is distinct from it. If, however, it is the generic form (<s>ākṛti</s>) that is denoted by the word, then the individual too does not enter into the denotation; rather, the universal, being the form, though distinct from the individual by nature, does not experience cognition without the individual — and to this extent alone does the analogy hold, not entirely. [Objection:] But how can the individual, which enters into a single cognition [along with the universal], be non-denoted? For denotedness means being the object of the cognition produced by the word, and the individual too has that status — so how can it be non-denoted? Listen with attention — [this is] the very essence of the <s>Prābhākara</s> position: True, the universal and individual are objects of a single awareness. Nevertheless, this must be considered: how does this awareness arise as having both as its objects? Is it the operation of the word alone that accounts for its having both as objects? Or does the word operate with respect to its own nature for the universal alone, while for the individual — since the universal, being non-denotative of the individual, is incapable of conveying the individual in any other way — [the individual is conveyed through the universal]? Now, among infinite individuals, since grasping the relation [of word and individual] is impossible, and since even regarding individuals characterized by the generic form, although grasping the relation is easy, still since the individual is known from the word only as possessing that form, and since there is no cause for the universal being merely an indicative mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), and since in the absence of a distinctive sign (<s>cihna</s>) the connection with action is impossible — the operation of the word is determined to be in the generic form (<s>ākṛti</s>). Therefore the generic form does not convey the individual; rather, the word itself, by being denotative of that [generic form], is said to be 'from the generic form to the individual.' Thus, for connected denotation, since the connection is grasped through the meaning itself, this connection is not separately denoted. Therefore the denotation is intertwined (<s>vyatiṣakta</s>), not a denotation of the intertwining [itself]; while isolated (<s>niṣkṛṣṭa</s>) denotation does not occur — for intertwining is understood from the intertwined, since denotation of the intertwined is impossible without intertwining. The meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>-words is this: words, having denoted the connected [meaning], cease their operation and do not separately denote the connection. But those who cognize the connected also cognize the connection.

children.translated_text: For their refutation:
Those who declare the denotable of words to be connected with the universal alone —
how would connection with a fixed specific obtain for them? [18]

Those proponents of connected denotation who say thus — 'The word denotes its meaning through the relation established in the usage of the learned, and the ascertainment of relation is through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>); and these two are not possible regarding specific connection (<s>viśeṣānvaya</s>); for the verb is observed in concomitance with action in general, not deviating from any [specific] causal factor' — to refute them:

children.text: darśitamidaṃ---viśeṣānvaye 'pyākāṅkṣā-sannidhi-yogyatopādhivaśena sambandhagrahaṇaṃ sukaramiti, tadabhidhāyakataiva yuktā padānām /
children.translated_text: This has been shown: even in the case of specific connection, the grasping of relation is easy by virtue of the conditions of <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy), <s>sannidhi</s> (proximity), and <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness); therefore, the denotative capacity of words for that [specific connection] is proper.

children.text: yadi cāsau neṣyate, tadā vākyārthapratipattireva nopapadyate, viśeṣānvayarūpatvādvākyārthasrū // 18 //
children.translated_text: And if that is not accepted, then even the cognition of sentence-meaning would be impossible, since sentence-meaning has the nature of specific connection. [18]

children.translated_text: [Objection:] But [one may argue that] the universal connection, once stated, will draw in the specific connection, since the universal, being incapable of being cognized without a specific, necessarily implies the cognition of specific connection. To this he says:
Even though the specific is drawn in, like individual and universal,
a determined specific is not cognized in that manner. [19]

Just as the universal, even while drawing in the individual, does not draw in a specifically determined individual, so here too — since a determined specific is not obtained, the cognition of sentence-meaning having the nature of a determined specific connection is impossible. [19]

children.text: tenā'kāṅkṣite yogye ca viśeṣe padāntareṇa1213 sannidhāpite 'pi, tadanvayabodhakapramāṇābhāvāt tadanvayo na pratīyetaiva /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even when an expected and fit specific is brought into proximity by another word, since there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for conveying the connection with it, the connection would not be cognized at all.
Hence <s>ākāṅkṣā</s>, <s>sannidhi</s>, and <s>yogyatā</s> would be entirely useless.

children.text: viśeṣānvayavādinastu mate sambandhagrahaṇaṃ pratyupādhitvena praviṣṭāni tāni 1214vākyārthapratipattāvupayujyante // 20 //
children.translated_text: But in the view of the proponent of specific connection, since those [three conditions] have entered as auxiliary conditions for the grasping of relation, they are useful in the cognition of sentence-meaning. [20]

In the view of the proponents of universal-connected-denotation, words have their capacities terminating in that [universal connection] alone, and the capacity of word-meanings to convey connection is not accepted.
He says thus:
Having entered as auxiliary conditions in the <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) for the cognition of relation,
in the theory of specific connection, <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness) and such are helpful. [21]

children.text: padānāṃ padārthāntarasambaddhassvārtho bodhya ityasyāṃ vyupattāvupādhitvena yogyatvādikamanupraviṣṭaṃ1215 viśeṣānvitābhidhānavādipakṣe upakārakam, na sāmānyānvitābhidhāne-iti darśitaṃ prāk // 21 //
children.translated_text: In the <s>vyutpatti</s> that words convey their own meaning as connected with another word-meaning — in the position of the proponent of specific connected denotation, <s>yogyatā</s> and such, having entered as auxiliary conditions, are helpful; not so in universal connected denotation — this was shown previously. [21]
He states a further objection:
Moreover, when the association of the universal is already established by the force of things themselves,
those who wish to accept that as what is denoted have labored the word in vain. [22]

children.text: kriyā-kārakasvabhāvālocanayāpi kārakamātreṇa, kriyāmātreṇa cānvayāvagamasiddheḥ, vṛthā sāmānyānvayābhidhāyakatā śabdasyāṅgīkriyata iti // 22 // 1216//
children.translated_text: Since, by considering the nature of action and causal factors alone, the cognition of connection is accomplished through the mere causal factor and the mere action, the denotative capacity of the word for universal connection is accepted in vain. [22]

or the verbal root alone, or the unconnected word-meanings,
or the cognition of universal connection — which is the cause of the cognition of sentence-meaning?

children.translated_text: How then is the inherent nature (<s>autpattikatva</s>) of the sentence and sentence-meaning established? Through the usage of the learned.
True.
It has been said: 'through that which has parts' [i.e., through words].

children.text: iti mahāmahopādhyāyaśrīmacchālikanāthamiśrapraṇītāyāṃ prakaraṇapañcikāyāṃ savṛttikāyā vākyārthamātrṛkāyā upoddhāto nāma prathamaḥ paricchedassamāptaḥ //
children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrīmac-Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, with the commentary, the first section (<s>pariccheda</s>) named '<s>Upoddhāta</s>' (Prelude) of the <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s> (Matrix of Sentence-Meaning) is concluded.

Words alone, endowed with parts, are capable of conveying sentence-meaning — proponents of specific connection [hold this]. Thus the summary verses. And so it has been said: Does a word have a meaning? Indeed it does.
[Section 2]
SECTION 2
Now the second section of the <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s> with commentary.

children.text: 1218upoddhātabhūtamanvitābhidhānaṃ prasādhya, apūrvaṃ kāryaṃ vedavākyānāmartha iti sādhayitukāmaḥ pūrvapakṣaṃ tāvadāha---
children.translated_text: Having established connected denotation (<s>anvitābhidhāna</s>) as the prelude, wishing to establish that the unprecedented [ritual effect] (<s>apūrva</s>) as duty (<s>kārya</s>) is the meaning of Vedic sentences, he first states the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s>:
[Objection:] Now, given that words require <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) in order to denote meaning,
how do the optative (<s>liṅ</s>) and other [suffixes] express an effect (<s>kārya</s>) not knowable by any other means of knowledge? [1]
The <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prior position) regarding <s>kārya</s> (duty/effect).

children.translated_text: Because that very [objection] is unestablished. Only action (<s>kriyā</s>) as duty (<s>kārya</s>) is understood from Vedic sentences, and through the force of <s>vyutpatti</s>, the unprecedented <s>apūrva</s> as an effect is cognized merely as an unwarranted mental fabrication.

children.text: tasmādagṛhītasambandho liṅādiḥ kathamapūrvaṃ kāryamabhidhatte, tathā ca kathaṃ 1221tadvākyārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, how can <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes, whose relation [with <s>apūrva</s>] has not been grasped, denote the unprecedented effect? And how then can that be the sentence-meaning?
For only the denoted meaning can be the sentence-meaning. [1]

In the <s>Apūrvādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Sūtra</s> 2.1.2], it was stated that the meaning of <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes is <s>apūrva</s> (the unprecedented). And <s>apūrva</s> is accepted as unfit for other means of knowledge. But regarding what is unfit for other means of knowledge, grasping the [word-meaning] relation is impossible, since that presupposes the prior grasping of the relatum. For the capacity of the word regarding a specific meaning is inferred from observing practical usage regarding that specific meaning. And when <s>apūrva</s> is not accessible to any <s>pramāṇa</s>, neither through direct experience nor through inference can the <s>vyutpatti</s> regarding it be accomplished. Thus, since there is no specific practical activity regarding <s>apūrva</s> that could serve as the basis for grasping the word-meaning relation regarding it, how is the <s>vyutpatti</s> of <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes regarding <s>apūrva</s> possible?
And thus:
How can other words too, in some [context], denote their own meaning
as connected with that unseen [<s>apūrva</s>], which is far removed from the path of <s>vyutpatti</s>? [2]

children.text: tasminnapratīyamāne tadanvitasyāpratīteḥ, tatra saṃbandhāvadhāraṇānupapatterdūranirastaṃ śabdāntarāṇāṃ tadanvitasvārthabodhakatvamiti // 2 //
children.translated_text: Since, when that [<s>apūrva</s>] is not cognized, what is connected with it is also not cognized, and since the ascertainment of relation regarding it is impossible, the capacity of other words to convey their own meaning as connected with it is entirely precluded. [2]

It is replied: When, for example, a single elder speaks,
'<s>Caitra</s>, fetch water!' — <s>Caitra</s> fetches water. [3]

children.translated_text: Since [activity] is understood when that [object] exists — but for me, that is made known through another means of knowledge — this is the difference between us.

children.text: tena yat buddhvā pravṛttirmama, tadasyānena śabdena boddhyata iti śabdasya pravṛttihetubhūtārthāvabodhakatāmavadhārayati // 3 1//
children.translated_text: Therefore, that having known which I act — that same thing is made known to this [learner] by this word. Thus, he determines the capacity of words to convey the meaning that is the cause of activity. [31]

Then one who wishes to learn [the language], observing [this], understands thus: the activity of that elder towards a specific meaning, immediately upon hearing a sentence containing <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes, [must have been] preceded by a cognition [of the meaning] — this activity of his, being of such nature, is self-directed. And [one who wishes to learn language observes:] That cognition, which precedes this activity, whose content is just such [a specific connected meaning], is produced by the word alone — since there is no other cause for it. For the elder was not previously cognizing through perception or inference the fetching of water by <s>Caitra</s>. And this cognition has as its content the specific connected [meaning] — namely, <s>Caitra</s>'s fetching of water. And no word other than <s>liṅ</s> and such suffixes can produce such cognition with such content. For words like '<s>Caitra</s>,' '<s>jala</s>' (water), etc. are observed in concomitance with their respective meanings in other sentences as well, and are not invariably concomitant with the productive force (<s>bhāvanā</s>) as their meaning. Therefore, since the productive force is the exclusive meaning of <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes, and since the sentence-meaning — being the action of a specific agent with specific instruments regarding a specific object — is comprehended from the sentence, the <s>vyutpatti</s> of all words including <s>liṅ</s> is accomplished.

children.translated_text: And thus they say:
"In which [category] — substance (<s>dravya</s>) and the like — would self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) be included?
Even when analyzed threefold, the determination of its being a purificatory rite (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is [upheld].

He, acting by himself independently of words, inquires: 'What did I know when I acted?' By 'on another occasion' — the state prior to the acquisition of word-meaning (<s>vyutpatti</s>) is referred to. What was cognized by the unlearned child in himself as the cause of activity, that very same thing is postulated as the cause for the learned person as well — nothing else; this is the meaning. Refutation of the impulsion-nature (<s>bhāvanatva</s>) of word and word-operation: Therefore, the view that the word itself, in the form of the injunctive suffix (<s>liṅ</s>) and the like, is the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) as the cause of activity, or that its operation is so — is refuted. Since neither of those is observed by the child in himself as the cause of activity. And due to their extreme weakness, these two views are not presented and refuted directly. For if the very form of the injunctive suffix (<s>liṅ</s>) etc. were the impeller, then everyone who hears it would invariably act — but this is not observed, since some act sometimes [and not always]. As for the view that the operation of the injunctive suffix is the cause of activity — let the gods accept that; we mortals with fleshly eyes are not capable of fathoming such a domain of proof. Presentation of <s>śābdabhāvanā</s> (verbal impulsion): What is this verbal impulsion (<s>śābdabhāvanā</s>)? We reply: It is in the form of the operation of the injunctive suffix and the like; it is favorable to the coming-into-being of human activity; it is postulated as an impulsion (<s>preraṇā</s>) having the cognition [of the injunction] as its instrument, endowed with the 'what-is-to-be-done' aspect (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) characterized by the laudatory praise (<s>prāśastya</s>) expressed in explanatory passages (<s>arthavāda</s>). 'Through the injunction of self-study (<s>svādhyāyādhyayana</s>), all prescribing [passages] and the self (<s>ātman</s>) — designated by the word <s>svādhyāya</s> — are enjoined: "he should bring into being."' (<s>Tantravārttika</s>, p. 114). There, upon the query 'for what purpose,' human activity is connected. Upon the expectancy 'by what means,' the knowledge of the injunction itself is accepted as the instrument, by fitness. For the verbal impulsion, being known, produces activity; and by fitness, the knowledge of laudatory praise arising from explanatory passages (<s>arthavāda</s>) enters the 'what-is-to-be-done' aspect. For the injunctive capacity, when failing, is supported by the knowledge of laudatory praise. And the objective impulsion (<s>arthabhāvanā</s>) — which is the object [of verbal impulsion], having the form of human operation, delimited by the thing-to-be-brought-about such as heaven etc., having as its instrument the material-means (<s>karaṇa</s>) obtained from <s>Vedic</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, and customary usage, and expressible by the same verbal cognition — serves as its content. Refutation of this: That is wrong. There is no evidence whatsoever that the injunctive suffix and the like have such an operation. If one says 'human activity occurring immediately after the injunctive suffix is the evidence' — no, since activity is not observed elsewhere [i.e., in non-Vedic contexts] as being based on that [verbal impulsion]. For activity is observed to be based on something [specific]; having observed that very thing, one can infer it, but not a verbal operation whose causal status has never been previously established. If one claims that the injunctive suffix itself is the evidence — that is mere boldness, since what has not been grasped in relation [to its meaning] cannot be a designator. For when the relatum has not been determined, there is a failure of the understanding of relation. And how, then, are all prescribing passages and the self enjoined through the injunction of self-study (<s>svādhyāyādhyayana</s>)? The injunction impels the person toward the objective impulsion (<s>arthabhāvanā</s>). And one who is impelled by something is enjoined by it. But it is impossible for non-conscious injunctions to serve as enjoiners. If [it is said that] they are not [directly] enjoined — that too is untenable, since in verbal impulsions, all words are already agents by their own nature, and there is no need for enjoinment. If non-personal [injunctions] are not enjoined to impel, but rather to convey meaning — that too does not work, since the same [problem of] requiring an enjoinee applies there equally. And the injunction of self-study is accepted as prescribing the study of syllables as its meaning. And thus they say:
And in the enumeration of what is to be purified, the purification of syllables is indeed appropriate.

children.text: svādhyāyāṃ hi sphuṭaṃ karma sākṣātsaṃskriyate ci saḥ" //
children.translated_text: For in self-study, the ritual act is clearly and directly purified."

children.translated_text: As it has been said:
"The grasping of the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) and the impulsion (<s>bhāvanā</s>) by a single cognition has been established.
From the verbal root's meaning, the relation is first determined."

And the purificatory injunction does not enjoin the thing to be purified, since its subsidiary status (<s>śeṣitva</s>) is established by another means of knowledge. But the purificatory injunction, which culminates in purification, would not postulate an effect for the thing to be purified. And since the self is both enjoined and not enjoined by the injunction of study — the impossibility of both alternatives. Examination of whether human activity is the thing-to-be-brought-about (<s>bhāvya</s>): How is human activity its thing-to-be-brought-about? Not, first, because of its immediate production, since there would be the consequence of the knowledge of the injunction not being an instrument. For human activity would then be the fruit of the action. And an action does not require an instrument for producing its own fruit. Nor does walking require an instrument for bringing about conjunction and disjunction. One might think: the injunctive word, having generated the knowledge of the injunction, then initiates its own operation in the form of impulsion, assisted by the instrument [i.e., the knowledge]. And there is no absence of instrumentality, since instrumentality consists in the accomplishment of the action. That is extraordinary [i.e., absurd]. For no object's own cognition is observed as a cause of production. Refutation of the laudatory-praise-knowledge as the 'what-is-to-be-done' aspect: Thus, the 'what-is-to-be-done' status (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) of the laudatory praise expressed in <s>arthavāda</s> is also subverted. For its being so is [only] through fitness. And in the origination of impulsion performed by the word, the fitness of that [laudatory praise] to serve as the favor-granting instrument of the cognition cannot be ascertained. But in activity performed by a person, there could be the ascertainment of its fitness, since activity in what is praised is observed in people. One might think: if activity in the unpraised is impossible, then impulsion itself is not possible. That is wrong. It is well known in the world that the accomplishment of an action does not depend on the possibility of a result; rather, the accomplishment of the result depends on the accomplishment of the action. For this very reason, in that view, even when there is no result, since impulsion is established, there would be activity. If the result too is part of the 'what-is-to-be-done' aspect, like laudatory praise, then in its absence too, impulsion would not be accomplished — then let the result alone serve as the complement of the 'what-is-to-be-done' aspect; what need is there of laudatory praise? True, it exists also [as a complement] — so it should not be abandoned. But then, when laudatory praise is not heard [in a given <s>Vedic</s> passage], let there be no dependence on it. And consequently, the postulation of its extension (<s>atideśa</s>) and so on becomes untenable; the postulation of instrument-and-what-is-to-be-done for a bare injunction — like the <s>darvihoma</s> — is also mere postulation. And the <s>darvihoma</s> example is unestablished, since even there, only the assistance of the 'what-is-to-be-done' consisting of the <s>Vedic</s> material, deity, <s>Smṛti</s>-and-custom-derived sipping (<s>ācamana</s>) and the like is intended. For the same thing cannot both be the helper and the helped with respect to itself. Now, if the word does indeed perform impulsion, but activity does not arise from that alone, but rather when there is knowledge of it — then let activity be the result of knowledge alone, not the result of impulsion, since it exists when [knowledge] exists and does not exist when it does not. And thus it is established that <s>śābdabhāvanā</s> (verbal impulsion) is not the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>). Moreover, sound (<s>śabda</s>) is a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>) — this must be accepted by one who holds the doctrine of contact-making sense organs (<s>prāpyakāri indriya</s>). Otherwise, since the ear, which is space, cannot reach sound, and since contact (<s>prāpti</s>) takes the form of either conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) or inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), and since conjunction — being generated by the action of one, both, or another conjunction — is impossible between sound and space (both being substances that do not act on each other), by elimination, inherence is the contact; thus, sound is a quality of space. And its operation is not possible, since operations belong to substances. How then is the denotation-operation (<s>abhidhāna</s>) of sound relied upon? Let it be heard how: When the cognition regarding meaning arises in oneself immediately after the cognition regarding the word, when that is spoken of as caused by the word, then it is called 'designative' (<s>ābhidhānika</s>). For there can be agency even when the operation belongs to something else, like the motion [attributed to] the self. So there is no fault. And how is that [word] the object of both the word-operation and the objective impulsion (<s>arthabhāvanā</s>)? Because they are expressible by a single verbal cognition.
Slokavārttika, ch. 7, verses 79-80

— thus.
That is not so.
In this view, the denotation of <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive activity) by the verbal suffix is difficult to establish — hence:

The doubt regarding whether verbal forms (<s>ākhyāta</s>) denote <s>bhāvanā</s>:
But it is objected: the denotation of <s>bhāvanā</s> by all verbal forms is determined from their co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with <s>karoti</s> (does/makes).
For thus: <s>bhāvanā</s> is the instigating activity of the agent of the meaning to become (<s>bhavati</s>) — that itself is effort (<s>kṛti</s>).
Because what is being brought into being is precisely what is being done, and that [brought-about thing] is the object of effort.
From the observation of questions and answers such as What did he do? He cooked. What is he doing? He is cooking. What will he do? He will cook — it is understood that the meaning of <s>karoti</s> (doing) is expressed by all verbal forms.
Otherwise, when a question concerns the meaning of <s>karoti</s>, the answer would be untenable.
Since the meaning of <s>karoti</s> is not understood from roots ending in -<s>dhañ</s> etc., but is understood in the presence of the verbal suffix (<s>ākhyāta-pratyaya</s>) — it is determined that this meaning belongs to the verbal suffixes alone.

Refutation of that:
That is wrong.
If the meaning of the question What is he doing? (<s>kiṃ karoti</s>) is What is it that he is doing? and the answer is He is cooking (<s>pacati</s>), then <s>pacati</s> functions in the meaning He does cooking (<s>pākaṃ karoti</s>).
And thus the denotation of the <s>karoti</s>-meaning by verbal forms would be established.
But this is not so.
For when the specific activity denoted by the verbal root is not yet known, the question is about that very specific activity, and He is cooking is the answer.
And thus, the denotation by verbal forms of a <s>karoti</s>-meaning distinct from the root-meaning is not established.
All root-meanings, being favorable to the coming-into-being of something previously non-existent, have acquired the status of the <s>karoti</s>-meaning, and can therefore be asked about and indicated by <s>karoti</s> — so the question and answer concern that specific [root-meaning] alone.
Moreover, since the question and answer are accounted for even as having the specific activity denoted by the root as their domain, the denotation by verbal forms of a <s>karoti</s>-meaning beyond that cannot be maintained.
Furthermore, for agents like <s>Devadatta</s> etc. who act with deliberate effort, the question and answer would work [even if the question only concerns] the difference of activities.
But if the question What is he doing? concerns a <s>karoti</s>-meaning distinct [from the root], and the answer is He is going (<s>gacchati</s>), then since there would be no acknowledgment of an activity distinct from going, the answer would simply be untenable.
But if [the question] concerns a specific root-meaning, then even there it is tenable.
If one says: Even there, conjunction and disjunction are the root-meaning, while bodily movement (<s>parispanda</s>) is the suffix-meaning — even then, since the possibility of an activity distinct from the root-meaning exists, there is no impossibility.
That is not so. Because bodily movement itself is what is denoted by the root <s>gam</s>- (to go).
For thus: the root <s>gam</s>- is not used for mere conjunction or disjunction — since it is not used when a hawk separates from or conjoins with a post.
Nor for both — since there would be the unwanted usage for a hawk that flies up and lands on a post.
If one says: conjunction and disjunction produced in a single moment of action are what <s>gam</s>- denotes —
Then let the action itself be what is denoted; why is it placed in the category of qualifiers (<s>upādhi</s>)?
For in this way, the encumbrance of depending on a qualifier is simply avoided.
Moreover, the determination of word-meaning comes from the usage of the learned (<s>vṛddha-vyavahāra</s>).
And the usage of the learned is not untenable without the verbal forms denoting <s>bhāvanā</s>.
As for the question-and-answer [argument], it belongs to a time subsequent to the knowledge of the relation, and therefore the determination of the relata should not be based on it.
When the usage of verbal forms is accounted for by their merely expressing the number of the agent etc., no additional denotation can be posited.
Moreover, in <s>pākaṃ karoti devadattaḥ</s> (Devadatta does cooking), the word <s>pāka</s> conveys the cooking-meaning, <s>karoti</s> expresses the personal effort corresponding to it, while the verbal suffix merely states the singular number of the agent — thus its denotation of only that much is established.
Therefore it is reasonable that elsewhere too it functions in the same way.
Thus, the explanation of <s>pacati devadattaḥ</s> (Devadatta cooks) as <s>pākaṃ karoti</s> (he does cooking) —
That too is untenable.
Because in <s>pacati</s>, the explanation works by taking up through <s>karoti</s> as the stem the personal effort through whose relation the cooking-meaning is what is to be accomplished (<s>sādhya</s>).
Even where there is no [personal] effort, as in <s>ratho gamanaṃ karoti</s> (the chariot does going), the usage of <s>karoti</s> should be seen as figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>), meant to show that going is what is to be accomplished.
Since both options are equally viable.

Presentation and refutation of <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>'s view:
But one who says that in ordinary usage like <s>devadatta odanaṃ pacati</s> (Devadatta cooks rice), the denotation of effort distinct from the root-meaning is established from usage, and therefore verbal forms denote that [effort] —
He should be instructed thus:
Child! Do you not know that word-meaning is that which is obtainable by no other means?
Here, since the understanding of effort is accounted for even through the implication of the root-meaning, the denotation of effort by verbal forms cannot be resorted to.

Determination that only injunctive forms denote effort (<s>kṛti</s>):
But the <s>Prābhākaras</s> too accept <s>bhāvanā</s>-denotation — how then [do they explain this] for the verbal suffix?
We reply: we do not accept that all verbal suffixes denote <s>bhāvanā</s>. Rather, only the injunctive (<s>liṅ</s>) etc., which express what is to be done (<s>kārya</s>), are accepted as denoting effort (<s>kṛti</s>), because the obligatory (<s>kārya</s>) cannot be expressed otherwise without expressing effort.
For what is obligatory is related to effort, and without expressing effort, it would not be expressed.
For there is no possibility that effort is not expressed while the obligation is expressed.
If it be thought: Just as in <s>daṇḍī</s> (staff-bearer) the suffix does not denote the staff, yet the cognition of a person qualified by the staff arises — so here too [obligation could arise without effort being denoted] —
That is not so. Even there, without the staff being cognized, there is no cognition of its possessor. And there the word <s>daṇḍa</s> (staff) serves as the stem and is its indicator.
But that is not possible here, since roots are not restricted to denoting personal effort.
For it is a conscious person who understands the obligation through the injunctive etc.
And he cannot understand obligation related to his own effort by himself — therefore the expression of his effort must be sought.
And his effort has the form of exertion (<s>prayatna</s>).
And if there is absolutely no experience of it, then its denoters do not [function] — so this is not a case for the <s>daṇḍin</s>-analogy.
If it be thought: Just as the injunctive merely denotes the number of the agent etc., and the agent etc. are understood through the implication of the action — so here too the action implies the effort, and the injunctive need not denote it —
That is not so. Even though effort is implied by the action that is the root-meaning, how can the unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>) [obligation] be understood as dependent on it [the effort]?
When effort is [explicitly] expressed, then the unprecedented [obligation], being perceived as delimited by effort, is understood as dependent on effort for its accomplishment — not otherwise.
And the unprecedented [obligation] in its bare form, undelimited by effort, is not capable of implying effort.
For an entity is implied only when its relation [to the implying entity] is already known.
And without the word [expressing effort], there is no cause for understanding the relation of the unprecedented [obligation] with effort.
Therefore, how could it [the obligation] imply effort?

Therefore, for those [injunctive suffixes] that express the unprecedented obligation, the expression of effort must necessarily be resorted to — this has been established most carefully in the <s>Viṣayakaraṇīya</s>. But enough of excessive digression.

Let alone actions in the world such as going and not-going —
even suckling at the breast, an action that produces satisfaction,

Now, I do not engage in action having understood mere action, nor mere result, nor the mere relation of action and result.
Even upon understanding the means-end relation of action and result, engagement does not follow.
Because one does not engage in eating that causes satisfaction if it is past or present [and not being performed]. Even regarding a future means of satisfaction, if there is no performance — as in the case of one called <s>sāmudra-vidā</s> [who knows but does not act].
The understanding of the person's inclination, though suspected as a cause of engagement, is set aside since the one who wishes to learn the linguistic convention [seeks] independent engagement.
Rather, having understood the obligatory nature (<s>kāryatā</s>), I have engaged. Realizing this is my obligation — I have engaged in all cases.
as long as this is my obligation is not determined —
there was never any engagement of mine in that.

brahmasiddhikato matenā'śaṅkā /
