iṣṭasādhanataiva tu kāryatā, na parā kācit, saiva pravṛttiheturvidhirucyate /

children.translated_text: Thus he says:
The means to the desired is what the wise call injunction (<s>vidhi</s>);
for from that [alone comes] determination etc., not causelessly, nor from [mere verbal] denotation.

An objection according to the view of the <s>Brahmasiddhi</s>:
Here another says: True, engagement arises from the understanding of obligation alone.
But obligation is nothing other than being a means to the desired (<s>iṣṭa-sādhanatā</s>); that itself, being the cause of engagement, is called injunction (<s>vidhi</s>).
p. 115] — thus.
Similarly: Since actions are not the desired means for a person, there is another impeller;
they declare <s>dharma</s> to be the cause of engagement and call it the injunctive command (<s>pravartanā</s>).

<s>Vidhiviveka</s>, verse 26, p. 243
— thus.
When the action is a desired means for the agent, the worldly cognition is: this is to be done;
but regarding the opposite, [the cognition is]: this is not to be done — therefore, in that domain —

Refutation of that:
Here, first, this much should be said: the past and present [actions] do have the character of being means to the desired, yet they are not determined as obligatory.
Therefore, obligation (<s>kāryatā</s>) is one thing, and being a means to the desired (<s>iṣṭa-sādhanatā</s>) is another.

children.text: tathā pravṛttirapi tanmātrāvagamāyattā na bhavatītyupekṣyaiva tāvat taṃ, phalasādhanatā---kāryatayorbhedaṃ vinirdiśati---
children.translated_text: Similarly, engagement too does not depend on the understanding of that [means-to-desired] alone. Setting that aside for now, he states the difference between being-a-means-to-the-result (<s>phala-sādhanatā</s>) and obligation (<s>kāryatā</s>):

children.text: 1254phalasādhanatā nāma yā sā naiva ca kāryatā /
children.translated_text: Being a means to the result is one thing, and obligation is another;
obligation is being accomplishable through effort (<s>kṛti-sādhyatva</s>), while being a means to the result
is being instrumental (<s>karaṇatva</s>) in producing the result — these two differ from each other.
Even though both are located in a single entity, there is nonetheless a difference in their essential nature.

children.text: tadeva hi vastu phalaṃ pratyupāyabhāvātphalasādhanamityucyate, kṛtyadhīnātmalābhatayā ca kāryamiti // 7 //
children.translated_text: For that very entity is called a means to the result because of its being an instrument with respect to the result, and obligatory because of its dependence on effort for its realization.
Why is the understanding of obligation limited to means-to-the-desired alone, and not elsewhere? To this he says:

children.text: kintu svayaṃ kleśarūpaṃ karma yatkāryatāṃ vrajet // 8 //
children.translated_text: Rather, action that is by nature toilsome — that becomes obligatory.
Being a means to the result is the cause of that [obligation]; hence obligation
invariably accompanies the existence of that [means-to-result], and manifests precisely then.

tatra na tāvatsvayaṃ sukharūpaṃ karma, sukhasādhanamapi cenna syāt, na tasya kṛtiṃ prati prādhānyāvagamo1257 ghaṭate /
ataḥ karmasu kāryatvāvagamaḥ phalasādhanatāvagamanibandhana iti, jñāpakakoṭiniviṣṭā phalasādhanatā 1258kāryatāmanurudhyate, na tvasau tadātmaiva /
tathā cāsādhanasyāpi sukhasyaivāsti kāryatā /
sukhaṃ hi sarvaḥ kāryatayāvaiti, na tasya phalasādhanatāmapekṣate /
tena phalasādhanatottīrṇakāryatāvagamena me pravṛttiriti niścitya, vyutpitsamānaścaitraṃ pravarttamānaṃ dṛṣṭvānuminoti--caitro 'pi kāryabodhātpravartate---iti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, having determined 'My activity is based on the cognition of what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>) that transcends the means to fruit,' the one seeking conventional understanding, seeing <s>Caitra</s> acting, infers: '<s>Caitra</s> too acts from the cognition of what-is-to-be-done.'

children.text: caitrasya 1259pravṛttiḥ--dharmiṇī, kāryabodhapūrvikā--iti sādhyo dharmaḥ, buddhipūrvakatve sati pravṛttitvānmadīyapravṛttivaditi /
children.translated_text: <s>Caitra</s>'s activity is the subject (<s>dharmin</s>); 'preceded by cognition of what-is-to-be-done' is the property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>) — because it is activity involving prior cognition, like my own activity.
And the optative (<s>liṅ</s>) and other [suffixes], as designators of the meaning that is the cause of activity, designate precisely what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>),
since it is that very thing, once cognized, that is the immediate cause of activity. [9]

For actions are by nature causes of the production of suffering.
The understanding of their obligatory nature (<s>kāryatā</s>) depends on the understanding of their being means to a result (<s>phala-sādhanatā</s>).
For obligation is not merely being of a nature dependent on effort for accomplishment; rather, what is called obligatory is that which, being the principal [motivation] for effort, has its existence dependent on effort.
And that which is principal for effort is that with reference to which effort operates.
Now, the operation of effort is not tenable with reference to suffering, or a cause of suffering, nor with reference to what is neither suffering nor a cause of suffering.
Rather, [it operates] with reference to pleasure, or a cause of pleasure.
Now, action itself is not of the nature of pleasure; and if it were not a means to pleasure either, the understanding of its being principal for effort would not work.
Therefore, the understanding of obligation in actions depends on the understanding of their being means to a result. Thus, being-a-means-to-the-result, being in the category of an indicator (<s>jñāpaka</s>), accompanies obligation — but it is not identical with it.
And thus, even pleasure that is not a means [to anything else] does have obligatory nature.
For everyone understands pleasure as obligatory; one does not require its being a means to a result [for that understanding].

children.translated_text:
Although desire (<s>icchā</s>) is the cause of activity, still it is not what is designated by the optative and such. Because the cognition of it is not required for activity. For once arisen, it is the cause of activity — not once cognized.
But even so, how is the conventional understanding of the optative and such in what-is-to-be-done [established]? To this he says:
Just as other words are conventionally understood in their own meanings
through the method of agreement and difference (<s>āvāpa-uddhāra</s>), so too the optative and such in what-is-to-be-done. [10]

Upon hearing a sentence containing the optative and such, having inferred the specific cognition of what-is-to-be-done from the activity that corresponds to it, one determines the causal role of the sentence.

children.text: tatrāpi 1262kor'thaḥ kena 1263śabdenābhihita iti vivecane, liṅānadyāvāpe1264 kāryāvagatidarśanāt, taduddhāre cādarśanāt, ta eva kāryāvagatiṃ kurvantīti śabdāntaravalliṅādīnāṃ kāryavācakatvavyutpattisiddhiḥ // 10 //
children.translated_text: There too, in the discrimination of which meaning is designated by which word, since the cognition of what-is-to-be-done is observed when the optative and such are included (<s>āvāpa</s>), and not observed when they are excluded (<s>uddhāra</s>), it is they alone that produce the cognition of what-is-to-be-done — thus, like other words, the conventional understanding of the optative and such as designators of what-is-to-be-done is established. [10]

children.text:
nanu lokavyavahārāt liṅādayo vācakatayā vyutpādyamānāṃ praiṣādiṣvevavacakatayā vyutpattimarhanti /
tatraiva teṣāṃ prayogadarśanādityaśaṅkyā'ha---

children.translated_text: For it is what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>) alone that, by the speakers who are superior, equal, or inferior,
receives the designation of command (<s>praiṣa</s>) and such, due to the difference in relation to the person to be prompted. [11]

But the optative and such, being conventionally understood as designators from worldly usage, deserve conventional understanding only as designators of commands (<s>praiṣa</s>) and such — since their use is observed only there. Anticipating this objection, he says:

children.text: pravarttyapuruṣāpekṣayā jyāyasā vaktrā pratipādyamānaṃ kāryaṃ praiṣa iti vyapadiśyate /
children.translated_text: What-is-to-be-done, when presented by a superior speaker in relation to the person to be prompted, is designated as a command (<s>praiṣa</s>).
When by an equal —

children.text: dya'mantraṇaṃ, hīnenādhyeṣaṇamiti, praiṣādipratipādakā api liṅādayaḥ 1266kāryameva pratipādanti, nār'thāntaram // 11 //
children.translated_text: it is invitation (<s>āmantraṇa</s>); when by an inferior, it is request (<s>adhyeṣaṇa</s>). Thus, even when presenting commands and such, the optative and such present only what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>), not anything else. [11]
But how is it determined that it is what-is-to-be-done alone that receives the designation of command and such? To this he says:
For it is what-is-to-be-done alone that is the single cause of activity everywhere.
Due to its invariable concomitance with activity, the meaning of the optative and such is ascertained. [12]

children.text: pravṛttirhi bālena svātmani kāryāvagamapūrvikā pratipanneti, sarvapuruṣānapi pravarttamānāndṛṣṭvā kāryāvagamameva bālaḥ kalpayatīti, praiṣādīnāmapi pravṛttiḥ kāryāvagamanibandhaneti, kāryameva praiṣādivyapadeśayogīti siddham /
children.translated_text: For the child, having understood from his own experience that activity is preceded by the cognition of what-is-to-be-done, upon seeing all persons acting, infers the cognition of what-is-to-be-done [in them too] — thus it is ascertained as the meaning of the optative and such.

children.text: vastutastu praiṣādīnāmapi 1267pravṛttyavyabhicāritvātkāryasya ca pravṛttiṣu sarvāsu hetubhūtatvātpraiṣādiṣvapi liṅādīnāṃ kāryamevār'tha iti niścīyate // 12 //
children.translated_text: In truth, even for commands and such, since what-is-to-be-done is invariably concomitant with activity, and since what-is-to-be-done is the cause in all activities, the meaning of commands and such is only what-is-to-be-done.

children.translated_text: He summarizes:
Thus, the optative and such are conventionally understood even in what-is-to-be-done as the meaning,
and likewise other words are understood in their own meanings as connected with that. [14]

When effort exists, [the effect] comes into being; when it does not exist, it does not — thus achievability-through-effort (<s>kṛtisādhyatā</s>) is first understood through inference. That for the sake of which effort is directed — that is the principal of effort; and effort is exertion (<s>prayatna</s>). And since that is knowable by mental perception, the specific purposive nature of effort too is knowable by perception alone. Therefore, what-is-to-be-done is cognized through both perception and inference — like bathing and cooking. Nothing is impossible here.
Even so, how is the optative and such established as designating what-is-to-be-done that is unknowable by other means? Anticipating this, he introduces <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>:
But here it should be examined: is that what-is-to-be-done of the nature of action (<s>kriyā</s>),
or is it something different from that? ...........................
...................... There, following worldly practice — [15]
What then is the determination? To this he says:
Although action is to be known by another means of knowledge as what-is-to-be-done —

children.translated_text: Upon hearing the optative and such, having understood that the root is employed for the purpose of meaning of that character, the cognition of the root-meaning as what-is-to-be-done is accomplished.

children.text: yathā laḍādibhyo varttamānādyadhyavasāyaḥ, teṣvapi 1273vartamāner'the varttamānāddhātorlaḍityeva sūtrārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as from the present tense (<s>laṭ</s>) and such, the determination of present time and such [is made], even there the sūtra-meaning is simply: 'the present tense follows a root in the sense of present [time].'

children.text: kartrādisaṃkhyāmātravācitvameva kevalaṃ laḍādīnāmiva liṅādīnāmapyartha iti, kriyaiva kāryatayā vede 'pyavagamyata iti, yadyapi vivekāsamarthānāmavagatirbhavati1274 /
children.translated_text: Just as the optative and such, like the present tense and such, merely designate the number of agents and such — so action alone is cognized as what-is-to-be-done even in the Veda. Although this understanding belongs to those incapable of discernment —
nevertheless, when the sixth-<s>adhyāya</s> conclusion is established in the Veda — [16]

For in ordinary life, upon hearing a sentence containing the optative and such, since the cognition of what-is-to-be-done directed toward a specific action is produced by the optative and such, as evidenced by the observation of the performance of that specific action — this is proper, since the cognition and the activity have the same object. For a child does not, having cognized one thing as what-is-to-be-done, engage in another.
Moreover, when action as what-is-to-be-done is accepted as conveyed by sentences containing the optative and such, there would indeed be parsimony of postulated capacities. For thus: let the verbal root (<s>dhātu</s>) alone state its own meaning; and the optative and such that follow the root are taken as designating that meaning under such a character [i.e., as what-is-to-be-done].
the 'desirer of heaven' (<s>svargakāma</s>) and such are accepted as the person to be enjoined (<s>niyojya</s>) in relation to what-is-to-be-done,
and it is established that they are to be expressed by words like '<s>svargakāma</s>' and such. [17]

children.text:
ṣaṣṭhādye hyetaduktam---liṅādiprayoge tāvatkāryāvagatirastīti nirvivādam /
kṛtisādhyañca kāryaṃ bhavati /

children.translated_text: Given an agent, [the effort] comes into being.
And the agent comes into being only when there is cognition of what-is-to-be-done related to oneself, not otherwise.

children.text: tena yadyapi lokānusāreṇa kriyāyā eva kāryatayā bodhyamānāyā vākyārthatvāt, tadanvayitvāccetareṣāmapi1278 padārthānām, kārakatvādṛte cānyasya kriyānvayitvāsambhavāllohitoṣṇīṣanyāyena viśeṣaṇabhūtasvargakāmanāsamarpaṇaparatayā kartṛviśeṣaṇatvena svargakāmasyānvayo 'vagamyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, although following worldly practice, since action itself as what-is-to-be-done is the sentence-meaning, and since the other word-meanings are connected with it, and since the syntactic connection of anything other than a <s>kāraka</s> (case-relation) with action is impossible — by the <s>lohitoṣṇīṣa</s>-principle (red-turban principle), the connection of the 'desirer of heaven' is understood as a qualifier of the agent, serving to present the qualifying desire for heaven.

Nevertheless, the connection should be described only through the function of presenting the cognizer of what-is-to-be-done related to oneself — thus the status of presenting the <s>niyojya</s> (person to be enjoined) alone is accepted. [17]

For in the sixth <s>adhyāya</s> this has been stated: it is indisputable that upon the use of the optative and such, there is a cognition of what-is-to-be-done. And what-is-to-be-done is achievable through effort.
Even so, why? He says:
And the what-is-to-be-done is that which the person-to-be-enjoined cognizes as belonging to himself.
Even so, why? He says:
Heaven and such, due to the connection with desire, are understood precisely as what-is-to-be-accomplished (<s>sādhya</s>). [18]

children.text: sādhyaviṣayaiva hi sarvatra kāmanā bhavati, tena tatsambandhātsādhyabhūtaṃ svargādi kāmyamānatayā puruṣaṃ viśinaṣṭi---
children.translated_text: For desire everywhere has what-is-to-be-accomplished as its object; therefore, heaven and such, being what-is-to-be-accomplished due to that connection, qualify the person by being desired —
Therefore, qualified by the specific desire for heaven and such as what-is-to-be-accomplished,
he alone is able to cognize as what-is-to-be-done that which is the means to the desired [end]. [19]

children.translated_text: To this we reply: For one who desires heaven and such, only that can be cognized as what-is-to-be-done which is conducive to the accomplishment of what is desired.

children.text: anyathā hi tatkāminā satā tatkāryatayānavabuddhaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: For otherwise, it would not be cognized as what-is-to-be-done by the one desiring it.
For one who has not abandoned the connection with that desire knows the means [to the desired end] as what-is-to-be-done.

children.text: tasmādyatkāmino yatkāryatayopadiśyate, tattasnaya kāmyasya 1282sādhanamiti niyojyakāryānvayānupapattyaiva gamyate // 19 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, that which is taught to a desirer as what-is-to-be-done — that is the means to what he desires. Thus, the impossibility of the connection of what-is-to-be-done with the person-to-be-enjoined [is refuted].

Presentation of the view of <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>:
Here someone says: Although the status of heaven and such as what-is-to-be-accomplished is understood through the connection with desire, still the cognition of what-is-to-be-accomplished by the means-to-be-done at hand is entirely without <s>pramāṇa</s>, since even what is achievable by other means has the status of being achievable. And it is not the case that whatever is desired necessarily has a means. For one whose mind is carried away by a succession of fantasies, there is nothing that does not become an object of desire. And yet not everything has a means — some even desire omniscience, yet there is no way to it.
But then, for one who desires it, agency in accomplishing the non-means would not be possible. How would it not be possible? For even those desiring to go to a village are seen engaging in random activities. Moreover, every person indeed desires prosperity, yet is mostly seen engaging in sensory objects that are contrary to it.
Refutation of that:
This being so, what is the result? He says:
If the optative and such there were to convey action alone as what-is-to-be-done,
the syntactic connection with the person-to-be-enjoined (<s>niyojya</s>) would be lost at that very point. [20]
How so? He says:
For action (<s>kriyā</s>), being momentary, is not capable of producing
heaven and such, which exist in a different time and are desired. [21]
And that [action], being incapable of producing what is desired, being momentarily destructible,
does not deserve the connection of what-is-to-be-done with the person-to-be-enjoined who desires the fruit. [22]

children.text:

tatra yadi vidhyuddeśagatassvargaśabdastathāvidhaprītiparatayā na varṇyate, tadātiparokṣār'thavādapadānāṃ vṛttirādṛtā na bhavediti, tadānuguṇyena tādaśyāmeva prītau svargaśabdaḥ prayukta iti niścītate /
tathābhūtā1287 ca sā niyatameva deśāntarabhogyā /

children.translated_text: Therefore, action, being quickly perishable, cannot serve as a means for it; thus the capacity of action, which perishes quickly, to serve as a means [for svarga] is not tenable.

children.text: yasmin hi pūrvavarttini yanniṣpādyate, tattasya sādhanamitilokapratītiḥ /
children.translated_text: For in whatever thing existing earlier something is accomplished, that is the means to it — this is the ordinary understanding.

children.text: ata eva ca vinaṣṭasyāpi karmaṇaśśāstreṇa sādhanatvaṃ bodhata iti ye bruvate, te 'pi nirastāḥ /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, those who say that even destroyed action can be taught as a means by scripture are also refuted.

children.text: evaṃ cāsāvāśutaravināśinī kriyā svargakāminā niyojyena saha kāryatayā sambandhuṃ nār'hati, svargaṃ prati sādhanatvānupapatteḥ // 20 //
children.translated_text: And thus, that quickly perishable action does not deserve to be connected as what-is-to-be-done with the person-to-be-enjoined who desires heaven, since it is unable to produce heaven.

That action is opposed to what-is-to-be-done is established by another <s>pramāṇa</s>. For motion (<s>parispanda</s>), whose termination is the arising of conjunction with a subsequent location, is quickly perishable; and heaven is to be enjoyed in a definite other place and at a definite other time.
Presentation of the view of <s>Maṇḍana Miśra</s>:
But it has been established in the sixth <s>adhyāya</s> that '<s>svarga</s>' (heaven) merely means 'pleasure' (<s>prīti</s>), since the word '<s>svarga</s>' is used for substances that are means to pleasure. And the use of it for them is not based on their own nature alone, since in the absence of pleasure the term is not applied. Nor can the designation of being a means to pleasure be achieved without designating pleasure itself; if the designation of pleasure is accepted, then it is simply a word denoting pleasure.
Since the use [of the word] for the means of pleasure can be explained through figurative usage (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), there is no need for postulating a separate denotative capacity. And since '<s>svarga</s>' is an unanalyzable word (<s>akhaṇḍa-śabda</s>), the <s>daṇḍī</s>-principle does not apply, because it is possible for the word '<s>daṇḍa</s>' contained within [<s>daṇḍī</s>] to convey [the meaning of] 'stick' [but <s>svarga</s> has no such analyzable component].
And the immediacy of pleasure after action is also not possible.
Refutation of that:
We reply: The use of the word '<s>svarga</s>' as merely meaning pleasure is not feasible in the injunctions of <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and such, since in the <s>arthavādas</s> (laudatory passages), pleasure that is unmixed with suffering and enjoyable for a long time and to be attained through desire is heard. If the word '<s>svarga</s>' occurring in the context of the <s>vidhi</s> (injunction) is not explained as referring to such pleasure, then the sense of the <s>arthavāda</s> passages with their exceedingly remote meanings would not be honored — thus, in conformity with that, the word '<s>svarga</s>' is determined to be used for pleasure of precisely that nature. And such pleasure is necessarily to be enjoyed in another place.
Therefore, by the words expressing injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), that which is what-is-to-be-done,
being enduring in a different time and distinct from action — that is stated. [23]

children.translated_text: And effort (<s>kṛti</s>) for people is precisely <s>prayatna</s> (volitional effort).

children.text: na ca cāsau bhāvārthamantareṇāstīti, 1298tatsambaddha evocyataiti bhāvārthādhikaraṇe [ 2. 1 . 1 ] sthitam /
children.translated_text: And that [effort] does not exist without the <s>bhāvārtha</s> (thing to be brought into being); therefore, it is stated as connected with it — this has been established in the <s>Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.1.1].
And the <s>bhāvārtha</s>, being connected, delimits it — this has been determined in the <s>Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.2.1].

children.text: viṣayabhūtaśca bhāvārthaḥ karaṇībhavatīti bādaryadhikaraṇe evoktam, svakāryasādhane bhāvārthe puruṣasyaiśvaryamiti ca tatraivāktam // 23 //
children.translated_text: And the <s>bhāvārtha</s>, being the object, becomes the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) — this has been stated in the <s>Bādarādhikaraṇa</s> itself; and that the person has mastery (<s>aiśvarya</s>) over the <s>bhāvārtha</s> in accomplishing its own effect has also been stated there. // 23 //

But let the action (<s>kriyā</s>) itself be stated as the <s>kārya</s> (what is to be done); let it itself be the means for the fruit. Thus its connection with the <s>niyojya</s> (person to be enjoined) is indeed possible. But how can it, being momentary, support the capacity to produce <s>svarga</s> (heaven), which is to be experienced in another body? We reply: It is better to postulate a longer duration for that very action, due to the impossibility otherwise, than to postulate an <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen entity) that is unheard of and beyond that [action]. Or alternatively, let it be accepted that the action itself has an enduring capacity (<s>śakti</s>). But both of these cannot be postulated, since they contradict other means of knowledge. For only what is non-contradictory can be postulated to establish what is directly cognized. And the longer duration of action, which perishes quickly, contradicts other <s>pramāṇas</s>. Presentation and refutation of the <s>Vārttika</s> view: And when the possessor of the capacity has passed away, the capacity too has passed away — this is established by other <s>pramāṇas</s> — hence that capacity too cannot be postulated as enduring. Moreover, when the substrate has ceased, in what does the capacity reside? If in the self (<s>ātman</s>) — the capacity belonging to one thing does not reside in another, since this contradicts other <s>pramāṇas</s>. Moreover, when the possessor of the capacity does not exist, a fruit from the capacity alone is not proper. For the possessor of the capacity is the means, not the capacity alone — otherwise, it would not be capacity-ness. Doubt regarding the deity's grace as the cause of the fruit: But let the ritual action (<s>yāga</s>) etc., being a means of propitiating the deity, be stated as the <s>kārya</s>; through the proximity to the deity, it is fully capable of producing the fruit even at a later time. The deity, capable of bestowing the fruit, is propitiated through ritual actions; when propitiated, she is pleased; and when pleased, she unites the performers with the fruit even at a later time. Refutation of that: This is not so, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the thesis that sacrifices and such cause the propitiation of deities. For there is no valid evidence that sacrifice is a means of propitiating the deity. But is it not remembered that sacrifice is precisely for the worship of the deity? And all worship is for the purpose of propitiating the one worshipped — this is understood. We reply: <s>Smṛti</s> (remembered tradition) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, precisely because it is <s>smṛti</s>. And the description of meaning by <s>smṛtis</s> depends on another <s>pramāṇa</s>, since they follow that. And it has been said that the deity-propitiating capacity of sacrifice is not known through any other <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, the identity of sacrifice as worship of the deity — since sacrifice is the abandonment of a substance for the sake of a deity — is to be understood as secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>); worship too functions only for the sake of the one worshipped. Moreover, the deity who is propitiated by ritual actions must receive the propitiation — and the comprehension of sacrifice-as-worship performed by a person in various places as pertaining to the deity contradicts <s>pramāṇa</s>. And the fact that the deity has a body enabling reception, and that the deity has been propitiated through the beginningless Veda — this too contradicts other <s>pramāṇas</s>, because its beginninglessness is impossible. And in the <s>Devatādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 9.1.4], this matter has been refuted in detail — hence not much effort is needed here. Doubt regarding sacrifice as purifying the person: Or perhaps the action, being a cause of purifying the person (<s>puruṣa-saṃskāra</s>), is stated by the word as the <s>kārya</s>; and from that purification of the person connected with the one desiring heaven and such, the fruit will arise at a later time. That is not so, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for sacrifice and such being causes of personal purification. For neither through another <s>pramāṇa</s> nor through scripture (<s>śabda</s>) is the person-purifying capacity of sacrifices and such ascertained — thus it has been stated in '<s>karmāṇyārambhabhāvyatva</s>' etc. [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 11.1.20]. Doubt regarding action as the <s>kārya</s>: But let the action itself be stated as the <s>kārya</s>, and let the fruit-producing capacity belong to it alone. Due to its otherwise-inexplicability, let something else produced by it, suitable for the arising of the fruit, enduring, and inhering in the self, be postulated — but let it not be stated as what <s>liṅ</s> and such [verbal suffixes] denote. Establishment of the own view that the <s>kārya</s> is what <s>liṅ</s> etc. denote: We reply: That which is postulated due to the otherwise-inexplicability is what establishes [the conclusion]. But the fruit-producing capacity of the action is not established through something else postulated as produced by the action and producing the fruit. For the means-of-the-means does not become its means, nor does an intermediate function (<s>avāntara-vyāpāra</s>) or a capacity (<s>śakti</s>) discharge that means-status. For the means-status of things possessing capacity is through their connection with the function. And there is no intermediate function of ritual actions that is distinct and inhering in the self, nor is there a capacity — hence it is not proper that it be known through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). Rather, when <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> is established, it is well-said that the <s>kārya</s>, distinct from the action, enduring even at a later time, connected with the <s>niyojya</s>, is stated by <s>liṅ</s> and similar [suffixes] alone — due to its suitability for connection with the <s>niyojya</s>. Description of the essence of the Guru's doctrine: Here is the procedure. In the <s>Codanā-sūtra</s>, the 'to-be-done'-ness (<s>kāryārthatā</s>) has been established. In the sixth [<s>adhyāya</s>], first [<s>pāda</s>], the <s>niyojya</s> — such as the one desiring heaven — has been derived as connected with that very <s>kārya</s>. And that the desire for heaven is the qualifier of the <s>niyojya</s> has been derived in the eleventh [<s>adhyāya</s>], first [<s>pāda</s>] [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 11.1.1]. And that the <s>kārya</s> is the cause of the arising of the desire that qualifies the <s>niyojya</s> has been established in the <s>Bādarādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 3.1.3]. And that <s>kārya</s> of such a nature is not in the form of action, because action cannot produce the fruit. Through the mediation of deity-propitiation, there is no fruit-producing capacity — this has been derived in the <s>Devatādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 9.1.4]. Through the mediation of person-purification, there is none — this has been stated in '<s>karmāṇyārambhabhāvyatva</s>' etc. The action or its capacity does not endure — this has been established in the <s>Apūrvādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Darśana</s> 2.1.2]. Therefore, the <s>kārya</s>, without precedent in other means of knowledge, inhering in the self, connected with the <s>niyojya</s>, is stated by <s>liṅ</s> and similar [suffixes] — this is established through many principles. And the <s>kārya</s> is accomplished through effort (<s>kṛti</s>).
He states the fitness of the enduring <s>kārya</s> for connection with the <s>niyojya</s>:
For that [<s>kārya</s>], enduring across time, is capable of accomplishing <s>svarga</s> (heaven) and such;
And its connection with the <s>niyojya</s> who desires [heaven] would also be established. // 24 //

children.text: nanu bhāṣyakāraḥ---pratyayārthaṃ prayatnamityāha1299, na kriyādibhinnaṃ kāryamiti yo manyate, taṃ pratyāha---
children.translated_text: Now, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>) says that the suffix-meaning is effort (<s>prayatna</s>), and does not accept a <s>kārya</s> distinct from action and such. To address that, he says:
The <s>kārya</s>, which is distinct from action and such, is not known through other means of valid knowledge;
Therefore, being without precedent in other <s>pramāṇas</s>, it is called <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented). // 25 //
And 'niyoga is the sentence-meaning' is the declaration of the <s>Prābhākaras</s> — to address this he says:
That which, having the nature of what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>), enjoins the <s>niyojya</s> and prompts him regarding its own self —
Is called <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) by those well-versed in <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>. // 26 //
Definition of <s>niyoga</s> (injunction): But even so, <s>apūrva</s> would be the sentence-meaning, not <s>niyoga</s>.
Even so, how does it have the status of sentence-meaning? To this he says:
Since the <s>kārya</s> alone is the principal [element], its status as sentence-meaning is proper;
For the sentence states precisely that, as connected with the <s>niyojya</s>. // 27 //

children.translated_text: Why does another, unrelated [injunction] not fall within the scope of a different <s>niyoga</s> (injunction)? Because the cognition of connection with two duties is impossible.
For a single entity cannot be cognized as simultaneously connected with two duties.

And that other <s>niyoga</s> in the subsidiary rites (<s>prayāja</s>) and such, being stated subsequently, is denoted by its own word as a subsidiary (<s>aṅga</s>) of the eligibility-injunction alone.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the assignment to two objects — but enough with excessive elaboration. [27]

For it has been stated: what is presented as the principal — that is the sentence-meaning. And the <s>kārya</s> is stated as the principal; hence it alone has the status of sentence-meaning. Statement that the designation connected with the <s>niyojya</s> is general: And the designation connected with the <s>niyojya</s> is general, because the designation of injunctions whose scope is the establishment of fire (<s>ādhāna</s>), study (<s>adhyayana</s>), subsidiary elements, and principal rites — which are devoid of a <s>niyojya</s> — is accepted. For the commentators (<s>vivaraṇakāras</s>) accept a separate injunction (<s>niyoga</s>) even regarding the establishment of fire, because of the absence of recognition of a <s>kratu</s>-injunction. For in the absence of proximity, the recognition of that injunction is not possible. Nor is the recognition possible through an invariable connection with <s>kratu</s> mediated by fire, as in the case of <s>paṇatā</s> and such — because before the establishment of fire, the meaning of words like <s>Āhavanīya</s> is not known, and hence the connection with <s>kratu</s> is not understood. But for ladles (<s>juhū</s>) and such, since they are denoted by words expressing generic form, the recognition of the <s>niyoga</s>-injunction is possible even before the [specific] injunction. But since the fires too are to be accomplished, how can two things-to-be-accomplished be connected in one sentence? We reply: Even here, the <s>niyoga</s> alone is the principal thing to be accomplished, because the fires have the status of non-desired objects (<s>anīpsita-karma</s>). Even with the non-desired-object status, since the fruit produced by the fire-establishment inheres in the fire, through the usage of words like <s>Āhavanīya</s> designating what possesses that [fruit], and since <s>Āhavanīya</s> and such fires are useful for the <s>kratu</s>, the person's activity is established for the purpose of accomplishing that — hence the injunction connected with the <s>niyojya</s> is sufficient. Similarly, in the injunction of study (<s>adhyayana</s>), since performance is obtained through the prompting of the injunction of making a teacher (<s>ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi</s>), the designation is devoid of a <s>niyojya</s> — this is established. And the injunctions of production of principal rites too, having achieved their purpose through the very performance directed by the qualification-injunction, do not require the search for designation connected with a <s>niyojya</s>. Presentation of subsidiary injunctions in the <s>prayājas</s> and such: The injunctions of production of subsidiary elements too, since they have as their scope the <s>prayājas</s> and such that have been applied [to the principal ritual], are accomplished as subsidiaries of the qualification-injunction alone — so what need is there of designation connected with a <s>niyojya</s> for them? But how do the injunctions of <s>prayājas</s> and such have applied objects? We reply: When <s>prayāja</s> and other sentences are heard in the proximity of the injunction with qualification, they cannot produce another injunction regarding their own object, because of the possibility of being restatements (<s>anuvāda</s>), like the threshing and such. Rather, they merely present the bare form qualified by their own suitable word-meanings. And that, being in need of a purpose, is connected with the injunction with qualification that serves as its purpose — thus the <s>liṅ</s>-word present in the qualification-sentence alone designates its own meaning as connected with that. And that connection of the <s>prayājas</s> and such is said to be through mere contextual grasping of the 'for-the-sake-of-this' relation. And the assignment of instrumental helpfulness for the <s>apūrva</s>, which expects instrumental helpfulness — that is the function of the context (<s>prakaraṇa</s>). And the assignment of their instrumental-helpfulness-producing capacity — that is through proximate mention (<s>aupādānika</s>). Doubt and resolution regarding that: Is there then no separate injunction in the <s>prayājas</s> and such? It is not that there is none — because since those momentary [rites] cannot serve as instrumental helpers collectively, a separate injunction must necessarily be accepted. The <s>liṅ</s> and such [suffixes] that were previously suspected of being restatements now state a separate injunction. For this very reason, it is not accepted that the words like <s>yajya</s> in the subsidiary sentences designate their own meaning as connected with the qualification-injunction, like the threshing and such. For if so, since the form of the subsidiary sacrifice at the stage of production would not be the object of a separate injunction because it is not differentiated from anything else, there would be no separate-injunction-object status. But at the stage of production, since the designation is in the mode of non-differentiation from anything else, the separate-injunction-object status is proper.

children.text: nanu niyogasya kāmyamānaphalasādhanatvābhyupagamāt, phalasyeva prādhānyāt, tasyaiva vākyārthatvaṃ1316 yuktamityata āha---
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Since <s>niyoga</s> is accepted as a means to the desired fruit, and since the fruit alone has primacy, the fruit alone should be the sentence-meaning. To this he says:
For the establishment of the person enjoined (<s>niyojya</s>), the means conducive to his own accomplishment,
even something like heaven (<s>svarga</s>) and such, the duty (<s>kārya</s>) is primary for us. [28]
The doubt and its removal regarding whether <s>niyoga</s> (injunction) is subordinate.

children.text: yattadapūrvaṃ kāryam, tasya niyojyānvayaṃ vinā kāryatvānupapatteḥ, anuṣṭhānaṃ vinā tadasambhavāt, kartrā ca vinā tadanupapatteḥ, adhikāreṇa1317 ca vinā kartturabhāvāt, niyojyatvaṃ vinā tadayogāt, akāmasādhane ca 1318kāmino niyogānavagamāditi, ātmasiddhyarthameva niyogaḥ kāmyamānaphalasiddhihetutvamavalambate, svāmivat /
children.translated_text: That unprecedented duty (<s>apūrva kārya</s>) — since its status as duty is impossible without connection with the person enjoined, since that is impossible without performance, since performance is impossible without an agent, since the agent does not exist without eligibility (<s>adhikāra</s>), since eligibility is impossible without being a person enjoined, and since the injunction (<s>niyoga</s>) of a desiring person is not understood when it is not a means to desire — therefore, <s>niyoga</s>, for the sake of its own establishment alone, resorts to being the means of accomplishing the desired fruit, like a master.

children.text: yathā'tmana eva saṃvidadhānassvāmī garbhadāsasyopakaroti, tathā niyogo 'pi niyojyasyeti, na 1319prādhānyapracyutiḥ // 28 //
children.translated_text: Just as a master, while providing for himself, benefits a slave born in his house, so too does <s>niyoga</s> [benefit] the person enjoined — hence there is no loss of primacy. [28]

children.text: nanu niyogasya phalasādhanatvāt, tasya ca setikarttavyatākakaraṇanibandhanasiddhitvāt, tadanuṣṭhānānantaraṃ niyogasiddheḥ phalasiddhissyāt, anantaraṃ niyogo 1320na niṣpadyate, tarhi kriyāyāmatītāyāṃ kutastatsiddhirityatrā'ha---
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Since <s>niyoga</s> is a means to the fruit, and since its accomplishment depends on the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) together with its procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>), the accomplishment of the fruit should follow upon the accomplishment of <s>niyoga</s> immediately after performance. If <s>niyoga</s> is not accomplished immediately, then how can its accomplishment come about when the action has passed? To this he says:

children.text: viṣayānuṣṭhitau satyāṃ siddho na hi vidhiḥ phalam /
children.translated_text: When the object has been performed, the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) is indeed accomplished; and the fruit
is produced at that very time, subject to the cooperation of auxiliary factors. [29]

children.text: tatra yānyaṅgāpūrvāṇi, tāni sambhūta pradhānotpattyapūrveṣūpakurvanti, tasmācca paramāpūrvaṃ niṣpadyate /
children.translated_text: There, the subsidiary <s>apūrva</s>s, having come together, assist in the principal-production <s>apūrva</s>s, and from that, the supreme <s>apūrva</s> is produced.

And those subsidiary <s>apūrva</s>s of the <s>dīkṣaṇīyā</s> and such — among them too, one production-<s>apūrva</s> is the subsidiary extended through remote assistance, and another subsidiary <s>apūrva</s> should be understood like the principal.
By this approach, everything else should also be reasoned out.

children.text: itthaṃ yadyapi karmānuṣṭhānānantarameva niyogasiddhiḥ, tathāpi yat phalasyānantarābhavanam, tat upapattyā kalpyate---iti // 29 //
children.translated_text: Thus, even though the accomplishment of <s>niyoga</s> occurs immediately after the performance of the ritual act, the non-immediate arising of the fruit is postulated through reasoning. [29]

This is the doctrinal position here: The principal-production-injunctions and the subsidiary-production-injunctions are accomplished by the mere performance of their respective objects when the appropriate auxiliary subsidiaries come together.
[Objection:] But if so, the causal efficacy of <s>apūrva</s> regarding the fruit would be undermined. To this he says:
The dependence on auxiliary factors does not undermine its causality;
'Lest it be undermined' — this is the reason for postulating the cooperation [of auxiliary factors] everywhere. [30]

children.translated_text: It has been said that fruit is useful for producing the cognition of duty.

children.text: nanu yathā śabdātkāryāvagatiḥ, tathā niṣphalatvādanumānenākāryatāpratītirapīti, kathaṃ pravṛttyupapattiḥ ? na /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But just as the cognition of duty arises from the word, so too, due to the absence of fruit, the cognition of non-duty through inference also arises — so how is activity possible? [Reply:] No.
Because inference cannot establish itself when it contradicts scripture (<s>āgama</s>).

children.text: anyathā yadi kaścitkalpite phale na pravartate, tadā kiṃ karttavyam // 30 //
children.translated_text: Otherwise, if someone does not act even regarding a postulated fruit, then what is to be done? [30]

The meaning is: 'thus.' 'Therefore, both personal effort (<s>puruṣakāra</s>) and destiny (<s>daiva</s>) are the means to the fruit' — thus the teachers say. <s>Daiva</s> (destiny) means <s>apūrva</s>. And what is to be depended upon as the cooperating factor is what is meant by the term '<s>puruṣakāra</s>' (personal effort). Doubt and its resolution regarding the non-statement of <s>niyoga</s> in obligatory rites and such: [Objection:] If so, let the denotation of the unprecedented duty (<s>apūrva kārya</s>) by <s>liṅ</s> and such be in desire-dependent (<s>kāmya</s>) rites, but how in obligatory (<s>nitya</s>), occasional (<s>naimittika</s>), and prohibitory (<s>niṣedha</s>) contexts? For the <s>Prābhākara</s>s do not accept the arising of fruit in those cases. For the fruit is not connected as a fruit [in those cases], but as a qualifier of the eligible person (<s>adhikāriviśeṣaṇa</s>). And when a qualifier of the eligible person such as life is already obtained, what need is there to seek for a fruit? Nor is there impossibility of activity without a fruit, since activity depends merely on the cognition of duty related to oneself. From the independent word, even without a fruit, the cognition of duty related to oneself [arises], since that much alone is understood in the world as the cause of activity.

children.text:
nanu phalodayānabhyupagame ca prācyamārgāsambhavāt, nityādiṣvapūrvakāryābhidhānamapramāṇakaṃ syāt, tatrā'ha---
evaṃ kāmādhikārārthaparyālocanayotthitā /
vyutpattissarvavākyārthapratipattinibandhanam // 31 // 1325//
children.translated_text: [Objection:] And if the arising of fruit is not accepted, since the <s>prācya</s> (eastern/prior) approach would be impossible, the denotation of the unprecedented duty in obligatory rites would be without a <s>pramāṇa</s>. To this he says: Thus, the <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) that arose from the examination of desire-dependent and eligibility-related [contexts] is the basis for the cognition of the meaning of all sentences. [31]
It has been stated that [assigning] multiple meanings is improper.

children.text: tena kāmādhikāre siddhe 'pūrvakāryābhidhāyakatve, nityādiṣvapi sa evār'tho virodhābhāvādāśrīyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the denotative capacity for unprecedented duty (<s>apūrvakāryābhidhāyakatva</s>) is established in desire-dependent contexts, the same meaning is resorted to in obligatory rites and such as well, due to the absence of contradiction.

children.text: nityādhikārānuguṇyena tu kriyākāryatvābhidhānaṃ kāmyeṣvanupapannamiti, sarvatrāpūrvameva1327 vākyārthaḥ---iti // 31 //
children.translated_text: But the denotation of action (<s>kriyā</s>) as duty, which would suit the obligatory context, is impossible in desire-dependent rites; therefore, <s>apūrva</s> alone is the sentence-meaning everywhere. [31]

children.text:
tatraitadeva tāvadvaktavyam---na kevalaṃ vede lokavyavahārādeva śabdārthāvadhāraṇam, kintu prasiddhārthapadasambandhādapi padārthāntarānvayayogyārthābhidhāyakateti1328 sthite, tadanurūpārthābhidhāyakatā nirṇīyata eva /
etacca yavavarāhādhikaraṇe [mī. da. 1. 3. 5.] vyutpāditam 1329vyavahārata eva sambandhāvadhāraṇādubhayathāpi padāntarārthādhyavasānaṃ bhavatyeva, tena vaidikavākyaśeṣānvayārhatālocanena dīrghaśūkādyarthatvameveti rāddhāntaḥ /
tathā trivṛcchabde, yūpā--havanīyādiṣu ca śaktyavadhāraṇāt /
loke 'pi cāyaṃ vyavahāro bahulamupalabhyate /
tathā sati vaidikaniyojyānvayayogyatayā liṅādīnāmapūrvakāryābhidhāyakatvanirṇayo nānupapannaḥ /
ayañcāparo viśeṣaḥ---yalliṅādiyuktānāṃ vākyānāṃ kāryārthatvam, tattāvadvṛddhavyavahārādeva siddham, kintu liṅādipratyayānāṃ yadvacyaṃ1330 kāryam, taccāpūrvaṃrūpamityetāvanmātraṃ vaidikapadasambandhādavasīyate--iti // 31 // 1331//
children.translated_text: On this point, this much should be said: Not only is the ascertainment of word-meaning from ordinary usage [applicable] in the Veda, but also, since it is established that from the connection with words of known meaning, words denote meanings fit for connection with other word-meanings, the denotative capacity for a corresponding meaning is indeed determined. And this was explained in the <s>Yavavarāhādhikaraṇa</s> [<s>Mīmāṃsā Sūtra</s> 1.3.5]: since the ascertainment of relation is from ordinary usage itself, in both ways [direct and extended], the determination of another word-meaning obtains; therefore, by considering the fitness for connection with the rest of the Vedic sentence, the meaning as long-awned barley and such is the established conclusion. Similarly, in the word <s>trivṛt</s>, in <s>yūpa</s> (sacrificial post), <s>āhavanīya</s> (fire), and such, the ascertainment of capacity [is thus established]. And in the world too, this usage is widely observed. This being so, the determination of the denotative capacity of <s>liṅ</s> and such for unprecedented duty, by virtue of fitness for connection with the Vedic person enjoined, is not impossible. And there is this further distinction: that sentences containing <s>liṅ</s> and such have duty-as-meaning — this much is established from the usage of the learned alone; but that the duty which is the denotable of <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes has the form of <s>apūrva</s> — just this much is ascertained from the connection with Vedic words. [31]
He now presents the one-sided (<s>ekadeśin</s>) view in order to refute it:
Others say that <s>vyutpatti</s> (conventional understanding) [regarding <s>liṅ</s>] is from ordinary usage alone,
regarding a duty (<s>kārya</s>) not knowable by other means and distinct from action (<s>kriyā</s>). [32]

children.text:
asyār'thaḥ---kecidevamāhuḥ---liṅādiyuktavākyaśravaṇe pravṛttidarśanāt, kāryāvagatinibandhanatvātpravṛtteḥ, kāryamātrameva teṣāmarthaḥ, na 1332kriyā /
vaidikaliṅādeḥ kārye śaktinirṇayaḥ /

children.translated_text: [Objection:] But if so, the <s>vyutpatti</s> would be established from the Veda itself. Anticipating this objection, he says:
The <s>vyutpatti</s> regarding the meaning of duty is indeed following ordinary usage;
but only the determination [that it has the form of <s>apūrva</s>] arises from reflection on Vedic sentences. [33]

The meaning is: Some say thus — since activity is observed upon hearing a sentence containing <s>liṅ</s> and such, and since activity is based on the cognition of duty, mere duty alone is the meaning of those [suffixes], not action (<s>kriyā</s>). The determination of the capacity of Vedic <s>liṅ</s> and such for duty [follows].

children.text: tasyāṃ śabdasya pravṛttyanupayogitvāditi, kriyāniṣkṛṣṭakāryābhidhāyitā laukikavyavahārādeva nirṇīyate--iti // 33 //
children.translated_text: Since the word is not useful for activity [regarding mere action], the denotative capacity for duty extracted from action (<s>kriyāniṣkṛṣṭakārya</s>) is determined from ordinary usage alone. [33]
He declares that this is improper:

children.text: sitetara iva tveṣa pakṣaścittaṃ na karṣati /
children.translated_text: But this position, like its opposite, does not attract the mind,
being soiled by the course of the moonlight-and-sun fallacy (<s>candrātapāmalanyāya</s>). [34]
He says how:
When duty (<s>kārya</s>) is not knowable by other means, how could one who stands beside [i.e., in ordinary usage]
comprehend the practical activity based on it, prior to [hearing] the word? [35]
Without knowing the practical activity, how can the cognition based on it
be known? And how can the capacity of the word [be determined] otherwise? [36]

children.text:
idamatrā'kūtam /
yadyapi kāryamātrameva pravṛttyupayogīti tāvanmātrameva śabdārthaḥ, tathāpi tasya loke kriyāgatasyaiva pravarttakatvadarśanād, śakyate kriyāśritatā pratyetum /
yathā'kṛtimātrasya śabdārthatve 'pi vyaktyāśritatāpi na pratikṣipyate, tathā kriyāśritatvaṃ pramāṇāntarapramitaṃ na pratikṣepamarhati /
children.translated_text: Just as, even when the generic form (<s>ākṛti</s>) alone is the word-meaning, dependence on the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is not rejected, so too the dependence on action, known through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, should not be rejected.
Therefore, the denotative capacity for a duty distinct from action is unestablished.

children.text: yadi paraṃ tannibandhanavyavahāra eva1334 syāt, tadā taddarśanāttaddhetubhūtapratipattyanyathānupapattyānumānena śabdasya vācakatvādhyavasānaṃ bhavet /
children.translated_text: If, however, there were practical activity based on that [duty distinct from action], then from observing it, by inference from the impossibility of the cognition that is its cause being otherwise, the denotative capacity of the word would be determined.

children.text: na caitadasti,tasya śabdādanyataḥ prāganavagamāttannibandhanavyavahārāpratipattiḥ1335, tadapratipattau ca taddhetubhūtapratipattyananumānānna śaktikalpanopapattiḥ // 34 //
children.translated_text: But this does not exist, since that [duty], not being known from anything other than the word prior [to hearing it], the practical activity based on it is not perceived, and when that is not perceived, the inference from the cognition that is its cause is not established, so the postulation of capacity is impossible. [34-36]

The purport here is: Even though mere duty alone, being useful for activity, is the word-meaning, still, since in the world it is observed that only what resides in action motivates [people], its dependence on action can be understood.
He elaborates the purport:
Let the cognition of mere duty be inferred [as the cause] of activity;
but that the duty is action itself — this is ascertained from worldly observation. [37]

children.text: lokapratītaṃ kriyārūpatvañca na śakyate 'pahnotumiti, kāryamātrārthatve kriyaiva kāryatayā liṅādyartha iti niścīyate, na punaḥ pramāṇāntarādapūrvam-iti // 37 //
children.translated_text: And the action-nature known in the world cannot be denied; hence, if mere duty is the meaning, action itself is determined as the duty that is the meaning of <s>liṅ</s> and such — not the unprecedented [<s>apūrva</s>] through another <s>pramāṇa</s>. [37]

children.translated_text: To them he replies:
Even in the case of activity that is observed from the teacher's statements about Vedic meaning,
the same method of ascertaining the relation applies there too. [38]

The doubt and its resolution regarding action-as-duty according to another view: Others say — through observing the activity based on the statement of the teacher who teaches the meaning of the Veda, <s>liṅ</s> and such are conventionally understood regarding a supra-sensory duty (<s>atīndriya kārya</s>). If even from the teacher's statement, action itself is understood as duty, then since action is inherently painful, without the connection with another human end (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), the activity of one who desires pleasure would never be possible. And there is no human end in the <s>sandhyā</s> worship and such [obligatory rites]. Therefore, a duty distinct from action is understood from the teacher's statements.

children.text: ācāryavākyaśravaṇādapi śiṣyāṇāṃ yā sandhyopāsanādau pravṛttiḥ, tatrāpi bālassvaviṣayanirūpitaṃ kriyākāryatvāvagamameva kāraṇatvena parikalpayet, phalaṃ vinā ca tadanupapatteḥ phalāvagamamapi sambhāvayet /
children.translated_text: Even regarding the activity of students in <s>sandhyā</s> worship and such that follows the hearing of the teacher's statement, the child would postulate as the cause the cognition of action-as-duty alone, as determined in the relevant context, and would also conjecture the cognition of fruit due to the impossibility [of activity] without it.
Following worldly <s>vyutpatti</s>, while understanding the Vedic meaning too, he would postulate fruit even in obligatory, occasional, and prohibitory contexts.

children.text: sa eva vālyadaśāyāṃ vyutpannassvayamācāryapadavīmadhiruḍho vedārthaṃ pratītya, śiṣyebhya upadiśan kriyāmeva kāryatayā pratipādayet, nāpūrvaṃ kāryam--iti // 39 //
children.translated_text: That very person, having acquired <s>vyutpatti</s> in childhood, himself having ascended to the position of teacher, having understood the Vedic meaning, while teaching students, would convey action itself as duty, not the unprecedented <s>apūrva</s> as duty. [39]
He concludes:
Therefore, <s>vyutpatti</s> in the meaning of mere duty is from worldly usage;
but its form as unprecedented [<s>apūrva</s>] is from following Vedic sentences. [39]
Having established the denotative capacity for unprecedented duty, he raises an objection:
[Objection:] But in this position too, contradiction with the world is observed,

children.text: sarvathaiva1341 yato loke kriyā kāryaiva gamyate // 40 //
children.translated_text: since in every way, in the world, action alone is understood as duty. [40]
He resolves:
This would be so — [that] action and <s>apūrva</s> are both worldly —
if the cognition and usage regarding action-as-duty were contradicted [by our position]. [41]

children.text: yadi kriyākāryatvagocarau laukikau pratipatti-prayogāvapūrvakāryābhidhāyitvapakṣāṅgīkāre virudhyete, tato lokaviruddhatvaṃ syādasmatpakṣasya /

children.translated_text: But this is not the case — he says:

children.text: apūrvaṃ hi kriyāsādhyaṃ sādhitā sādhanaṃ kriyā /
children.translated_text: For <s>apūrva</s> is accomplished by action, and the accomplished action is the means;
therefore, unprecedented-duty-ness is consistent with action-as-duty. [42]

If the worldly cognition and usage regarding action-as-duty were contradicted by the acceptance of the denotative capacity for unprecedented duty, then our position would be contradicted by the world.
For the world expresses through words what is known through other <s>pramāṇa</s>s;
therefore, the usage in the sense of action-as-duty is accompanied by the [right] characteristic. [43]

children.text: pratipatti-prayogau hi nāvaśyaṃ śrautavṛttyanusāriṇāveva, lakṣaṇayāpi loke1344 taddarśanāt /
tena yadyapyuktena nyāyenāpūrvameva kāryaṃ liṅādīnāmabhidheyam, tathāpi tasya kriyākāryatvāvyabhicārāt, tatra lakṣaṇayā tayornānupapattiḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, although by the stated reasoning the unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>) alone is the denoted meaning of <s>liṅ</s> and other [injunctive suffixes], nevertheless, since that [unprecedented effect] is invariably an effect of action (<s>kriyākārya</s>), there is no impossibility of [understanding] those two [action and apūrva] through secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) in that [context].

children.text: yattu śrautapadārthe kārye loke liṅādi na prayujyata iti /
children.translated_text: As for the [objection] that <s>liṅ</s> and other suffixes are not employed in the world with the directly denoted meaning of duty (<s>kārya</s>) —
that is because [<s>apūrva</s>], being of the nature of the unprecedented, is not cognized through any other means of knowledge, while worldly usage pertains to what is [already] cognized.

children.text: kriyāsādhyantvapūrvam, sādhitā ca satī kriyā sādhanaṃ bhavatītyapūrveṇa saha kriyākāryatvaṃ1345 nityasambaddhamiti, śakyate tallakṣayitum // 42 - 43 //
children.translated_text: Action (<s>kriyā</s>) is the means of accomplishing <s>apūrva</s>, and action, once accomplished, becomes the instrument — thus, the character of being an effect of action (<s>kriyākāryatva</s>) is always connected with <s>apūrva</s>, and therefore that [action as duty] can be indicated through secondary meaning. [42-43]
For understanding and usage do not necessarily follow only the directly denoted meaning (<s>śrautavṛtti</s>); they are observed in the world through secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) as well.

children.text: yadyeṣā1346 lakṣaṇā, kimiti tarhi loko nāvagacchatītyāha---
children.translated_text: If this is secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), why then does the ordinary person not recognize it [as such]? To this he says:
The non-recognition of the secondary meaning is due to not having determined the primary meaning (<s>mukhyārtha</s>).
But those who are skilled in the primary meaning — for them the cognition of secondary meaning arises. [44]

children.text: mukhyamarthamaviditvā lākṣaṇikamapyarthaṃ śrautamiva manyante, mlecchā iva yava-varāhādyartham /
children.translated_text: Without knowing the primary meaning, people take even the secondary meaning to be directly denoted, like <s>mlecchas</s> (non-Sanskrit speakers) [who take] the meaning of words like <s>yava</s> (barley) and <s>varāha</s> (boar) [without knowing the original meaning].
But for discriminating investigators who distinguish the primary meaning, the cognition of secondary meaning [arises]. [44]
He concludes:
Therefore, the Vedic sentence expresses an effect (<s>kārya</s>) not knowable through other means of knowledge, connected with other meanings —
this is the summary that has been stated. [45]

children.translated_text: He states the title, the author, and the purpose of the work: This <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s> (Matrix of Sentence-Meaning) [has been composed] by <s>Śālikanātha</s>, following the Guru <s>Prabhākara</s> in the <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> tradition, for the instruction of the well-disposed. Composed by <s>Śālika</s> [<s>Śālikanātha</s>] himself, who wished to benefit those of good conduct,
this is the commentary (<s>vṛtti</s>) on the <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s>.
Thus, in the <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s> with commentary, composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrīmac-Śālikanātha Miśra</s>, the second section (<s>pariccheda</s>) is concluded.
And thus is concluded the <s>Vākyārthamātṛkā</s>, the eleventh <s>prakaraṇa</s> (chapter) in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s>.
Now the twelfth <s>prakaraṇa</s> named <s>Viṣayakaraṇīya</s> (Object and Instrument).
Declaration of the chapter's subject:
Having properly considered the doctrine of <s>Prabhākara</s>, this description of reasoning is composed by me
in order to distinguish the object (<s>viṣaya</s>) and the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>). [1]

children.translated_text: Since mere conjunction cannot be the meaning of <s>gam</s> (to go) — for there is no usage of 'goes' for conjunction arising from conjunction, nor is usage observed for disjunction arising from disjunction — neither mere conjunction nor mere disjunction is the denotation of <s>gam</s>. What is the use of this pedantic, childish prattle that enchants the minds of the immature?
This was properly composed by <s>Śālikanātha</s> for the purpose of benefiting the learned.
Or rather, having duly examined the doctrine of the Guru, this <s>Viṣayakaraṇīya</s> [was composed]. [2]

For action (<s>kriyā</s>), being momentarily destructible, cannot serve as a means for heaven and such which exist in a different time — hence it is established that the optative and such convey what-is-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>) as something enduring in a different time and distinct from action — namely, <s>apūrva</s> (the unprecedented effect).

Statement of the established doctrine:
What-is-to-be-done is called that which is desired by effort (<s>kṛti</s>). Effort is the activity of the self — personal exertion (<s>puruṣa-prayatna</s>) — these are synonymous. And the <s>ātman</s>, being conscious, enters into syntactic connection with what-is-to-be-done as a cognizer. And since nothing produced by another's activity can be cognized as what-is-to-be-done in relation to oneself, the effort that is one's own activity — to be ascertained by mental perception — [is the relevant factor]. Therefore, the <s>ātman</s> considers only what is produced by that effort as what-is-to-be-done, namely <s>apūrva</s>.
Effort itself, being the activity of the self which is the agent (<s>bhāvayitṛ</s>) who is the motivator of the <s>apūrva</s> that is to come into being, is designated by the word <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force).
And since the designation of what-is-to-be-done by the optative and such is not possible without designating effort — they also designate effort, and also <s>apūrva</s>. Nor is the simultaneous designation of multiple things a fault, since it is understood thus, and since it is in harmony.
For the what-is-to-be-done-designating capacity of the optative and such has been established by <s>pramāṇa</s>. In harmony — because effort, being subordinate, [is designated] in relation to what-is-to-be-done of the nature of <s>apūrva</s> which is the principal word's referent. And the optative and such, even as designators of what-is-to-be-done, undisputedly designate also the number of agents and such.
Nor does <s>bhāvanā</s> alone become the sentence-meaning merely by being designated. Since the meaning of <s>bhāvya</s> (what is to be produced), namely <s>apūrva</s>, is designated subordinately, and since <s>apūrva</s> is designated principally — it alone is the sentence-meaning. Nothing is impossible here.
For this very reason, the usage of the venerable <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śabara</s>) in various places is: 'Personal exertion — the instrument — is called the producer of <s>apūrva</s> (<s>bhāvana</s>).'

Presentation of the verbal root meaning as object (<s>viṣaya</s>):
That what-is-to-be-done of such a nature must surely be delimited by some existent meaning (<s>bhāvārtha</s>). For effort does not exist without an existent meaning. Every personal exertion necessarily depends on some existent meaning; without it, there is no effort.
Therefore, the existent meaning, being invariably concomitant with effort, delimits the <s>apūrva</s> to be produced by effort. Its being an object (<s>viṣaya</s>) consists precisely in its delimiting function.
'Where alone something exists and not elsewhere — that is its object' — so say the knowers of the object-relation. And: 'Existence-not-elsewhere is the meaning of the word object.' Therefore, the <s>bhāvya</s> (what is to be produced) is the meaning, and the object is the meaning — since it is <s>bhāvya</s> alone that is the domain of personal exertion.
Therefore, the existent meaning — the ritual-action word (<s>karmaśabda</s>) — first deserves to be co-employed with the designators of what-is-to-be-done in the capacity of conveying the object, since [the object] is a prerequisite for cognition. For the unprecedented <s>apūrva</s> cannot be cognized as what-is-to-be-done without an object. And what-is-to-be-done, once cognized, has an expectation for a means.
Therefore, the syntactic connection of existent meanings with <s>apūrva</s> is not in the inferior capacity of means, but [the venerable <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>], considering it to be the means of cognition, says thus: 'For cognition of the injunction (<s>niyoga</s>) does not arise from an injunction without an object' [<s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>].

Determination of the verbal root meaning as instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>):
And that injunctive meaning (<s>vidhyartha</s>), of the nature of what-is-to-be-done, once cognized as delimited by the existent meaning that has become the object, requires a procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>), since this is observed even with respect to other things to be accomplished.
There, that very existent meaning, having become the object, is determined as the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), since it is pervaded by effort. For whatever is objectified by whatever effort directed toward another purpose — that alone is the instrument there.
Just as — the axe, being pervaded by the two efforts of raising and striking directed toward the act of splitting wood, is the instrument of those two, which obtain the designation of 'splitting' through their delimitation by the fruit of splitting expressed by the root <s>chidi</s> (to cut) — so too here, the existent meaning, being pervaded by the personal exertion directed toward the purpose of <s>apūrva</s>, is the instrument in that very exertion which has the form of <s>apūrva-bhāvanā</s> (production of the unprecedented).
But how can the existent meaning, whose nature is obtained through effort, be the instrument in <s>bhāvanā</s>? For by being produced, it would be the object (<s>karman</s>) rather. We reply: The verbal root meaning is not the object there, since it is the object of effort directed toward <s>apūrva</s>. For all <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations) other than the agent are pervaded by the agent's activity, yet they do not thereby become objects (<s>karman</s>), since they are not desired as ends.
And sometimes, even what is not desired as an end serves as the object — as in '<s>agnihotraṃ juhoti</s>' (he offers the <s>Agnihotra</s>).
The instrument, although not possible in its bare form-cessation, nevertheless the <s>apūrva-bhāvanā</s>-character is dependent on it — hence no impossibility. Just as with the axe. For the axe is not the object (<s>karman</s>) but is the instrument, since it is not desired as an end. Because the splitting-character of the raising and striking [movements] depends on it.
For when the raising and striking, empowered by the association with the axe, produce the fruit of splitting, they enter into the causal role with respect to splitting.
Hence the justification of the third-case designation in '<s>udbhidā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Udbhid</s>) [<s>Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa</s> 29.7.2.3] — since sacrifice is the instrument in the <s>apūrva-bhāvanā</s>, and the word '<s>udbhid</s>' is its name.
And thus, <s>apūrva</s> and fruit have one and the same <s>bhāvanā</s>, since personal exertion is one. And the instrument is one alone, since the existent meaning being pervaded by that <s>bhāvanā</s> has one single character of what-is-to-be-produced.
For this very reason, the <s>Prābhākaras</s> [say that] this is the augmentation of what-is-to-be-accomplished (<s>sādhya-vivṛddhi</s>).

Summary of the object-status and instrument-status of the verbal root meaning:
If what has become the object has the status of instrument — well then, in 'he should sacrifice with the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>' (new-and-full-moon sacrifices), since those collectively mentioned are collectively the prerequisite for cognition, and since the object-status is one, there would be one instrument only — and consequently the connection with the procedure through differentiation would not be possible.
We reply: The words of the wise ones, endowed with longevity and scriptural learning, have not been properly grasped. The meaning is: that very thing which has become the object is the instrument, not anything else — in virtue of being a prerequisite for cognition.
And the object-status [is determined] through the prerequisite for cognition, and that obtains as the designation determines it, since designation is the means of cognition.
Therefore, from collective designation, the object-status is of the collectively [mentioned things]; but the instrument-status is connected with the accomplishment of the injunction, and that should be understood according to its own nature. For the instrumental capacity of the means depends on their own nature, and when the nature differs, the instrumental capacity differs.
And since in the instrumental capacity, being the domain of effort constitutes instrument-status — through differentiation there is differentiated instrument-status.
But then, when instrument-status is accepted for each individually, why are not the instruments, independent of each other, causes of the accomplishment of the injunction? Not so — because the accomplishment of the injunction depends on the instruments as heard [in scripture]. There, many instruments are heard for it — hence its accomplishment is precisely so.
And the accomplishability by multiple instruments of a single [effect] is observed — as with going, [which can be accomplished] by horse, palanquin, or chariot.
If it is said that there the intermediate activities of the causes differ — here too we affirm that the intermediate activities, being unprecedented productions, are different. For this very reason, since the instrument-status differs due to their differentiation, there is no confusion of the <s>dharmas</s> of ghee, herbs, and <s>sānnāyya</s> offerings, even though they are all directed toward the ultimate <s>apūrva</s>. Because <s>dharmas</s> are established in the capacity of means to <s>apūrva</s>, and because <s>apūrva</s> differs [for each].
But those who do not accept an <s>apūrva</s> intervening between sacrifices and <s>bhāvanā</s> — for them the instrument-status of sacrifices is difficult to establish. Since <s>apūrva</s>, having no activity-nature, and instrument-status arising from the connection with activity — [the two are incompatible].
If it is said that the instrument-status is figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>) — then how can there be a connection with procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>)? For the instrument is connected with the procedure. And what is figurative is not truly an instrument — for in what is figurative, the properties of the primary meaning do not obtain.

Even those who maintain that <s>bhāvanā</s> is designated in all verbal forms — their view too does not please us. For there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the designation of <s>bhāvanā</s> in the present tense (<s>laṭ</s>) and such, which do not designate what-is-to-be-done.

Refutation of the <s>Vārtika</s> view:
And the evidence presented — that in the question 'What does he do?' the answer 'He cooks' shows [<s>bhāvanā</s>] — that too is not probative. For this question is about the specific activity — 'What does he do?' And the answer 'He cooks' indicates precisely that [specific activity]. The mere utterance of the verbal root, which designates mere activity, is not made [in isolation], since a bare root-utterance is ungrammatical. And the utterance with another suffix would have no connection with the question.
For this very reason, the present tense and such are used for the activity even of non-conscious entities [like 'the chariot goes']. But the optative and such are employed only with reference to conscious beings.
Nor is the usage for non-conscious beings figurative — since it is not contradicted even in the primary sense. And if [the optative and such] merely designated the number of agents and such, then in usages like 'the chariot goes' the primary sense would follow [even for the optative].
Nor should one say: conjunction and disjunction alone are the meaning of the verbal root, while activity as motion is the meaning of the present tense in 'the chariot goes,' and hence the present tense has a primary meaning even for non-conscious entities. For since verbal roots are designators of action, the activity itself, being the first thing encountered, is the proper meaning of the root — not the secondary [results of] conjunction and disjunction.

children.translated_text: Thus ends the twelfth chapter named <s>Viṣayakaraṇīya</s> (Object and Instrument) in the <s>Prakaraṇapañcikā</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrīmac-Śālikanātha Miśra</s>.
Section 1
Now, in the <s>Aṅgapārāyaṇa</s> (Examination of Subsidiaries), the first section is devoted to the determination of subsidiaries that assist through convergence (<s>sannipatti</s>).
Declaration of the chapter's subject.
To resolve the doubt regarding subsidiaries, where multiple explanations are possible,
I shall expound the profound thought of Guru <s>Prabhākara</s>. [1]

children.translated_text: And thus the grammarians too have said: 'The clarified butter (<s>ājya</s>) becomes liquid through contact with fire — hence the use of the <s>cvi</s>-suffix and so on.'
But sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>) of the substance does not bring about a different state through the destruction of the previous state.
And here there is a verse: They call transformation (<s>vikāra</s>) the acquisition of a different state through the abandonment of the previous state;
purificatory rite (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is the mere arising of an excellence. [2]

The fourfold classification of subsidiaries (<s>aṅga</s>):
Here the class of subsidiaries is fourfold — of the nature of universal (<s>jāti</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), substance (<s>dravya</s>), and existent meaning (<s>bhāvārtha</s>). There, the existent-meaning type is also twofold: those that assist through convergence (<s>sannipattyupakāraka</s>) and those that assist remotely (<s>ārādupakāraka</s>).
The fourfold classification of convergent [subsidiaries]:
There, the convergence-assisting type is fourfold, distinguished as: production (<s>utpatti</s>), obtainment (<s>prāpti</s>), modification (<s>vikṛti</s>), and consecration (<s>saṃskṛti</s>) of what-is-to-be-accomplished (<s>sādhya</s>). Respectively, these take the form of blending (<s>saṃyavana</s>), milking (<s>dohana</s>), melting (<s>vilāpana</s>), sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>), and such.
There, by blending, a lump that did not previously exist is produced. Milk that already exists is obtained through milking. By melting, the prior solidified state is removed, and the other — the liquid state of ghee — is produced. For ghee, being earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>) since it possesses odor, is naturally in a solidified form, and becomes liquid through contact with fire. To this the venerable <s>Kāśyapa</s> [<s>Kaṇāda</s>] says: 'The liquidity of butter, lac, honey, and wax — being earthy — arises from contact with fire and is similar to [the liquidity of] water' [<s>Vaiśeṣika-darśana</s> 2.1.6].
